blocks.src:
> 本导读整理自 Socratopia 网站本书介绍页：https://www.socratopia.app/library/information-theory-en

Most information theory textbooks were written before deep learning. They prove the source coding theorem, derive channel capacity, and stop. Most modern machine learning textbooks invoke "cross-entropy" and "KL divergence" without saying where those quantities come from. This book sits in the gap between them, and it argues — with precise mathematical identity, not metaphor — that the bits Shannon counted in 1948 are the bits a frontier transformer counts today.

The central thread is the compression-prediction equivalence : a language model with cross-entropy C bits per token compresses text at exactly C bits per token when used as an arithmetic coder. Chapter 4 proves the identity, and Chapter 15 returns to it with concrete numbers — frontier models now hit 0.7 bits per character on English, landing inside Shannon's 1951 human-prediction estimate seventy years after he made it.

What makes the book unusual is its honesty about what information theory does not settle. Chapter 13 treats the famous Tishby "compression phase" alongside the Saxe critique that calls it an artifact of saturating activations. Chapter 14 leads with the McAllester-Stratos lower bound on mutual-information estimators — the cautionary fact that quietly invalidates many published "MI in deep learning" claims. Chapter 16 says plainly that quantum machine learning has produced no robust evidence of practical advantage as of 2026.

The capstone (Chapter 18) is a reference-design experiment, not a benchmark: train a 4M-parameter transformer on a laptop and verify, with your own data, that cross-entropy equals compression rate, that gzip loses by a factor of two, that hidden-layer mutual information rises with depth. Appendix D ships the complete runnable Python — TransformerLayer , training loop, arithmetic-coding compression check, MI probe, plus a 10-symptom failure-mode diagnostic table for when reproductions deviate.

For the reader who has met cross-entropy as "the loss function that PyTorch uses" and wants to understand why it is the loss function, this book is the ladder.

**Target audience**：Upper-undergraduate (junior/senior) and graduate students in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Applied Mathematics, Statistics, Machine Learning, and quantitative researchers in physics, biology, and economics who want a rigorous foundation in information theory connected to modern AI.

**Study hours**：180-240 hours for a full reading with all worked examples and a serious attempt at problem sets. Approximately one semester of graduate study, or two semesters at undergraduate pace.

When Claude Shannon published _A Mathematical Theory of Communication_ in 1948, no one imagined that within a single human lifetime his framework would become the mathematical core of an artificial intelligence revolution. Shannon was thinking about telephone wires and the corruption of bits in transit; today his equations describe how a transformer language model compresses the universe of plausible English sentences into a probability distribution. The same logarithm of probability that Shannon defined as self-information is the loss function of every modern classifier, every language model, every generative model in deployment. The bits Shannon counted in 1948 are the bits we count today.

This book is an attempt to teach information theory the way it should be taught in 2026 and beyond. The classical theory — entropy, source coding, channel coding, rate-distortion — remains the foundation, and we treat it rigorously. But every classical result is connected to its modern AI usage. When we prove the source coding theorem in Chapter 4, we immediately see why a language model's cross-entropy _is_ its compression rate. When we discuss KL divergence in Chapter 8, we see that cross-entropy minimization is the training objective of every neural classifier. When we develop variational methods in Chapter 10, we see that the VAE and its descendants rest on the ELBO inequality. The classical and the modern are not two separate halves of the field; they are one continuous story.


#### Who this book is for

The intended reader is an upper-undergraduate or graduate student in computer science, electrical engineering, applied mathematics, statistics, or a quantitative discipline who wants both rigorous information theory and the tools to read modern machine learning papers. The mathematical level is serious: theorems are stated precisely, proofs are given for major results, problem sets are challenging. Calculus, linear algebra, and probability are prerequisites; some programming experience is needed for the capstone in Chapter 18.

A motivated working professional — an ML engineer who learned the tricks of the trade without the foundations, a quantitative researcher curious about the field — will also find the book accessible. Each chapter opens with motivation and intuition before the mathematics, and the worked examples are detailed.

#### What makes this book different

Three commitments distinguish this book from existing treatments.

**First, the AI through-line.** Every classical chapter ends with a connection to a modern AI application. The reader should never be left wondering "why does this matter today?" The connection is precise, not vague: when we say "cross-entropy training is information-theoretic," we mean it as a mathematical identity, not as a metaphor.

**Second, honesty about limits.** Information theory has been around for 75 years; some of its claims about deep learning are contested. We are explicit about this. The "compression phase" of deep learning training (Chapter 13) is presented alongside the Saxe critique. Mutual information estimation in high dimensions (Chapter 14) is presented alongside the McAllester-Stratos lower bound. The reader leaves with a balanced view of what information theory does and does not tell us about modern AI.

**Third, the capstone.** Chapter 18 trains a small language model from scratch and analyzes it through every lens we have developed. By the end, the reader has not just read about information theory; they have computed cross-entropy on real text, verified the compression-prediction identity, estimated layer-wise mutual information, and watched a language model's training trajectory through information-theoretic eyes. This is where the book's claims become concrete.


#### Structure

The book is organized into seven parts.

* **Part I (Chapters 1-4): Foundations.** Entropy, mutual information, asymptotic equipartition, source coding.
* **Part II (Chapters 5-7): Channels and Capacity.** Channel coding theorem, practical codes.
* **Part III (Chapters 8-10): Distributions and Divergences.** KL divergence, information geometry, variational methods.
* **Part IV (Chapters 11-12): Rate-Distortion and Network.** Lossy compression and multi-user information theory.
* **Part V (Chapters 13-15): Modern AI Applications.** Information bottleneck, mutual information in deep learning, language models as compressors.
* **Part VI (Chapters 16-17): Quantum and Beyond.** Quantum information and open frontiers.
* **Part VII (Chapter 18): Capstone.** Build and analyze a small language model.

Three running threads weave the chapters together: the **compression-prediction duality** , the **cumulative capstone** (each chapter contributes a tool that the capstone uses), and the **history side-track** (200-400 words per chapter on the human story behind the mathematics).


#### How to read this book

A graduate reading of all 18 chapters takes about one semester. An undergraduate reading might cover Chapters 1-11 plus Chapter 15 in one semester and the rest in a follow-on course. A self-study reader is encouraged to take the chapters at their own pace; the book rewards depth over speed.

The exercises are essential. Each chapter has 8-12 problems at three difficulty levels (Concept Check, Application, Think Deeper). The Concept Check problems verify basic understanding; the Application problems develop technical fluency; the Think Deeper problems are open-ended and invite reflection. Selected solutions are in Appendix B.

The capstone (Chapter 18) requires programming. Code skeletons are in Appendix D. A reader who completes the capstone will have a trained language model and a working understanding of how its information-theoretic properties are measured.

#### A final note

Information theory is, in some sense, the most successful intellectual transplant of the twentieth century. Born from a question about telephone wires, it has become the mathematics of communication, computing, statistics, and now artificial intelligence. The seventy-five years from Shannon's 1948 paper to the modern frontier model is a continuous story, and this book is an attempt to tell that story coherently.

I have tried to write the textbook I wish had existed when I first encountered the field — rigorous but warm, technical but oriented toward what matters today, mathematical but never losing sight of why the mathematics is beautiful. Whether I have succeeded is for the reader to judge.

I leave you with the closing line of the capstone: _Information is not a thing. It is a relationship between what you know and what you don't._ Welcome to that relationship.

— SocraLab, 2026

* * *

* * *

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
In 1948, a 32-year-old engineer at Bell Telephone Laboratories published a paper that, in the space of about eighty pages, founded an entire branch of mathematics. The paper was titled _A Mathematical Theory of Communication_ , and the engineer was Claude Elwood Shannon. The paper invented the bit, defined entropy as a measurable quantity attached to any probability distribution, and proved two theorems whose limits still bound every wireless network, every storage device, and every learning algorithm built today. It is among the most cited works in twentieth-century science, and unlike many such papers, it is also strikingly readable. A motivated undergraduate can sit down with the original and follow most of it in a weekend.

This book begins where Shannon began: with the question of what information _is_ , mathematically. We will see that the answer is so general and so robust that it now describes not only telephone lines but lossless compressors, machine translation systems, deep neural networks, the channel capacity of optical fibers, and even the operation of the genome. The same definition that Shannon gave for measuring how many bits per second a noisy telephone wire can carry also tells us how surprising the next word in a sentence will be to a language model. Information, in Shannon's hands, became a quantity as definite as energy or mass.

Before any equations, hold one image in mind. Suppose a friend in another city is going to send you a single message about the outcome of an event. If the event was certain (the sun rose this morning), the message contains no information; you knew the answer already. If the event had two equally likely outcomes (a fair coin landed heads or tails), the message contains exactly one bit. If the event had a million equally likely outcomes (your friend chose one of a million names from a phone book at random), the message contains about twenty bits. The pattern is clear: the more uncertain you were before the message arrived, the more information the message carries when it does. Shannon's contribution was to make this pattern precise, to prove that there is essentially only one way to make it precise, and to derive deep consequences from the resulting definition.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
### 1.1 Why "Information" Needs a Mathematical Definition

The English word _information_ is one of the most abused words in technical writing. Engineers use it to mean signal; biologists use it to mean genetic message; philosophers use it to mean meaningful content. None of these usages is wrong, but none of them is precise enough to compute with. Shannon's first move was an act of disciplined narrowing. He set aside meaning entirely and proposed that the _amount_ of information in a message could be measured by the _uncertainty_ the message resolves.

This separation of meaning from quantity is the move that made the field possible. Two messages can carry the same amount of information by Shannon's definition while meaning entirely different things. The sentence "the patient has tuberculosis" and the sentence "the prime suspect was in Brussels" might both pin down a single answer chosen from a million possibilities, and so both contain about twenty bits, even though their semantic weight is incomparable. By refusing to talk about meaning, Shannon could talk about everything else: rate, capacity, error, redundancy, compression, channel limits.

There is a useful analogy with thermodynamics. Before Carnot, engineers spoke about heat in qualitative terms: hot, warm, fierce, gentle. Carnot did not deny the qualitative experience of heat, but he set it aside in favor of a quantity, the absolute temperature, which permitted a calculus of efficiency. Shannon did the same thing for information. He did not deny that meaning matters; he simply refused to let the lack of a meaning theory delay the construction of an information theory.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
#### A first guess at the right measure

If you knew nothing about the field and were asked to invent a measure of information, what might you try?

A first guess: count the number of possible messages. If there are MMM equally likely messages and you receive one, you have learned the answer to a question with MMM possibilities. The natural measure of "how big a question" is just MMM. This is the kind of move a beginner makes, and it is wrong, but instructively wrong.

To see why it is wrong, consider two independent events. A friend sends you the outcome of two independent coin flips. The first flip has 222 possible outcomes; the second also has 222. Together, they have 2×2=42 \times 2 = 42×2=4 possible joint outcomes. If your measure of information were just MMM, then the two-flip message would carry "four units" while one flip carries "two units." But intuitively, two independent flips carry exactly twice as much information as one flip, since they are independent. The right measure should _add_ under independence, not multiply.

The fix: take the logarithm. log⁡(M1⋅M2)=log⁡M1+log⁡M2\log(M_1 \cdot M_2) = \log M_1 + \log M_2log(M1​⋅M2​)=logM1​+logM2​. Independence in joint distributions becomes addition in log space. Define the information in a message that picks one of MMM equally likely options to be log⁡M\log MlogM, and additivity is automatic.

This was the proposal Ralph Hartley made in 1928, two decades before Shannon. Hartley's measure works for the easy case (equally likely outcomes) but fails for the typical case, in which different outcomes have different probabilities. If a friend tells you "it rained today" in Seattle, you learn very little; rain in Seattle is common. If a friend tells you "it rained today" in the Atacama desert, you learn a great deal; rain in the Atacama is exceedingly rare. Both messages are the same string, "it rained today," but they resolve different amounts of uncertainty.

Hartley's measure cannot distinguish them. We need one that can. Shannon's was the next move.


### 1.2 Self-Information

The right generalization is to attach an information value not to a _message_ but to an _outcome_. If outcome xxx has probability p(x)p(x)p(x), then receiving the news that xxx occurred resolves an amount of uncertainty that depends on p(x)p(x)p(x), specifically on how small p(x)p(x)p(x) is. The smaller p(x)p(x)p(x), the more surprising the message, and the more information it carries.

blocks.src:
#### Definition: Self-Information

For an outcome xxx with probability p(x)p(x)p(x), the **self-information** (or **surprise**) of xxx is

I(x)=log⁡1p(x)=−log⁡p(x).I(x) = \log \frac{1}{p(x)} = -\log p(x).I(x)=logp(x)1​=−logp(x).

In plain language, this means: the rarer the event, the more informative its occurrence. A certain event (p(x)=1p(x) = 1p(x)=1) has zero self-information. An impossible event (p(x)=0p(x) = 0p(x)=0) has infinite self-information in the limiting sense, but no message ever announces an impossible event, so this limit is harmless.

The base of the logarithm sets the unit. Base 2 gives bits. Base eee gives nats (natural units). Base 10 gives dits or hartleys. For computational and engineering purposes, bits are universal, and unless stated otherwise we will write log⁡\loglog to mean log⁡2\log_2log2​. The conversion is trivial: one nat is log⁡2e≈1.4427\log_2 e \approx 1.4427log2​e≈1.4427 bits.

Why is this the right definition? Three properties.

  1. **Monotonicity in ppp**: I(x)I(x)I(x) is a decreasing function of p(x)p(x)p(x). Rarer events are more informative. Common events less so. Good.
  2. **Additivity under independence** : If xxx and yyy are independent, so p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)p(x, y) = p(x) p(y)p(x,y)=p(x)p(y), then I(x,y)=−log⁡p(x,y)=−log⁡p(x)−log⁡p(y)=I(x)+I(y)I(x, y) = -\log p(x, y) = -\log p(x) - \log p(y) = I(x) + I(y)I(x,y)=−logp(x,y)=−logp(x)−logp(y)=I(x)+I(y). Information about independent events adds. Good.
  3. **Continuity** : I(x)I(x)I(x) varies smoothly with p(x)p(x)p(x). A small change in probability gives a small change in information. Good.

Up to choice of base, the logarithm is the _only_ function with these three properties on the appropriate domain. We will see in §1.4 a stronger axiomatic argument that pins down the choice even more tightly.


#### Worked Example 1: The Magic Coin

A friend has a coin that comes up heads with probability 0.990.990.99 and tails with probability 0.010.010.01. She flips it once and tells you the outcome.

If she says "heads," you have learned an outcome of probability 0.990.990.99. The self-information is

I(heads)=−log⁡20.99≈0.0145 bits.I(\text{heads}) = -\log_2 0.99 \approx 0.0145 \text{ bits}.I(heads)=−log2​0.99≈0.0145 bits.

You learned almost nothing. You expected heads.

If she says "tails," you have learned an outcome of probability 0.010.010.01. The self-information is

I(tails)=−log⁡20.01≈6.64 bits.I(\text{tails}) = -\log_2 0.01 \approx 6.64 \text{ bits}.I(tails)=−log2​0.01≈6.64 bits.

You learned a great deal. The rare event happened.

The two messages are physically identical (one syllable each), but their information content differs by a factor of about 460. The right measure of information, then, is not how long the message is; it is how much uncertainty it resolves.


### 1.3 Shannon Entropy

Self-information measures one outcome at a time. For most engineering purposes, what matters is the _average_ information of a source over all its possible outcomes. If you operate a teletype machine that emits one of 26 letters each second, you do not care about the surprise of a single particular letter; you care about the average surprise per letter, which determines the rate at which the source is generating information.

#### Definition: Shannon Entropy

The **Shannon entropy** of a discrete random variable XXX with probability mass function p(x)p(x)p(x) is

H(X)=E[I(X)]=−∑xp(x)log⁡p(x),H(X) = \mathbb{E}[I(X)] = -\sum_{x} p(x) \log p(x),H(X)=E[I(X)]=−x∑​p(x)logp(x),

where the sum is over all values xxx with p(x)>0p(x) > 0p(x)>0, and we adopt the convention 0log⁡0=00 \log 0 = 00log0=0 (justified by lim⁡p→0+plog⁡p=0\lim_{p \to 0^+} p \log p = 0limp→0+​plogp=0).

In plain language, this means: entropy is the average number of bits required to convey one outcome of XXX, in the long run, if you are using the most efficient possible code.

Entropy depends only on the _distribution_ ppp, not on the labels of the outcomes. Two random variables with completely different state spaces but identical probability vectors will have the same entropy. This is reassuring: the amount of uncertainty in a system is a property of how the probability is spread, not of what the outcomes are called.


#### A first computation: the binary entropy function

Consider a single binary random variable XXX with P(X=1)=pP(X = 1) = pP(X=1)=p and P(X=0)=1−pP(X = 0) = 1 - pP(X=0)=1−p. Its entropy is

Hb(p)=−plog⁡2p−(1−p)log⁡2(1−p).H_b(p) = -p \log_2 p - (1 - p) \log_2 (1 - p).Hb​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p).

This function, the **binary entropy function** , appears so often that it deserves its own name. Let us examine its behavior.

* At p=0p = 0p=0: both terms are 000 (using 0log⁡0=00 \log 0 = 00log0=0). Hb(0)=0H_b(0) = 0Hb​(0)=0. The outcome is certain (always 000); no information needed.
* At p=1p = 1p=1: same reasoning. Hb(1)=0H_b(1) = 0Hb​(1)=0. Always 111.
* At p=1/2p = 1/2p=1/2: Hb(1/2)=−12log⁡12−12log⁡12=−log⁡12=1H_b(1/2) = -\frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{2} = -\log \frac{1}{2} = 1Hb​(1/2)=−21​log21​−21​log21​=−log21​=1 bit.
* At p=0.99p = 0.99p=0.99: Hb(0.99)=−0.99log⁡0.99−0.01log⁡0.01≈0.0144+0.0664≈0.0808H_b(0.99) = -0.99 \log 0.99 - 0.01 \log 0.01 \approx 0.0144 + 0.0664 \approx 0.0808Hb​(0.99)=−0.99log0.99−0.01log0.01≈0.0144+0.0664≈0.0808 bits per coin flip.

So a fair coin flip carries one bit. A heavily biased coin (99/1) carries less than a tenth of a bit per flip on average, since most flips just say "heads" and surprise no one. The function is symmetric around p=1/2p = 1/2p=1/2, where it attains its maximum.

The shape of Hb(p)H_b(p)Hb​(p) is a smooth bump from (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) up to (1/2,1)(1/2, 1)(1/2,1) and back down to (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0), concave throughout. This concavity is not an accident; it is the source of many of the inequalities that follow in later chapters.

#### Worked Example 2: Entropy of an Eight-Sided Die

A fair eight-sided die has p(x)=1/8p(x) = 1/8p(x)=1/8 for each x∈{1,2,…,8}x \in \\{1, 2, \ldots, 8\\}x∈{1,2,…,8}. Its entropy is

H(X)=−∑x=1818log⁡218=−log⁡218=3 bits.H(X) = -\sum_{x=1}^{8} \frac{1}{8} \log_2 \frac{1}{8} = -\log_2 \frac{1}{8} = 3 \text{ bits}.H(X)=−x=1∑8​81​log2​81​=−log2​81​=3 bits.

Three bits per roll — exactly enough to specify one of eight outcomes. This makes sense: each roll is equivalent to three independent fair coin flips.

Now suppose the die is loaded: p(1)=1/2p(1) = 1/2p(1)=1/2, and p(2)=p(3)=…=p(8)=1/14p(2) = p(3) = \ldots = p(8) = 1/14p(2)=p(3)=…=p(8)=1/14. The entropy is

H(X)=−12log⁡12−7⋅114log⁡114=12+12log⁡214≈0.5+1.904≈2.40 bits.H(X) = -\frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{2} - 7 \cdot \frac{1}{14} \log \frac{1}{14} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \log_2 14 \approx 0.5 + 1.904 \approx 2.40 \text{ bits}.H(X)=−21​log21​−7⋅141​log141​=21​+21​log2​14≈0.5+1.904≈2.40 bits.

The loaded die is more predictable, and so its entropy is lower. The maximum-entropy distribution on a fixed set of outcomes is always the uniform one. We will prove this rigorously in §1.5.


#### Worked Example 3: Entropy of English Text

What is the entropy of an English letter? Naively, with 26 letters and a space, you might guess log⁡227≈4.75\log_2 27 \approx 4.75log2​27≈4.75 bits per letter. But not all letters are equally common. Using letter frequencies for English (roughly: eee at 12%12\%12%, ttt at 9%9\%9%, aaa at 8%8\%8%, and so on), the entropy of a single letter drops to about 4.074.074.07 bits. If you account for the fact that pairs of letters are not independent (after qqq, the next letter is almost certainly uuu; after ttt, often hhh; and so on), the entropy per letter falls to around 3.33.33.3 bits for digrams. Trigrams give about 3.13.13.1 bits. In a famous experiment in 1951, Shannon estimated the entropy of English at the level of long-range structure to be roughly 1.01.01.0 to 1.51.51.5 bits per letter. This means English has a redundancy of about 75%75\%75%. This bound is, as we will see in Chapter 4, the fundamental limit on lossless text compression. Modern transformer language models, which we treat in Chapter 15, push the empirical estimate down to roughly 0.70.70.7 bits per character on diverse English text, which is a striking confirmation that Shannon's analysis was on the right track and a striking demonstration of how good modern predictive models have become.

blocks.src:
### 1.4 Why This Definition? Four Axioms

The definition H(X)=−∑pilog⁡piH(X) = -\sum p_i \log p_iH(X)=−∑pi​logpi​ is not arbitrary. It is essentially forced by a small set of natural requirements. Shannon and, more rigorously, Khinchin showed that any function HHH satisfying four axioms must equal −∑pilog⁡pi-\sum p_i \log p_i−∑pi​logpi​ up to a positive multiplicative constant (which corresponds to choice of log base).

Let H(p1,…,pn)H(p_1, \ldots, p_n)H(p1​,…,pn​) be a real-valued function defined on probability distributions. The axioms are:

**Axiom 1 (Continuity)** : HHH is a continuous function of (p1,…,pn)(p_1, \ldots, p_n)(p1​,…,pn​).

A small perturbation of the probabilities should produce a small perturbation of the entropy. This is clearly desirable for any reasonable measure of uncertainty.

**Axiom 2 (Monotonicity in nnn for the uniform distribution)**: For the uniform distribution p1=⋯=pn=1/np_1 = \cdots = p_n = 1/np1​=⋯=pn​=1/n, the entropy H(1/n,…,1/n)H(1/n, \ldots, 1/n)H(1/n,…,1/n) is a monotonically increasing function of nnn.

The more equally likely outcomes there are, the more uncertain the source. A uniform distribution over four outcomes is more uncertain than a uniform distribution over two.

**Axiom 3 (Recursivity / Grouping)** : If we group some outcomes together (say, outcomes nnn and n−1n - 1n−1), the entropy decomposes according to the rule

H(p1,…,pn−2,pn−1,pn)=H(p1,…,pn−2,pn−1+pn)+(pn−1+pn)⋅H(pn−1pn−1+pn,pnpn−1+pn).H(p_1, \ldots, p_{n-2}, p_{n-1}, p_n) = H(p_1, \ldots, p_{n-2}, p_{n-1} + p_n) + (p_{n-1} + p_n) \cdot H\left(\frac{p_{n-1}}{p_{n-1} + p_n}, \frac{p_n}{p_{n-1} + p_n}\right).H(p1​,…,pn−2​,pn−1​,pn​)=H(p1​,…,pn−2​,pn−1​+pn​)+(pn−1​+pn​)⋅H(pn−1​+pn​pn−1​​,pn−1​+pn​pn​​).

This says: the uncertainty of a coarse-grained question plus the conditional uncertainty given the coarse answer equals the uncertainty of the fine-grained question. This is the property of a sensible entropy: it should not matter whether we resolve the question all at once or in two stages.

**Why does Axiom 3 do most of the work?** Axioms 1 and 2 are essentially regularity conditions — continuity rules out pathological functions, monotonicity fixes the sign — and Axiom 4 is just a choice of unit. The entire functional form of HHH comes from Axiom 3. Here is the intuition. Recursivity says that the answer to "how uncertain is the source?" cannot depend on how you choose to interrogate it. You may ask a single question with nnn possible answers, or first ask a binary question and then a follow-up; the _expected_ number of bits to resolve the source must be the same either way. That requirement is enormously restrictive. Concretely, the recursion forces H(1/n,…,1/n)H(1/n, \ldots, 1/n)H(1/n,…,1/n) to be a function f(n)f(n)f(n) satisfying f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)f(mn) = f(m) + f(n)f(mn)=f(m)+f(n) for all positive integers m,nm, nm,n — every uniform distribution can be decomposed into a uniform choice over mmm groups followed by a uniform choice within a group. Combined with the monotonicity of Axiom 2, the only continuous solution to this Cauchy-type functional equation is f(n)=clog⁡nf(n) = c \log nf(n)=clogn. From there, applying recursivity to non-uniform distributions extends the formula to −c∑pilog⁡pi-c \sum p_i \log p_i−c∑pi​logpi​, and Axiom 4 fixes c=1c = 1c=1 (with log base 2). So Axiom 3 is doing almost all the work; the others just make the answer well-posed and dimensioned.

blocks.src:
**Axiom 4 (Normalization)** : H(1/2,1/2)=1H(1/2, 1/2) = 1H(1/2,1/2)=1, so that one fair binary question carries one unit of entropy.

This is a choice of unit, fixing the log base to 2.

**Theorem (Khinchin / Shannon)** : The unique function satisfying Axioms 1 through 4 is

H(p1,…,pn)=−∑i=1npilog⁡2pi.H(p_1, \ldots, p_n) = -\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log_2 p_i.H(p1​,…,pn​)=−i=1∑n​pi​log2​pi​.

The full proof is technical and was first given in complete form by Khinchin in the 1950s. Shannon's original 1948 derivation used a slightly different axiom set but reached the same conclusion. The point for our purposes is that the formula is not a guess. Once you decide that information should be continuous, monotone in the number of equally likely options, and consistent under grouping, the formula is forced.

This kind of axiomatic uniqueness is rare in applied mathematics. It is the main reason information theory has the universal applicability it does: any reasonable definition of average uncertainty for a probability distribution is equivalent, up to scale, to Shannon's.


#### Common Misconception

Many readers, on first encountering Shannon entropy, conflate it with one of two adjacent quantities and so misuse it:

* **Misconception** : "Entropy is just log⁡\loglog of the number of outcomes."

This is true only for the uniform distribution. For non-uniform distributions, entropy is strictly less than log⁡n\log nlogn, and equals log⁡n\log nlogn only when all outcomes are equally likely. The entropy of a loaded die over eight faces is less than three bits, as our worked example showed.

* **Misconception** : "Entropy measures the information content of a _specific_ outcome."

No — that is self-information, I(x)=−log⁡p(x)I(x) = -\log p(x)I(x)=−logp(x). Entropy is the _average_ of self-information over the distribution: H(X)=E[I(X)]=∑p(x)I(x)H(X) = \mathbb{E}[I(X)] = \sum p(x) I(x)H(X)=E[I(X)]=∑p(x)I(x). The entropy of XXX is one number that summarizes the whole distribution, not a function of any particular outcome.

When teaching information theory, these two misconceptions account for perhaps half of all early errors. Bear them in mind.


### 1.5 Properties of Entropy

We collect here the most useful elementary properties of entropy. Most are direct consequences of the convexity of −xlog⁡x-x \log x−xlogx, which we will use repeatedly throughout the book.


#### Property 1: Non-negativity

H(X)≥0.H(X) \geq 0.H(X)≥0.

**Proof** : Each term −p(x)log⁡p(x)-p(x) \log p(x)−p(x)logp(x) is non-negative when 0≤p(x)≤10 \leq p(x) \leq 10≤p(x)≤1, because log⁡p(x)≤0\log p(x) \leq 0logp(x)≤0 on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. The sum of non-negative terms is non-negative. □\square□

Equality holds if and only if XXX is deterministic, that is, p(x)=1p(x) = 1p(x)=1 for one outcome and zero for the rest.

blocks.src:
#### Property 2: Maximum entropy on a finite set

For a discrete random variable XXX on a set of nnn outcomes,

H(X)≤log⁡n,H(X) \leq \log n,H(X)≤logn,

with equality if and only if XXX is uniformly distributed.

**Proof** : This follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the concave function log⁡\loglog. For any probability distribution ppp,

H(X)=∑xp(x)log⁡1p(x)≤log⁡∑xp(x)⋅1p(x)=log⁡n,H(X) = \sum_x p(x) \log \frac{1}{p(x)} \leq \log \sum_x p(x) \cdot \frac{1}{p(x)} = \log n,H(X)=x∑​p(x)logp(x)1​≤logx∑​p(x)⋅p(x)1​=logn,

where we used Jensen's inequality on the concave function log⁡\loglog. Equality in Jensen's inequality holds when the argument is constant, that is, when 1/p(x)1/p(x)1/p(x) is the same for all xxx, which means p(x)=1/np(x) = 1/np(x)=1/n for all xxx. □\square□


#### Property 3: Concavity in the distribution

H(p)H(p)H(p) is a concave function of ppp. That is, for two probability distributions ppp and qqq and λ∈[0,1]\lambda \in [0, 1]λ∈[0,1],

H(λp+(1−λ)q)≥λH(p)+(1−λ)H(q).H(\lambda p + (1 - \lambda) q) \geq \lambda H(p) + (1 - \lambda) H(q).H(λp+(1−λ)q)≥λH(p)+(1−λ)H(q).

**Proof** : The function f(t)=−tlog⁡tf(t) = -t \log tf(t)=−tlogt is concave on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] (verify by differentiation: f′′(t)=−1/(tln⁡2)<0f''(t) = -1/(t \ln 2) < 0f′′(t)=−1/(tln2)<0). The entropy is a sum of f(p(x))f(p(x))f(p(x)), and the sum of concave functions is concave. □\square□

This concavity has a beautiful interpretation: mixing two distributions can only increase the entropy. Intuitively, mixing produces a more uncertain combined distribution; you have to first decide which distribution you sampled from.


#### Property 4: Joint entropy decomposition

For a pair (X,Y)(X, Y)(X,Y), the **joint entropy** is

H(X,Y)=−∑x,yp(x,y)log⁡p(x,y).H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(x, y).H(X,Y)=−x,y∑​p(x,y)logp(x,y).

This is just the entropy of the joint distribution, treated as a single random variable on the product space. It satisfies

max⁡(H(X),H(Y))≤H(X,Y)≤H(X)+H(Y),\max(H(X), H(Y)) \leq H(X, Y) \leq H(X) + H(Y),max(H(X),H(Y))≤H(X,Y)≤H(X)+H(Y),

with the right inequality an equality if and only if XXX and YYY are independent.

We will return to joint entropy and to its richer cousins, conditional entropy and mutual information, in Chapter 2.

blocks.src:
### 1.6 Worked Example 4: Twenty Questions and the Optimal Strategy

The game of Twenty Questions illustrates entropy concretely. Player A thinks of an object; Player B may ask up to twenty yes-or-no questions to guess what it is.

Each yes-or-no question can resolve at most one bit of information (when the answer is equally likely to be yes or no; less when it is biased). Twenty questions can therefore resolve at most twenty bits, which is enough to distinguish among 220≈1062^{20} \approx 10^6220≈106 objects.

A good Player B asks questions whose answers are as close to fifty-fifty as possible. "Is it bigger than a breadbox?" is a classically good question because, conditioned on what we know so far, both answers are roughly equally likely. A poor question ("is it the Empire State Building?") has very skewed answer probabilities (overwhelmingly no, slightly yes if the answer happens to be "yes"). The expected information from the poor question is much less than one bit.

This is the operational meaning of entropy: it is the average number of yes-or-no questions you need to ask to determine the value of XXX, provided you are using the optimal asking strategy. We will make this operational interpretation precise in Chapter 4 with the Source Coding Theorem, which says that you can encode XXX in expectation with as few as H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol, and no fewer. Twenty Questions is the friendly first taste.


### 1.7 Differential Entropy: A First Sketch

Most of this chapter has assumed XXX is discrete. For continuous random variables (say, a Gaussian), the obvious analog is

h(X)=−∫f(x)log⁡f(x) dx,h(X) = -\int f(x) \log f(x) \, dx,h(X)=−∫f(x)logf(x)dx,

where fff is the density. This quantity is called **differential entropy**. It is useful but subtle: unlike discrete entropy, differential entropy can be negative (a tightly peaked density has f(x)>1f(x) > 1f(x)>1 on parts of its support, and so log⁡f(x)>0\log f(x) > 0logf(x)>0 there, giving a negative integrand). Differential entropy also depends on the choice of measure: change variables and the entropy changes.

For most of this book the discrete case is what we need. We will pick up differential entropy seriously in Chapter 9, when we discuss continuous-source rate-distortion.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
### 1.8 Historical Note: Shannon at Bell Labs

It would be a disservice to begin this book without a short portrait of the man whose ideas it is built around.

Claude Elwood Shannon (1916-2001) grew up in Gaylord, Michigan, the son of a probate judge. His first scientific role model was his uncle, an inventor. As an undergraduate at Michigan, Shannon studied electrical engineering and mathematics. His master's thesis at MIT, completed in 1937 when he was 21, applied Boolean algebra to relay circuits and is sometimes called the most important master's thesis of the twentieth century. It established that the algebra Boole had invented for logic in 1854 could describe the behavior of telephone switching circuits and digital computers. Without this insight, the architectural language of digital computing would have had to be invented from scratch by someone else.

Shannon joined Bell Labs in 1941. The wartime years were spent on cryptography and on fire-control problems for anti-aircraft batteries. After the war, he turned to the problem that would make him famous: how much information could be reliably transmitted across a noisy channel? The 1948 paper, _A Mathematical Theory of Communication_ , was the answer.

Shannon's personal style was famously playful. He rode a unicycle in the Bell Labs hallways. He juggled, sometimes while riding the unicycle. He built a series of small machines in his home workshop, including a chess-playing program (one of the first), a maze-solving mechanical mouse named Theseus, a calculating machine that worked in Roman numerals, and a flame-throwing trumpet. He once described his philosophy of research as "I just wondered how things were put together."

Shannon was not a prolific publisher. His complete _Collected Papers_ fits in one volume of about a thousand pages. But what he published changed the character of communication, computing, and statistics permanently. His papers are also extraordinarily clear: he wrote in plain English, his proofs are usually more illuminating than mechanically necessary, and he was generous about giving credit. The best advice anyone can give a student of information theory is to read the original 1948 paper alongside any modern textbook.

The field he created — information theory — is now the mathematical foundation of every modern communication system, every compression scheme, every machine learning loss function, and every cryptographic protocol. One paper, one man, one framework that has lasted seventy-five years.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
### 1.9 An AI Connection: Cross-Entropy and Modern Loss Functions

We close this opening chapter with a glance forward, because every chapter in this book closes with a glance forward.

When you train a neural network classifier on, say, the MNIST handwritten digits, the standard loss function is _cross-entropy_. We will define cross-entropy carefully in Chapter 8, but its essence is already in this chapter. If ppp is the true distribution over class labels (a one-hot vector for a single example: probability one on the true digit, zero elsewhere) and qqq is the model's predicted distribution, then the cross-entropy loss is

H(p,q)=−∑yp(y)log⁡q(y).H(p, q) = -\sum_y p(y) \log q(y).H(p,q)=−y∑​p(y)logq(y).

For a one-hot ppp with the truth at position y∗y^*y∗, this collapses to −log⁡q(y∗)-\log q(y^*)−logq(y∗) — exactly the _self-information_ of the truth under the model's distribution. The model is being penalized in proportion to how surprised _it_ is by the right answer.

A model that gives the right answer probability close to one incurs negligible loss; a model that gives it probability close to zero is hammered. Training proceeds by gradient descent on the parameters of qqq to drive the average self-information of the correct labels down toward the entropy of the data — the irreducible floor below which no model can go. The gap between the model's cross-entropy and the true entropy is exactly the **Kullback-Leibler divergence** D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q), a quantity we will explore in Chapter 8 and use throughout the book.

So when a deep learning paper reports that a language model achieves a cross-entropy of 2.52.52.5 bits per token, what is being said is: the model resolves the next-token uncertainty to within 2.52.52.5 bits per word on average. Modern frontier language models push this number into the range of 0.70.70.7 to 1.01.01.0 bits per character on diverse English text, which is comparable to Shannon's 1951 estimate of the entropy of English. Whether this means the models have "learned the entropy of English" or merely "memorized enough of the corpus to compress it well" is a debate we will return to in Chapter 15.

For now, hold the connection lightly. Entropy is the floor; cross-entropy is the achieved cost; their gap is the room a model has left to improve. Every modern AI system is operating somewhere in this picture.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We have introduced the central object of the book: Shannon entropy, defined for a discrete random variable XXX with distribution ppp by H(X)=−∑xp(x)log⁡p(x)H(X) = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x)H(X)=−∑x​p(x)logp(x). We saw why this definition is essentially forced by four natural axioms (continuity, monotonicity, recursivity, normalization). We saw its basic properties: non-negativity, maximization at the uniform distribution, and concavity. We examined three worked examples: a magic coin, a loaded die, and the entropy of English text. We previewed the AI connection that runs through the book: that cross-entropy loss in modern deep learning is the same quantity, in the same units, that Shannon defined in 1948.

The next chapter extends entropy from a single random variable to a pair: joint, conditional, and mutual information, proving the chain rule that organizes all of subsequent information theory.

A reader who has finished this chapter should be able to:

* Compute the entropy of any discrete distribution
* Explain why the logarithm is the right base operation for information measure
* State the four axioms that pin down Shannon entropy uniquely
* Distinguish self-information from entropy, and entropy from joint entropy
* Begin to see why every modern machine learning loss function is, at heart, an entropy

We will revisit entropy in every subsequent chapter. By Chapter 18, when we train a small language model and measure its perplexity, the entire arc will close: the bits Shannon defined will be the bits we count.

We will see in Chapter 3 (the AEP) that this fact is not just an arithmetic identity but an operational one: with high probability, an i.i.d. sequence falls in a "typical set" of about 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X) sequences, all roughly equiprobable.

**Q4.** A news service categorizes the day's lead story as one of: "politics" (p=0.4p = 0.4p=0.4), "economics" (p=0.2p = 0.2p=0.2), "sports" (p=0.2p = 0.2p=0.2), "science" (p=0.1p = 0.1p=0.1), "other" (p=0.1p = 0.1p=0.1). Hint

Compute H(X)H(X)H(X). The expected number of optimal yes-or-no questions is between H(X)H(X)H(X) and H(X)+1H(X) + 1H(X)+1 (Source Coding Theorem, Chapter 4).

**Answer:**

H(X)=−0.4log⁡0.4−0.2log⁡0.2−0.2log⁡0.2−0.1log⁡0.1−0.1log⁡0.1.H(X) = -0.4 \log 0.4 - 0.2 \log 0.2 - 0.2 \log 0.2 - 0.1 \log 0.1 - 0.1 \log 0.1.H(X)=−0.4log0.4−0.2log0.2−0.2log0.2−0.1log0.1−0.1log0.1.

Numerically:

* −0.4log⁡0.4≈0.529-0.4 \log 0.4 \approx 0.529−0.4log0.4≈0.529
* −0.2log⁡0.2≈0.464-0.2 \log 0.2 \approx 0.464−0.2log0.2≈0.464 (twice)
* −0.1log⁡0.1≈0.332-0.1 \log 0.1 \approx 0.332−0.1log0.1≈0.332 (twice)

Sum: H(X)≈0.529+0.928+0.664≈2.12H(X) \approx 0.529 + 0.928 + 0.664 \approx 2.12H(X)≈0.529+0.928+0.664≈2.12 bits.

You should expect to ask between 2.122.122.12 and 3.123.123.12 yes-or-no questions on average to guess the lead story, with a clever strategy. A naive binary search over five categories costs ⌈log⁡25⌉=3\lceil \log_2 5 \rceil = 3⌈log2​5⌉=3 questions; a Huffman-style strategy that asks about the most likely category first will do better on average. We will compute the exact optimum in Chapter 4.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Why does Shannon's definition of information ignore meaning? Could a different definition of "information" (one that incorporated semantics) be useful, or is the meaning-free version definitive?

**Discussion:** Shannon's choice was strategic. Meaning is hard; uncertainty resolution is mathematical. By restricting attention to the latter, Shannon made the field tractable. The cost is that two messages with identical bit-content can have wildly different importance to a recipient. "Your house is on fire" and "the chess piece is on E5" might both be 100-bit messages, yet only one demands action.

Several twentieth-century thinkers tried to extend Shannon's framework to incorporate semantics. Carnap and Bar-Hillel proposed _semantic information_ in the 1950s, defined relative to a logical language; their framework computes "how much" a sentence rules out from the space of possible worlds. It is a beautiful idea but has not had operational uptake comparable to Shannon's. The lesson seems to be that extending information theory to handle meaning requires committing to a particular language and ontology, which kills the universality that made Shannon's framework powerful.

In modern AI, there are echoes of this debate. Language models trained to minimize cross-entropy are being asked to do far more than compress text: they are also being asked to encode meaning, reasoning, world knowledge. The success and failure modes of these models tell us something about what cross-entropy minimization captures and what it does not. A model that confidently produces fluent nonsense has very low cross-entropy on its own outputs but has clearly failed at the task we care about. This is a hint that pure information-theoretic optimization, while necessary, is not sufficient for the goals of modern AI.

The question is open and active. For now, take the operational view: Shannon's bits are the right primitive, and meaning is a question we add on top.

**Q2.** Suppose a hostile party can manipulate a probability distribution before you observe a sample from it. How might they choose the distribution to minimize the entropy you can extract? To maximize it? What does this tell you about entropy as a measure of information _availability_ versus information _resolution_?

**Discussion:** A hostile party who wants to minimize the information you extract should make the distribution as deterministic as possible, concentrating all the probability on one outcome. Then your samples carry essentially no information; you knew the answer in advance. To maximize the entropy you extract, the hostile party should make the distribution as uniform as possible.

This duality — uncertainty as both a friend (it is what makes a sample informative) and a foe (it is what makes a system hard to predict) — runs through the field. In communication, we want the channel input to be high-entropy (so the transmitter can convey many bits) and the channel error to be low-entropy (so the receiver can decode reliably). In machine learning, we want the data distribution to have rich structure (high conditional entropy of detail given context, low entropy of label given features). The beauty of Shannon's framework is that the same quantity H(X)H(X)H(X) measures all of these things, and the rules for combining them (chain rules and data-processing inequalities) are universal.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Shannon Idea: Measuring Information
blocks.src:
**Q3.** Consider a variant on the entropy axioms: drop Axiom 4 (normalization). What functions then satisfy the remaining three axioms? What does this tell you about the role of "choice of unit" in physics and information theory?

**Discussion:** Without normalization, the function H=−c∑pilog⁡piH = -c \sum p_i \log p_iH=−c∑pi​logpi​ for any c>0c > 0c>0 satisfies the remaining axioms. In other words, removing normalization is exactly removing the choice of unit (bits versus nats versus dits). Choice of unit is universal in physics: temperature can be measured in Kelvin, Celsius, Fahrenheit, Rankine; energy in joules, ergs, calories. Each unit corresponds to a multiplicative constant. The axiomatic uniqueness of entropy _up to a multiplicative constant_ is exactly the statement that information is a real physical quantity with a natural definition, and the only choice is what we measure it in.

This connects information theory to thermodynamics in an unexpected way. The thermodynamic entropy S=−kB∑piln⁡piS = -k_B \sum p_i \ln p_iS=−kB​∑pi​lnpi​ is the same formula with kBk_BkB​ (Boltzmann's constant) playing the role of unit. Many physicists and information theorists have argued, most famously E. T. Jaynes in 1957, that thermodynamic entropy is a special case of Shannon entropy, applied to the distribution over microstates. We will encounter this perspective again in Chapter 9 when we discuss the maximum-entropy principle in statistical mechanics.


### Connections to Subsequent Chapters

This chapter laid the foundations: self-information, entropy, the axioms, the basic properties. Almost every subsequent chapter builds on these definitions.

* **Chapter 2** generalizes from one variable to a pair (joint, conditional, and mutual information) and proves the chain rule that all of subsequent theory rests on.
* **Chapter 3** proves the Asymptotic Equipartition Property, which gives entropy its operational interpretation as the asymptotic per-symbol description length.
* **Chapter 4** proves the Source Coding Theorem, which says H(X)H(X)H(X) is the fundamental limit of lossless compression.
* **Chapter 8** introduces KL divergence, of which cross-entropy and likelihood-based machine learning are direct applications.
* **Chapter 15** returns to the entropy of natural language and connects modern language model perplexity to Shannon's 1951 estimate.

A reader who has internalized this chapter can read any of those chapters with the necessary background. The thread that will stay with us is: every quantity in information theory is, at root, the entropy of a carefully chosen distribution.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
Chapter 1 gave us entropy H(X)H(X)H(X), the average uncertainty of a single random variable. That was enough to prove that the entropy of English is bounded, to motivate lossless compression, and to show why cross-entropy is the right training loss. But a single random variable does not capture much of what we want to say about information. The interesting questions arise when two or more variables are present and we want to ask how much one tells us about the other. How much does the weather tell us about whether someone will carry an umbrella? How much does the previous word in a sentence narrow down what the next one will be? How much does the result of one medical test reduce our uncertainty about the disease another test would diagnose? Each of these questions has a precise information-theoretic answer, and the machinery to give that answer is the subject of this chapter.

We extend the definition of entropy from one variable to two, in the form of joint entropy, then refine it to conditional entropy (the leftover uncertainty about YYY once XXX is observed), and finally to mutual information (the reduction in uncertainty about YYY provided by knowledge of XXX). Mutual information will turn out to be the central quantity of the rest of this book. Channel capacity in Chapter 5 is the maximum of I(X;Y)I(X;Y)I(X;Y) over input distributions; the source coding theorem of Chapter 4 connects mutual information to redundancy; modern self-supervised learning, which we treat in Chapter 14, is largely an exercise in maximizing mutual information between learned representations and their context.

This chapter is short on stories and long on identities. The chain rules and inequalities introduced here will recur in nearly every subsequent chapter. They are worth memorizing.


### 2.1 Joint Entropy

For two random variables XXX and YYY with joint distribution p(x,y)p(x, y)p(x,y), the joint entropy is the entropy of the pair, treated as a single random variable on the product space:


#### Definition: Joint Entropy

H(X,Y)=−∑x,yp(x,y)log⁡p(x,y).H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(x, y).H(X,Y)=−x,y∑​p(x,y)logp(x,y).

In plain language, this means: H(X,Y)H(X, Y)H(X,Y) is the number of bits needed on average to specify both XXX and YYY jointly, when an optimal code is used. It depends on the joint distribution, not on the marginals alone.


#### A first observation: independence is the maximum

If XXX and YYY are independent, then p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)p(x, y) = p(x) p(y)p(x,y)=p(x)p(y), and the joint entropy decomposes:

H(X,Y)=−∑x,yp(x)p(y)[log⁡p(x)+log⁡p(y)]=H(X)+H(Y).H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x) p(y) [\log p(x) + \log p(y)] = H(X) + H(Y).H(X,Y)=−x,y∑​p(x)p(y)[logp(x)+logp(y)]=H(X)+H(Y).

If XXX and YYY are dependent, then H(X,Y)<H(X)+H(Y)H(X, Y) < H(X) + H(Y)H(X,Y)<H(X)+H(Y). Knowing XXX reduces our uncertainty about YYY, so we do not need a full H(Y)H(Y)H(Y) bits on top of H(X)H(X)H(X) to specify the pair. The slack between H(X)+H(Y)H(X) + H(Y)H(X)+H(Y) and H(X,Y)H(X, Y)H(X,Y) is exactly the mutual information I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y), which we will define in §2.4.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Worked Example: Two correlated coins

Two coins are flipped, but they are glued together in a strange way: they always come up either both heads or both tails, with each outcome equally likely. So p(HH)=p(TT)=1/2p(HH) = p(TT) = 1/2p(HH)=p(TT)=1/2, and p(HT)=p(TH)=0p(HT) = p(TH) = 0p(HT)=p(TH)=0.

Marginal distributions: P(X=H)=P(X=T)=P(Y=H)=P(Y=T)=1/2P(X = H) = P(X = T) = P(Y = H) = P(Y = T) = 1/2P(X=H)=P(X=T)=P(Y=H)=P(Y=T)=1/2. So H(X)=H(Y)=1H(X) = H(Y) = 1H(X)=H(Y)=1 bit.

Joint distribution: only two of the four outcomes have nonzero probability, each with probability 1/21/21/2. So

H(X,Y)=−12log⁡12−12log⁡12=1 bit.H(X, Y) = -\frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{2} = 1 \text{ bit}.H(X,Y)=−21​log21​−21​log21​=1 bit.

The pair is _one bit_ , not two, because perfectly correlated random variables together carry only as much information as one of them. The data redundancy is total. We will use this kind of example again in Chapter 12 when we discuss distributed source coding.


### 2.2 Conditional Entropy

Often we want to ask: given that we already know XXX, how much uncertainty about YYY remains? This is the conditional entropy.


#### Definition: Conditional Entropy

The **conditional entropy** of YYY given XXX is

H(Y∣X)=∑xp(x)H(Y∣X=x)=−∑x,yp(x,y)log⁡p(y∣x).H(Y \mid X) = \sum_x p(x) H(Y \mid X = x) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(y \mid x).H(Y∣X)=x∑​p(x)H(Y∣X=x)=−x,y∑​p(x,y)logp(y∣x).

In plain language, this means: H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X) is the average uncertainty about YYY once XXX has been observed. The averaging is over the distribution of XXX; for each particular value xxx, we compute H(Y∣X=x)=−∑yp(y∣x)log⁡p(y∣x)H(Y \mid X = x) = -\sum_y p(y \mid x) \log p(y \mid x)H(Y∣X=x)=−∑y​p(y∣x)logp(y∣x), which is the entropy of the conditional distribution p(y∣x)p(y \mid x)p(y∣x), and then average.

This is not symmetric: in general, H(Y∣X)≠H(X∣Y)H(Y \mid X) \neq H(X \mid Y)H(Y∣X)=H(X∣Y). Knowing the disease often pins down the symptom; knowing the symptom rarely pins down the disease.


#### Property 1: Conditional entropy is non-negative

H(Y∣X)≥0,H(Y \mid X) \geq 0,H(Y∣X)≥0,

with equality if and only if YYY is a deterministic function of XXX. The proof is immediate from the non-negativity of H(Y∣X=x)H(Y \mid X = x)H(Y∣X=x) for each xxx.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Property 2: The chain rule

This is the workhorse identity of information theory.

**Chain rule for entropy:**

H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y).H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y).H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y).

In plain language, this means: the joint entropy of (X,Y)(X, Y)(X,Y) is the entropy of XXX plus the leftover entropy of YYY given XXX. Equivalently, you can specify the pair by first specifying XXX (cost: H(X)H(X)H(X) bits) and then specifying YYY given that you know XXX (cost: H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X) bits on average).

**Proof:** Starting from the definition,

H(X,Y)=−∑x,yp(x,y)log⁡p(x,y).H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(x, y).H(X,Y)=−x,y∑​p(x,y)logp(x,y).

Use p(x,y)=p(x)p(y∣x)p(x, y) = p(x) p(y \mid x)p(x,y)=p(x)p(y∣x):

H(X,Y)=−∑x,yp(x,y)[log⁡p(x)+log⁡p(y∣x)]=−∑xp(x)log⁡p(x)−∑x,yp(x,y)log⁡p(y∣x).H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) [\log p(x) + \log p(y \mid x)] = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x) - \sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log p(y \mid x).H(X,Y)=−x,y∑​p(x,y)[logp(x)+logp(y∣x)]=−x∑​p(x)logp(x)−x,y∑​p(x,y)logp(y∣x).

The first term is H(X)H(X)H(X); the second is H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X). □\square□

The same argument with XXX and YYY swapped gives the second equality.


#### General chain rule

The chain rule extends to nnn variables:

H(X1,X2,…,Xn)=∑i=1nH(Xi∣X1,X2,…,Xi−1).H(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n H(X_i \mid X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{i-1}).H(X1​,X2​,…,Xn​)=i=1∑n​H(Xi​∣X1​,X2​,…,Xi−1​).

This is the most useful identity in the field; it lets us factor the joint entropy of any sequence into a sum of per-step uncertainties. Language models, in particular, are an autoregressive instantiation of this chain rule: they parametrize p(xi∣x1,…,xi−1)p(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1})p(xi​∣x1​,…,xi−1​) as a neural network, and the cross-entropy of the model on a corpus is precisely the average per-token surprise computed via the chain rule.


#### Property 3: Conditioning reduces entropy

A fundamental inequality:

H(Y∣X)≤H(Y),H(Y \mid X) \leq H(Y),H(Y∣X)≤H(Y),

with equality if and only if XXX and YYY are independent.

**Proof sketch:** Define mutual information I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X) (we will do this formally in §2.4); the claim is that I(X;Y)≥0I(X; Y) \geq 0I(X;Y)≥0. This is equivalent to saying the KL divergence D(p(x,y)∥p(x)p(y))≥0D(p(x, y) \| p(x) p(y)) \geq 0D(p(x,y)∥p(x)p(y))≥0, which is Gibbs' inequality (Chapter 8). Equality holds iff p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)p(x, y) = p(x) p(y)p(x,y)=p(x)p(y), i.e., independence. □\square□

This inequality is intuitively obvious: on average, knowing more cannot make you more uncertain. But there is a subtle and important point: it holds _on average over_ XXX, not for every value of XXX. For a particular outcome X=xX = xX=x, the conditional entropy H(Y∣X=x)H(Y \mid X = x)H(Y∣X=x) can exceed H(Y)H(Y)H(Y). Imagine YYY is a fair coin flip and XXX is "the coin showed an unusual face this morning." For most values of XXX, YYY is still pretty random, but conditioning on a rare or surprising XXX can sometimes leave more uncertainty about YYY than the marginal. The averaging over XXX is what enforces the inequality.

This subtlety is a perennial source of student confusion. Do not flatten "conditioning reduces entropy" into "more data always makes things less uncertain at every point."

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
### 2.3 Worked Example: Conditional Entropy in Diagnosis

A doctor has a patient with one of two conditions: a common ailment (probability 0.90.90.9) or a rare disease (probability 0.10.10.1). She runs a test XXX that has the following conditional distribution:

p(X=+∣common)=0.1,p(X=−∣common)=0.9,p(X = + \mid \text{common}) = 0.1, \quad p(X = - \mid \text{common}) = 0.9,p(X=+∣common)=0.1,p(X=−∣common)=0.9, p(X=+∣rare)=0.95,p(X=−∣rare)=0.05.p(X = + \mid \text{rare}) = 0.95, \quad p(X = - \mid \text{rare}) = 0.05.p(X=+∣rare)=0.95,p(X=−∣rare)=0.05.

The test is highly sensitive (true positive rate 0.950.950.95) and reasonably specific (true negative rate 0.90.90.9). What is the entropy of the disease before the test? After?

Let YYY be the disease and XXX the test result.

Before the test:

H(Y)=Hb(0.1)=−0.1log⁡0.1−0.9log⁡0.9≈0.469 bits.H(Y) = H_b(0.1) = -0.1 \log 0.1 - 0.9 \log 0.9 \approx 0.469 \text{ bits}.H(Y)=Hb​(0.1)=−0.1log0.1−0.9log0.9≈0.469 bits.

The marginal probabilities of the test:

p(X=+)=0.9⋅0.1+0.1⋅0.95=0.09+0.095=0.185,p(X = +) = 0.9 \cdot 0.1 + 0.1 \cdot 0.95 = 0.09 + 0.095 = 0.185,p(X=+)=0.9⋅0.1+0.1⋅0.95=0.09+0.095=0.185, p(X=−)=1−0.185=0.815.p(X = -) = 1 - 0.185 = 0.815.p(X=−)=1−0.185=0.815.

Posterior given a positive test:

p(Y=rare∣X=+)=p(X=+∣rare)p(rare)p(X=+)=0.95⋅0.10.185≈0.514.p(Y = \text{rare} \mid X = +) = \frac{p(X = + \mid \text{rare}) p(\text{rare})}{p(X = +)} = \frac{0.95 \cdot 0.1}{0.185} \approx 0.514.p(Y=rare∣X=+)=p(X=+)p(X=+∣rare)p(rare)​=0.1850.95⋅0.1​≈0.514.

Posterior given a negative test:

p(Y=rare∣X=−)=0.05⋅0.10.815≈0.0061.p(Y = \text{rare} \mid X = -) = \frac{0.05 \cdot 0.1}{0.815} \approx 0.0061.p(Y=rare∣X=−)=0.8150.05⋅0.1​≈0.0061.

So after a positive test, the patient has roughly even odds of the rare disease. After a negative, the rare disease is almost ruled out. The conditional entropy:

H(Y∣X=+)=Hb(0.514)≈0.9996 bits,H(Y \mid X = +) = H_b(0.514) \approx 0.9996 \text{ bits},H(Y∣X=+)=Hb​(0.514)≈0.9996 bits, H(Y∣X=−)=Hb(0.0061)≈0.052 bits,H(Y \mid X = -) = H_b(0.0061) \approx 0.052 \text{ bits},H(Y∣X=−)=Hb​(0.0061)≈0.052 bits, H(Y∣X)=0.185⋅0.9996+0.815⋅0.052≈0.185+0.042≈0.227 bits.H(Y \mid X) = 0.185 \cdot 0.9996 + 0.815 \cdot 0.052 \approx 0.185 + 0.042 \approx 0.227 \text{ bits}.H(Y∣X)=0.185⋅0.9996+0.815⋅0.052≈0.185+0.042≈0.227 bits.

Note that H(Y∣X=+)>H(Y)≈0.469H(Y \mid X = +) > H(Y) \approx 0.469H(Y∣X=+)>H(Y)≈0.469 bits: a positive test, in this case, _increases_ uncertainty (because it leaves the patient at roughly fifty-fifty between two diseases). But H(Y∣X=−)H(Y \mid X = -)H(Y∣X=−) is very low. The average, H(Y∣X)≈0.227H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.227H(Y∣X)≈0.227, is less than H(Y)≈0.469H(Y) \approx 0.469H(Y)≈0.469, as the inequality requires.

The information gained by the test is H(Y)−H(Y∣X)≈0.242H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.242H(Y)−H(Y∣X)≈0.242 bits. In other words, this test resolves about half a bit of disease uncertainty on average. This number, the **mutual information** , is the next subject of the chapter.


### 2.4 Mutual Information

We arrive at the central object of much of the rest of this book.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Mutual Information

The **mutual information** between XXX and YYY is

I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)−H(X∣Y).I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y).I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)−H(X∣Y).

Equivalently, expanding via the chain rule,

I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y).I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).

And in its most commonly used form,

I(X;Y)=∑x,yp(x,y)log⁡p(x,y)p(x)p(y)=D(p(x,y)∥p(x)p(y)).I(X; Y) = \sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x) p(y)} = D(p(x, y) \| p(x) p(y)).I(X;Y)=x,y∑​p(x,y)logp(x)p(y)p(x,y)​=D(p(x,y)∥p(x)p(y)).

The last form expresses mutual information as the KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals. It is the most convenient form for proofs.

In plain language, this means: I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) is the amount by which knowing XXX reduces the uncertainty about YYY (or vice versa, by symmetry). It is a measure of the dependence between XXX and YYY.


#### Properties

  1. **Non-negativity** : I(X;Y)≥0I(X; Y) \geq 0I(X;Y)≥0, with equality iff XXX and YYY are independent.
  2. **Symmetry** : I(X;Y)=I(Y;X)I(X; Y) = I(Y; X)I(X;Y)=I(Y;X). The information XXX carries about YYY is the same as the information YYY carries about XXX.
  3. **Bounding** : I(X;Y)≤min⁡(H(X),H(Y))I(X; Y) \leq \min(H(X), H(Y))I(X;Y)≤min(H(X),H(Y)). You cannot extract more information about YYY than YYY has, and you cannot extract more information from XXX than XXX has.
  4. **Self-mutual-information** : I(X;X)=H(X)I(X; X) = H(X)I(X;X)=H(X). A variable carries exactly its own entropy of information about itself.

The proofs of 1, 3, 4 are immediate from the formulas; symmetry is built into the symmetric form H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y)H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).


#### A picture worth memorizing

Information theorists often draw a Venn-diagram-like picture (verbally, since we have no figures): imagine two overlapping circles representing H(X)H(X)H(X) and H(Y)H(Y)H(Y). Their union is H(X,Y)H(X, Y)H(X,Y). Their intersection is I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y). The crescent of the H(X)H(X)H(X) circle outside the overlap is H(X∣Y)H(X \mid Y)H(X∣Y); the crescent of H(Y)H(Y)H(Y) outside the overlap is H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X). Every identity in this section can be read off this picture:

* H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−I(X;Y)H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - I(X; Y)H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−I(X;Y) (inclusion-exclusion).
* H(X∣Y)=H(X)−I(X;Y)H(X \mid Y) = H(X) - I(X; Y)H(X∣Y)=H(X)−I(X;Y) (subtract the overlap).
* I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y)I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y) (overlap from union and parts).

The Venn picture is _not_ a fully rigorous tool; for three variables it can mislead, because I(X;Y;Z)I(X; Y; Z)I(X;Y;Z) (the three-way version) can be negative. But for two variables it is a faithful and useful summary.


### 2.5 Conditional Mutual Information

The conditional version of mutual information answers: given knowledge of a third variable ZZZ, how much information about YYY does XXX provide?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Conditional Mutual Information

I(X;Y∣Z)=H(X∣Z)−H(X∣Y,Z).I(X; Y \mid Z) = H(X \mid Z) - H(X \mid Y, Z).I(X;Y∣Z)=H(X∣Z)−H(X∣Y,Z).

Equivalently:

I(X;Y∣Z)=∑zp(z)I(X;Y∣Z=z)=EZ[I(X;Y∣Z)].I(X; Y \mid Z) = \sum_{z} p(z) I(X; Y \mid Z = z) = \mathbb{E}_Z [I(X; Y \mid Z)].I(X;Y∣Z)=z∑​p(z)I(X;Y∣Z=z)=EZ​[I(X;Y∣Z)].

This is again non-negative, again symmetric in XXX and YYY, and again the natural quantity for many applications. In particular, conditional mutual information is the quantity controlled by the **data-processing inequality** , which we now state.


#### The Data-Processing Inequality

If X→Y→ZX \to Y \to ZX→Y→Z is a Markov chain (meaning ZZZ is conditionally independent of XXX given YYY), then

I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y).I(X; Z) \leq I(X; Y).I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y).

In plain language, this means: processing data can only destroy information, never create it. If ZZZ is computed from YYY (perhaps stochastically), then ZZZ carries at most as much information about XXX as YYY does. Information about XXX cannot increase under post-processing.

**Proof:** By the chain rule and symmetry of mutual information,

I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y∣Z).I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z).I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y∣Z).

Since X→Y→ZX \to Y \to ZX→Y→Z forms a Markov chain, I(X;Z∣Y)=0I(X; Z \mid Y) = 0I(X;Z∣Y)=0. And I(X;Y∣Z)≥0I(X; Y \mid Z) \geq 0I(X;Y∣Z)≥0. Therefore

I(X;Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y∣Z)≥I(X;Z).□I(X; Y) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z) \geq I(X; Z). \squareI(X;Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y∣Z)≥I(X;Z).□

The data-processing inequality is the formal statement of an extremely intuitive fact: nothing you do to your raw data can give you more information about the underlying state than the raw data itself contained. It bounds what every machine learning system can do. If a deep network's hidden representation TTT is a function of input XXX, then I(T;Y)≤I(X;Y)I(T; Y) \leq I(X; Y)I(T;Y)≤I(X;Y) — the network can extract at most as much information about labels YYY as the input XXX had to begin with. We will use this inequality in Chapter 13 when we treat the information bottleneck.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
### 2.6 Worked Example: Mutual Information in a Communication Channel

Consider a binary symmetric channel: input X∈{0,1}X \in \\{0, 1\\}X∈{0,1}, output Y∈{0,1}Y \in \\{0, 1\\}Y∈{0,1}, with probability of bit flip ϵ\epsilonϵ. So p(Y=0∣X=0)=p(Y=1∣X=1)=1−ϵp(Y = 0 \mid X = 0) = p(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) = 1 - \epsilonp(Y=0∣X=0)=p(Y=1∣X=1)=1−ϵ and p(Y=1∣X=0)=p(Y=0∣X=1)=ϵp(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) = p(Y = 0 \mid X = 1) = \epsilonp(Y=1∣X=0)=p(Y=0∣X=1)=ϵ.

Suppose the input is uniform: p(X=0)=p(X=1)=1/2p(X = 0) = p(X = 1) = 1/2p(X=0)=p(X=1)=1/2. Then by symmetry p(Y=0)=p(Y=1)=1/2p(Y = 0) = p(Y = 1) = 1/2p(Y=0)=p(Y=1)=1/2, and H(Y)=1H(Y) = 1H(Y)=1 bit.

Conditional entropy:

H(Y∣X)=∑xp(x)H(Y∣X=x)=Hb(ϵ).H(Y \mid X) = \sum_x p(x) H(Y \mid X = x) = H_b(\epsilon).H(Y∣X)=x∑​p(x)H(Y∣X=x)=Hb​(ϵ).

(Each conditional distribution puts probability ϵ\epsilonϵ on the wrong value and 1−ϵ1 - \epsilon1−ϵ on the right one.)

So the mutual information is

I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=1−Hb(ϵ).I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = 1 - H_b(\epsilon).I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=1−Hb​(ϵ).

Three sanity checks:

* When ϵ=0\epsilon = 0ϵ=0 (noiseless), Hb(0)=0H_b(0) = 0Hb​(0)=0, so I(X;Y)=1I(X; Y) = 1I(X;Y)=1 bit. The channel transmits one bit per use, perfectly.
* When ϵ=1/2\epsilon = 1/2ϵ=1/2 (maximum noise), Hb(1/2)=1H_b(1/2) = 1Hb​(1/2)=1, so I(X;Y)=0I(X; Y) = 0I(X;Y)=0. The output is independent of the input — a coin flip, and no information is transmitted.
* When ϵ=1\epsilon = 1ϵ=1 (deterministic flip), Hb(1)=0H_b(1) = 0Hb​(1)=0, so I(X;Y)=1I(X; Y) = 1I(X;Y)=1 bit again. A bit-flipping channel is just a relabeling; full information passes through, you just need to know to flip the output.

This computation is the foundation of Chapter 5, where we will define **channel capacity** as the maximum of I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) over all possible input distributions p(X)p(X)p(X). For the binary symmetric channel, the maximum happens at the uniform input, and the capacity is C=1−Hb(ϵ)C = 1 - H_b(\epsilon)C=1−Hb​(ϵ) bits per channel use.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
### 2.7 An AI Connection: Mutual Information in Self-Supervised Learning

A glance ahead. Modern self-supervised learning, in methods like SimCLR, MoCo, CPC, and CLIP, has made a striking move. Instead of training a network to predict a specific label, it trains the network to _maximize the mutual information_ between two views of the same data: two random crops of an image, an image and its caption, two consecutive frames of a video.

Concretely, given an encoder fff that produces a representation Z=f(X)Z = f(X)Z=f(X), and a paired view X′X'X′ with representation Z′=f(X′)Z' = f(X')Z′=f(X′), the InfoNCE loss is a lower bound on I(Z;Z′)I(Z; Z')I(Z;Z′). Training to minimize InfoNCE is training to push this lower bound up, that is, to make the representations Z,Z′Z, Z'Z,Z′ of paired views maximally informative about each other.

Why does this learn useful features? Roughly: features that capture invariances shared between views (the same object in different crops, the same scene in different frames) survive under maximization of mutual information. Features that vary independently between views are penalized. The approach has produced foundation models that rival or exceed supervised pretraining, with no human labels required.

We will treat all of this carefully in Chapter 14. For now, hold the connection lightly: the central object of self-supervised learning is mutual information, defined by exactly the formula we wrote in §2.4.

There is also a cautionary half to this story. Estimating mutual information from samples in high dimensions is statistically hard. The lower bounds used in InfoNCE are loose; the upper bounds are unstable. Many of the empirical wins of self-supervised learning have less to do with mutual information per se than with auxiliary effects of the loss (representation uniformity, alignment, and so on). Honest about limits: mutual information is a useful organizing principle, but it is not the whole story.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
### 2.8 Historical Note: From Shannon's 1948 Paper to the Modern Toolbox

The two-variable identities in this chapter — joint, conditional, and mutual information, the chain rule, the data-processing inequality — were nearly all in Shannon's 1948 paper. Shannon stated the chain rule for entropy and used mutual information implicitly throughout, although the term "mutual information" was popularized later. The data-processing inequality in its modern symmetric form is due to a series of refinements in the 1950s and 1960s by Kullback (whose KL divergence we treat in Chapter 8), Csiszár, and others.

The single most influential textbook to package these identities for a generation of students is Thomas M. Cover and Joy A. Thomas's _Elements of Information Theory_ (first edition 1991, second edition 2006). Cover's exposition popularized the "Venn diagram" picture of joint and conditional entropy that we sketched in §2.4 and made the chain rule a standard pedagogical tool. Cover spent his career at Stanford and was famously generous with his time for students; many practitioners of information theory in the 2000s learned the field from his lectures or his book.

The mutual information formulation also has earlier statistical roots. R. A. Fisher's information measure (1922), a different quantity that we will meet in Chapter 9, already encoded the idea that the slope of a log-likelihood carries information. The connection between Fisher information and Shannon mutual information was made rigorous by E. T. Jaynes (1957) and by the information-geometry program initiated by Shun-ichi Amari in the 1980s. Information theory and statistical inference were not separate disciplines; they were one field told in two languages.


### Common Misconception

Two confusions are very common at this stage.

* **Misconception** : "If I(X;Y)=0I(X; Y) = 0I(X;Y)=0, then XXX and YYY are uncorrelated, and conversely."

Mutual information being zero means XXX and YYY are _independent_ , which is strictly stronger than uncorrelated. Independence implies zero correlation, but uncorrelated random variables can have substantial mutual information. The standard counterexample: let XXX be uniform on {−1,0,1}\\{-1, 0, 1\\}{−1,0,1} and Y=X2Y = X^2Y=X2. Then E[XY]=E[X3]=0\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X^3] = 0E[XY]=E[X3]=0, so they are uncorrelated, but YYY is a deterministic function of XXX, so H(Y∣X)=0H(Y \mid X) = 0H(Y∣X)=0 and I(X;Y)=H(Y)>0I(X; Y) = H(Y) > 0I(X;Y)=H(Y)>0.

* **Misconception** : "Mutual information is symmetric, so it does not matter which variable we call the cause."

Mutual information is symmetric, but causal direction is not. I(X;Y)=I(Y;X)I(X; Y) = I(Y; X)I(X;Y)=I(Y;X) tells you nothing about whether XXX causes YYY or vice versa. The discipline of causal inference (Pearl, Spirtes, and others) lives in a different world from information theory; mutual information is symmetric on principle, and using it to detect causal direction requires extra assumptions.

Keep these straight. They are the two most common interview-style traps in the field.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

This chapter built out the two-variable theory: joint entropy H(X,Y)H(X, Y)H(X,Y), conditional entropy H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X), and mutual information I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y). We proved the chain rule, conditioning reduces entropy on average, and the data-processing inequality. We saw how each quantity acts in concrete settings: correlated coins, medical diagnosis, the binary symmetric channel.

Mutual information is the quantity we will return to most. It is the supremum of the channel coding theorem (Chapter 5), the loss in source coding (Chapter 4), the engine of self-supervised learning (Chapter 14), and the constraint at the heart of the information bottleneck (Chapter 13). Master the chain rule, the data-processing inequality, and the Venn-diagram picture, and you have the structural backbone of the rest of this book.

Looking back to Chapter 1: we defined entropy for a single variable; now we have its two-variable extensions and the inequalities that link them. Looking forward to Chapter 3: the next chapter will give entropy its operational meaning by proving the Asymptotic Equipartition Property — the statement that long sequences from a stochastic source are concentrated on a "typical set" of about 2nH(X)2^{nH(X)}2nH(X) sequences. That fact, more than any other, is the engine of every subsequent chapter.


### 2.X Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Two random variables XXX and YYY take values in {0,1}\\{0, 1\\}{0,1} with the following joint distribution: p(0,0)=0.4p(0, 0) = 0.4p(0,0)=0.4, p(0,1)=0.1p(0, 1) = 0.1p(0,1)=0.1, p(1,0)=0.1p(1, 0) = 0.1p(1,0)=0.1, p(1,1)=0.4p(1, 1) = 0.4p(1,1)=0.4. Compute H(X)H(X)H(X), H(Y)H(Y)H(Y), H(X,Y)H(X, Y)H(X,Y), H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X), and I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y).

Hint

First compute the marginals p(X)p(X)p(X) and p(Y)p(Y)p(Y), then use the formulas.

**Answer:** Marginals: p(X=0)=0.5p(X = 0) = 0.5p(X=0)=0.5, p(X=1)=0.5p(X = 1) = 0.5p(X=1)=0.5; same for YYY. So H(X)=H(Y)=1H(X) = H(Y) = 1H(X)=H(Y)=1 bit.

Joint: H(X,Y)=−2(0.4log⁡0.4)−2(0.1log⁡0.1)≈2(0.529)+2(0.332)=1.058+0.664=1.722H(X, Y) = -2(0.4 \log 0.4) - 2(0.1 \log 0.1) \approx 2(0.529) + 2(0.332) = 1.058 + 0.664 = 1.722H(X,Y)=−2(0.4log0.4)−2(0.1log0.1)≈2(0.529)+2(0.332)=1.058+0.664=1.722 bits.

Conditional: H(Y∣X)=H(X,Y)−H(X)=1.722−1=0.722H(Y \mid X) = H(X, Y) - H(X) = 1.722 - 1 = 0.722H(Y∣X)=H(X,Y)−H(X)=1.722−1=0.722 bits.

Mutual information: I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=1−0.722=0.278I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = 1 - 0.722 = 0.278I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=1−0.722=0.278 bits.

The variables have positive mutual information, indicating dependence: indeed, p(X=Y)=0.8>0.5p(X = Y) = 0.8 > 0.5p(X=Y)=0.8>0.5, the value under independence.

**Q2.** Show that I(X;X)=H(X)I(X; X) = H(X)I(X;X)=H(X) directly from the definition.

Hint

Use I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X∣Y)I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X∣Y) with Y=XY = XY=X.

**Answer:** H(X∣X)=0H(X \mid X) = 0H(X∣X)=0 (knowing XXX leaves no uncertainty about XXX). So I(X;X)=H(X)−H(X∣X)=H(X)−0=H(X)I(X; X) = H(X) - H(X \mid X) = H(X) - 0 = H(X)I(X;X)=H(X)−H(X∣X)=H(X)−0=H(X). A random variable carries exactly its own entropy of information about itself, no more, no less.

**Q3.** Verify the chain rule H(X,Y,Z)=H(X)+H(Y∣X)+H(Z∣X,Y)H(X, Y, Z) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X) + H(Z \mid X, Y)H(X,Y,Z)=H(X)+H(Y∣X)+H(Z∣X,Y) starting from the definition H(X,Y,Z)=−∑p(x,y,z)log⁡p(x,y,z)H(X, Y, Z) = -\sum p(x, y, z) \log p(x, y, z)H(X,Y,Z)=−∑p(x,y,z)logp(x,y,z).

Hint

Decompose p(x,y,z)=p(x)p(y∣x)p(z∣x,y)p(x, y, z) = p(x) p(y \mid x) p(z \mid x, y)p(x,y,z)=p(x)p(y∣x)p(z∣x,y) and apply the logarithm.

**Answer:** Using the factorization,

log⁡p(x,y,z)=log⁡p(x)+log⁡p(y∣x)+log⁡p(z∣x,y).\log p(x, y, z) = \log p(x) + \log p(y \mid x) + \log p(z \mid x, y).logp(x,y,z)=logp(x)+logp(y∣x)+logp(z∣x,y).

So

H(X,Y,Z)=−∑p(x,y,z)log⁡p(x)−∑p(x,y,z)log⁡p(y∣x)−∑p(x,y,z)log⁡p(z∣x,y).H(X, Y, Z) = -\sum p(x, y, z) \log p(x) - \sum p(x, y, z) \log p(y \mid x) - \sum p(x, y, z) \log p(z \mid x, y).H(X,Y,Z)=−∑p(x,y,z)logp(x)−∑p(x,y,z)logp(y∣x)−∑p(x,y,z)logp(z∣x,y).

Each sum simplifies: the first equals H(X)H(X)H(X) (sum out y,zy, zy,z to get p(x)p(x)p(x)); the second equals H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X); the third equals H(Z∣X,Y)H(Z \mid X, Y)H(Z∣X,Y). □\square□

**Q4.** Explain the difference between H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X) (averaged) and H(Y∣X=x)H(Y \mid X = x)H(Y∣X=x) (for a particular xxx). Give an example where one of the latter exceeds H(Y)H(Y)H(Y), even though the former cannot.

Hint

Conditioning on a particular value can increase uncertainty if that value points toward an ambiguous corner of the joint distribution.
