blocks.src:
**Answer:** H(Y∣X=x)H(Y \mid X = x)H(Y∣X=x) is the entropy of the conditional distribution given a particular outcome xxx; it can be smaller or larger than H(Y)H(Y)H(Y). H(Y∣X)H(Y \mid X)H(Y∣X) is the average of H(Y∣X=x)H(Y \mid X = x)H(Y∣X=x) weighted by p(x)p(x)p(x), and it satisfies H(Y∣X)≤H(Y)H(Y \mid X) \leq H(Y)H(Y∣X)≤H(Y) always.

A concrete example is the medical-diagnosis case from §2.3: a positive test gives H(Y∣X=+)≈1.0H(Y \mid X = +) \approx 1.0H(Y∣X=+)≈1.0 bit, which exceeds the marginal H(Y)≈0.469H(Y) \approx 0.469H(Y)≈0.469 bits, because conditioning on a positive result leaves the patient near 50/50 between two diseases. But the _average_ H(Y∣X)≈0.227H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.227H(Y∣X)≈0.227 is below H(Y)H(Y)H(Y), as the expected-value inequality requires. The negative-test branch dominates the average and pulls it down.

The takeaway: H(Y∣X)≤H(Y)H(Y \mid X) \leq H(Y)H(Y∣X)≤H(Y) is an _expected_ inequality. For each particular xxx, H(Y∣X=x)H(Y \mid X = x)H(Y∣X=x) can be larger, smaller, or equal to H(Y)H(Y)H(Y); only the expectation is constrained.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Two communications experts each independently estimate the entropy of an English letter from the same corpus. Expert A uses unigram statistics and gets H(Xt)=4.07H(X_t) = 4.07H(Xt​)=4.07 bits per letter. Expert B uses bigram statistics and computes the joint entropy of consecutive letters, getting H(Xt,Xt−1)=7.18H(X_t, X_{t-1}) = 7.18H(Xt​,Xt−1​)=7.18 bits per pair. Use the chain rule to derive Expert B's estimate of the per-letter entropy _given_ the previous letter, and explain why it is lower than Expert A's.

Hint

By the chain rule, H(Xt∣Xt−1)=H(Xt,Xt−1)−H(Xt−1)H(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) = H(X_t, X_{t-1}) - H(X_{t-1})H(Xt​∣Xt−1​)=H(Xt​,Xt−1​)−H(Xt−1​). Treat the source as stationary so that H(Xt−1)=H(Xt)=4.07H(X_{t-1}) = H(X_t) = 4.07H(Xt−1​)=H(Xt​)=4.07 bits.

**Answer:** By the chain rule and stationarity:

H(Xt∣Xt−1)=H(Xt,Xt−1)−H(Xt−1)=7.18−4.07=3.11 bits per letter.H(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) = H(X_t, X_{t-1}) - H(X_{t-1}) = 7.18 - 4.07 = 3.11 \text{ bits per letter}.H(Xt​∣Xt−1​)=H(Xt​,Xt−1​)−H(Xt−1​)=7.18−4.07=3.11 bits per letter.

Expert B's per-letter conditional entropy is lower than Expert A's marginal entropy because letters in English are not independent: after qqq, the next letter is almost always uuu; after ttt, often hhh. The mutual information per letter pair is

I(Xt;Xt−1)=H(Xt)−H(Xt∣Xt−1)=4.07−3.11=0.96 bits per pair.I(X_t; X_{t-1}) = H(X_t) - H(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) = 4.07 - 3.11 = 0.96 \text{ bits per pair}.I(Xt​;Xt−1​)=H(Xt​)−H(Xt​∣Xt−1​)=4.07−3.11=0.96 bits per pair.

Each letter shares about a bit of information with its predecessor. As we go to trigrams, four-grams, and longer contexts, the per-letter conditional entropy continues to drop, all the way down to roughly 1.01.01.0 bit per letter for very long contexts. We will return to this in Chapter 15 when we discuss language model perplexity.

This problem also illustrates Chapter 1's English-text computation in a more rigorous way: it is not that the unigram entropy was wrong; it is that the unigram entropy is the _upper bound_ on per-letter entropy, and conditioning on context drives it down toward the true entropy of English.

**Q2.** A stationary Markov chain on three states {a,b,c}\\{a, b, c\\}{a,b,c} has transition matrix

P=(0.50.5000.50.50.500.5),P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 & 0 \\\ 0 & 0.5 & 0.5 \\\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix},P=​0.500.5​0.50.50​00.50.5​​,

with stationary distribution π=(1/3,1/3,1/3)\pi = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)π=(1/3,1/3,1/3). What is the entropy rate H(Xt∣Xt−1)H(X_t \mid X_{t-1})H(Xt​∣Xt−1​)?

Hint

For a Markov chain, H(Xt∣Xt−1)=∑xπ(x)H(row x of P)H(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) = \sum_x \pi(x) H(\text{row } x \text{ of } P)H(Xt​∣Xt−1​)=∑x​π(x)H(row x of P).

**Answer:** Each row of PPP has entropy Hb(0.5)=1H_b(0.5) = 1Hb​(0.5)=1 bit (each row is "0.5, 0.5, 0", whose entropy is −0.5log⁡0.5−0.5log⁡0.5=1-0.5 \log 0.5 - 0.5 \log 0.5 = 1−0.5log0.5−0.5log0.5=1 bit; the zero entry contributes nothing). Averaging over the stationary distribution,

H(Xt∣Xt−1)=∑xπ(x)H(P(⋅∣x))=13⋅1+13⋅1+13⋅1=1 bit.H(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) = \sum_x \pi(x) H(P(\cdot \mid x)) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 1 + \frac{1}{3} \cdot 1 + \frac{1}{3} \cdot 1 = 1 \text{ bit}.H(Xt​∣Xt−1​)=x∑​π(x)H(P(⋅∣x))=31​⋅1+31​⋅1+31​⋅1=1 bit.

But H(Xt)=H(π)=log⁡3≈1.585H(X_t) = H(\pi) = \log 3 \approx 1.585H(Xt​)=H(π)=log3≈1.585 bits. So I(Xt;Xt−1)=0.585I(X_t; X_{t-1}) = 0.585I(Xt​;Xt−1​)=0.585 bits per pair.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
This is the **entropy rate** of the Markov chain, the long-run average per-symbol entropy. It plays the same role for non-i.i.d. sources that H(X)H(X)H(X) plays for i.i.d. sources, and it is the fundamental compression limit for the Markov source. We will pick up the entropy rate again in Chapter 4.

**Q3.** Verify the data-processing inequality on a simple example: let XXX be a fair coin flip, YYY be XXX corrupted by independent noise (flipped with probability ϵ=0.1\epsilon = 0.1ϵ=0.1), and Z=YZ = YZ=Y (no further processing). Compute I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) and I(X;Z)I(X; Z)I(X;Z).

Hint

Z=YZ = YZ=Y means I(X;Z)=I(X;Y)I(X; Z) = I(X; Y)I(X;Z)=I(X;Y), so the inequality holds with equality.

**Answer:** With Z=YZ = YZ=Y, I(X;Z)=I(X;Y)I(X; Z) = I(X; Y)I(X;Z)=I(X;Y) trivially.

I(X;Y)=1−Hb(0.1)≈1−0.469=0.531I(X; Y) = 1 - H_b(0.1) \approx 1 - 0.469 = 0.531I(X;Y)=1−Hb​(0.1)≈1−0.469=0.531 bits.

The data-processing inequality gives I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y)I(X; Z) \leq I(X; Y)I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y), and here we have equality, as expected. To see the inequality bite, replace Z=YZ = YZ=Y with ZZZ = a further noisy version of YYY (independent flip with probability ϵ′=0.1\epsilon' = 0.1ϵ′=0.1). Then I(X;Z)=1−Hb(0.19)I(X; Z) = 1 - H_b(0.19)I(X;Z)=1−Hb​(0.19), where 0.19=0.1⋅0.9+0.9⋅0.10.19 = 0.1 \cdot 0.9 + 0.9 \cdot 0.10.19=0.1⋅0.9+0.9⋅0.1 is the cumulative flip probability. Numerically, Hb(0.19)≈0.701H_b(0.19) \approx 0.701Hb​(0.19)≈0.701, so I(X;Z)≈0.299I(X; Z) \approx 0.299I(X;Z)≈0.299 bits — strictly less than I(X;Y)≈0.531I(X; Y) \approx 0.531I(X;Y)≈0.531, as the inequality requires.

**Q4.** Mutual information is non-negative for any pair of variables. The "interaction information" of three variables, I(X;Y;Z)=I(X;Y)−I(X;Y∣Z)I(X; Y; Z) = I(X; Y) - I(X; Y \mid Z)I(X;Y;Z)=I(X;Y)−I(X;Y∣Z), can be _negative_. Explain this in plain language and give an example.

Hint

Negative interaction information means that conditioning on ZZZ increases the dependence between XXX and YYY.

**Answer:** Negative interaction information arises when ZZZ is a "common effect" of XXX and YYY: conditioning on ZZZ creates apparent dependence between otherwise independent variables.

Classic example: let XXX and YYY be independent fair coins, and Z=X⊕YZ = X \oplus YZ=X⊕Y (XOR). Marginally, I(X;Y)=0I(X; Y) = 0I(X;Y)=0. But conditioned on ZZZ, XXX and YYY are perfectly correlated: knowing XXX and ZZZ determines YYY. So I(X;Y∣Z)=1>0I(X; Y \mid Z) = 1 > 0I(X;Y∣Z)=1>0, and I(X;Y;Z)=0−1=−1I(X; Y; Z) = 0 - 1 = -1I(X;Y;Z)=0−1=−1 bit.

This is the kind of phenomenon that breaks the naïve Venn-diagram intuition for three variables. The "overlap" of three sets, in the information-theoretic Venn diagram, is interaction information, and unlike Shannon entropy and mutual information, it can go negative. The XOR example is the cleanest illustration.

In causal-inference terms, this is "Berkson's paradox": conditioning on a common effect creates dependence between independent causes. A famous instance: in a hospital admissions sample, severity of disease A and severity of disease B may appear negatively correlated, even if they are independent in the population, because both raise the probability of admission. Information theory and causal inference give the same warning in different vocabularies.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Mutual information is a measure of dependence. So is correlation. Compare the two: when does each succeed and fail at detecting dependence? When would you prefer one over the other?

**Discussion:** Correlation measures _linear_ dependence: the angle between two variables in a normalized inner-product space. Mutual information measures _all_ dependence: any deviation of the joint from the product of marginals. Correlation is zero for the deterministic relation Y=X2Y = X^2Y=X2 when XXX is symmetric around zero; mutual information is positive (in fact, equals H(Y)H(Y)H(Y), the most it can be).

So mutual information is strictly more general. Why is correlation still used so much? Three reasons. First, correlation is computable in closed form from a small number of moments, only the means and covariance are needed. Mutual information requires estimating the full joint distribution, which in high dimensions is intractable. Second, for jointly Gaussian variables, correlation and mutual information are in one-to-one correspondence: I(X;Y)=−12log⁡(1−ρ2)I(X; Y) = -\frac{1}{2} \log(1 - \rho^2)I(X;Y)=−21​log(1−ρ2), so they carry the same information. Third, correlation has direct interpretation in linear regression and standard statistics; mutual information requires a bit of calibration before users develop intuition for the values.

The current methodological consensus is roughly: use correlation as a default tool when you suspect linear dependence and have lots of data; use mutual information when you want to be certain you are detecting all dependence, and have either small enough dimension or a specialized estimator (Chapter 14 covers MINE for the high-dimensional case). For nonlinear systems and modern machine learning, mutual information is typically the right primitive.

**Q2.** The data-processing inequality says that no post-processing of YYY can extract more information about XXX than YYY already had. But in machine learning, we often see that a _trained_ representation seems to "extract" useful structure that was buried in raw pixels. Reconcile.

**Discussion:** This is a beautiful tension and worth thinking about carefully. The data-processing inequality is rock-solid: no function of YYY carries more information about XXX than YYY does. So how can a learned representation T=f(Y)T = f(Y)T=f(Y) be "better" than YYY itself for a downstream task?

The answer is that "better for a task" and "more information about XXX" are different things. The learned representation TTT carries _less_ information than YYY, but the information it does carry is in a more _useful form_ — it has dropped irrelevant variation (lighting, camera angle, background clutter) and preserved task-relevant variation (object identity, semantic class). In information-theoretic language: I(T;Y)<I(Y;Y)=H(Y)I(T; Y) < I(Y; Y) = H(Y)I(T;Y)<I(Y;Y)=H(Y), but I(T;Ylabel)I(T; Y_{\text{label}})I(T;Ylabel​) might be close to I(Y;Ylabel)I(Y; Y_{\text{label}})I(Y;Ylabel​) — the representation has compressed away noise while preserving signal.

This is exactly the **information bottleneck** principle, which we treat in Chapter 13. The trade-off, minimize I(T;Y)I(T; Y)I(T;Y) to compress and maximize I(T;Ylabel)I(T; Y_{\text{label}})I(T;Ylabel​) to predict, is a Lagrangian whose optima are the "ideal representations" for a task.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
So the data-processing inequality is not violated; it is leveraged. Compressing away irrelevant information is exactly what makes a representation useful, even though it strictly reduces total information about the input.

**Q3.** Independence and zero mutual information are the same. Conditional independence and zero conditional mutual information are also the same. But "conditional independence given ZZZ" is a much stronger statement than "independence and conditional on ZZZ one of XXX or YYY is determined." Comment on the role of conditioning in the information-theoretic toolkit.

**Discussion:** Conditioning is the engine of inference. When we move from raw uncertainty (H(X)H(X)H(X)) to refined uncertainty (H(X∣Y)H(X \mid Y)H(X∣Y)), we are using YYY as evidence. When we condition on a third variable ZZZ, we are asking: holding ZZZ fixed, how dependent are XXX and YYY? The conditional mutual information I(X;Y∣Z)I(X; Y \mid Z)I(X;Y∣Z) answers this exactly.

Conditional independence is the structural backbone of probabilistic graphical models, of d-separation in Bayesian networks, of the Markov property of stochastic processes. In every one of these settings, I(X;Y∣Z)=0I(X; Y \mid Z) = 0I(X;Y∣Z)=0 is the precise quantitative version of "ZZZ screens off YYY from telling us anything more about XXX." Without this notion, every analysis would have to track the entire joint distribution; with it, we can decompose hopelessly large joint distributions into manageable conditional pieces.

In information theory specifically, conditional mutual information appears as the mortar between bricks. The chain rule for mutual information,

I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y),I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y),I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z∣Y),

is the mutual-information cousin of the entropy chain rule. The data-processing inequality uses it. Multi-terminal information theory (Chapter 12) uses it pervasively. The information bottleneck (Chapter 13) is essentially a constrained optimization over conditional mutual informations.

The lesson: master conditioning. Information theory rewards readers who internalize that every marginal quantity has a conditional twin and that the conditional twin is usually the more powerful statement.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Joint, Conditional, and Mutual Information
blocks.src:
### Connections to Subsequent Chapters

This chapter set up the central object of the rest of the book: mutual information, and its conditional variant. Almost every theorem from here on is a statement about mutual information.

* **Chapter 3** uses joint typicality (a corollary of the AEP for joint distributions) to count the size of typical (X,Y)(X, Y)(X,Y) pairs in terms of H(X,Y)H(X, Y)H(X,Y), H(X)H(X)H(X), and H(Y)H(Y)H(Y), and from that derives the mutual information I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) as a counting quantity.
* **Chapter 5** defines channel capacity C=max⁡p(X)I(X;Y)C = \max_{p(X)} I(X; Y)C=maxp(X)​I(X;Y) — the maximum mutual information over input distributions.
* **Chapter 6** proves that this capacity is achievable (Shannon's coding theorem), using exactly the joint typicality of Chapter 3.
* **Chapter 8** introduces KL divergence, of which I(X;Y)=D(p(X,Y)∥p(X)p(Y))I(X; Y) = D(p(X, Y) \| p(X) p(Y))I(X;Y)=D(p(X,Y)∥p(X)p(Y)) is a special case.
* **Chapter 13** uses conditional mutual information as the key quantity in the information bottleneck.
* **Chapters 14, 15** apply mutual information ideas in modern self-supervised learning and language modeling.

A reader who has internalized the chain rule, the data-processing inequality, and the Venn-diagram picture has the structural backbone of the rest of this book.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
Imagine flipping a fair coin one thousand times. There are exactly 210002^{1000}21000 possible sequences of heads and tails, a number with 301 decimal digits, far larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe. By any naïve accounting, you might think the outcome is one of an unimaginable variety. And it is, in the sense that any specific sequence of outcomes is essentially impossible to predict.

But here is the surprise. Of those 210002^{1000}21000 sequences, the overwhelming majority share one property: they have approximately five hundred heads and five hundred tails, give or take a few standard deviations. Sequences with seventy heads, or with all heads, or with the heads and tails alternating in a fixed period, are theoretically possible but practically never observed. The space of "typical" sequences is much smaller than the full space, yet containing essentially all the probability.

This is the **Asymptotic Equipartition Property** (AEP), and it is one of the most beautiful results in probability. It is the bridge between the abstract definition of entropy and the operational meaning of compression: the entropy H(X)H(X)H(X) is precisely the asymptotic per-symbol cost of describing a long sequence drawn from XXX, because long sequences are concentrated on 2nH(X)2^{nH(X)}2nH(X) typical ones, all of which are roughly equiprobable.

Of all the chapters in this book, Chapter 3 is the most "magic." From a single statement of the law of large numbers applied to log-probabilities, an entire operational theory of compression and channel coding falls out. We owe this perspective to Shannon (1948); the modern textbook proof is due to McMillan and Breiman.


### 3.1 The Statement of the AEP

Let X1,X2,…X_1, X_2, \ldotsX1​,X2​,… be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables drawn from a distribution p(x)p(x)p(x) on a finite alphabet X\mathcal{X}X. The probability of any particular sequence (x1,x2,…,xn)(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)(x1​,x2​,…,xn​) is

p(x1,x2,…,xn)=∏i=1np(xi).p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i).p(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)=i=1∏n​p(xi​).

Take the logarithm:

log⁡p(x1,…,xn)=∑i=1nlog⁡p(xi).\log p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(x_i).logp(x1​,…,xn​)=i=1∑n​logp(xi​).

The right-hand side is a sum of nnn i.i.d. random variables (each is log⁡p(Xi)\log p(X_i)logp(Xi​) for a random sample XiX_iXi​). By the weak law of large numbers, this sum converges in probability to n⋅E[log⁡p(X)]=−nH(X)n \cdot \mathbb{E}[\log p(X)] = -n H(X)n⋅E[logp(X)]=−nH(X). Dividing by nnn:

−1nlog⁡p(X1,…,Xn)→H(X)in probability.-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \to H(X) \quad \text{in probability}.−n1​logp(X1​,…,Xn​)→H(X)in probability.

This is the AEP in its sharpest form. Stated as a theorem:

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
#### Theorem (Asymptotic Equipartition Property)

If X1,X2,…X_1, X_2, \ldotsX1​,X2​,… are i.i.d. with distribution p(x)p(x)p(x), then for any ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0,

Pr⁡(∣−1nlog⁡p(X1,…,Xn)−H(X)∣>ϵ)→0as n→∞.\Pr\left(\left|-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - H(X)\right| > \epsilon\right) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.Pr(​−n1​logp(X1​,…,Xn​)−H(X)​>ϵ)→0as n→∞.

Equivalently, with high probability for large nnn,

2−n(H(X)+ϵ)≤p(X1,…,Xn)≤2−n(H(X)−ϵ).2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon)} \leq p(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \leq 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)}.2−n(H(X)+ϵ)≤p(X1​,…,Xn​)≤2−n(H(X)−ϵ).

In plain language, this means: a long i.i.d. sequence has probability approximately 2−nH(X)2^{-n H(X)}2−nH(X). All "typical" sequences (those satisfying the AEP bound) are roughly equiprobable.


### 3.2 Typical Sets

We can package the AEP into a definition that will be the workhorse of all subsequent coding arguments.


#### Definition: The Typical Set

For ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0 and n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N, the **typical set** Aϵ(n)A_\epsilon^{(n)}Aϵ(n)​ with respect to the distribution p(x)p(x)p(x) is

Aϵ(n)={(x1,…,xn)∈Xn:∣−1nlog⁡p(x1,…,xn)−H(X)∣≤ϵ}.A_\epsilon^{(n)} = \left\\{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathcal{X}^n : \left|-\frac{1}{n} \log p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) - H(X)\right| \leq \epsilon\right\\}.Aϵ(n)​={(x1​,…,xn​)∈Xn:​−n1​logp(x1​,…,xn​)−H(X)​≤ϵ}.

In plain language, this means: the typical set consists of those sequences whose empirical log-probability is close to the entropy.

The AEP tells us that for any ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0, the probability of seeing a typical sequence approaches one as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞. The typical set captures essentially all the probability.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
#### Properties of the Typical Set

The typical set has three key properties, all of which we will use throughout the book.

**Property 1** : For any ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0, Pr⁡(Aϵ(n))>1−ϵ\Pr(A_\epsilon^{(n)}) > 1 - \epsilonPr(Aϵ(n)​)>1−ϵ for sufficiently large nnn.

This is just the AEP rephrased.

**Property 2** : ∣Aϵ(n)∣≤2n(H(X)+ϵ)|A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \leq 2^{n(H(X) + \epsilon)}∣Aϵ(n)​∣≤2n(H(X)+ϵ).

The cardinality of the typical set is at most about 2nH(X)2^{nH(X)}2nH(X).

**Proof** : For any (x1,…,xn)∈Aϵ(n)(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in A_\epsilon^{(n)}(x1​,…,xn​)∈Aϵ(n)​, we have p(x1,…,xn)≥2−n(H(X)+ϵ)p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \geq 2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon)}p(x1​,…,xn​)≥2−n(H(X)+ϵ). Therefore

1≥∑(x1,…,xn)∈Aϵ(n)p(x1,…,xn)≥∣Aϵ(n)∣⋅2−n(H(X)+ϵ),1 \geq \sum_{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in A_\epsilon^{(n)}} p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \geq |A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \cdot 2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon)},1≥(x1​,…,xn​)∈Aϵ(n)​∑​p(x1​,…,xn​)≥∣Aϵ(n)​∣⋅2−n(H(X)+ϵ),

which gives ∣Aϵ(n)∣≤2n(H(X)+ϵ)|A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \leq 2^{n(H(X) + \epsilon)}∣Aϵ(n)​∣≤2n(H(X)+ϵ). □\square□

**Property 3** : For sufficiently large nnn, ∣Aϵ(n)∣≥(1−ϵ)2n(H(X)−ϵ)|A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \geq (1 - \epsilon) 2^{n(H(X) - \epsilon)}∣Aϵ(n)​∣≥(1−ϵ)2n(H(X)−ϵ).

The cardinality is also at least about 2nH(X)2^{nH(X)}2nH(X).

**Proof** : For sufficiently large nnn, Pr⁡(Aϵ(n))>1−ϵ\Pr(A_\epsilon^{(n)}) > 1 - \epsilonPr(Aϵ(n)​)>1−ϵ. Each typical sequence has probability ≤2−n(H(X)−ϵ)\leq 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)}≤2−n(H(X)−ϵ). So

1−ϵ<Pr⁡(Aϵ(n))=∑(x1,…,xn)∈Aϵ(n)p(x1,…,xn)≤∣Aϵ(n)∣⋅2−n(H(X)−ϵ),1 - \epsilon < \Pr(A_\epsilon^{(n)}) = \sum_{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in A_\epsilon^{(n)}} p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \leq |A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \cdot 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)},1−ϵ<Pr(Aϵ(n)​)=(x1​,…,xn​)∈Aϵ(n)​∑​p(x1​,…,xn​)≤∣Aϵ(n)​∣⋅2−n(H(X)−ϵ),

giving ∣Aϵ(n)∣≥(1−ϵ)2n(H(X)−ϵ)|A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \geq (1 - \epsilon) 2^{n(H(X) - \epsilon)}∣Aϵ(n)​∣≥(1−ϵ)2n(H(X)−ϵ). □\square□

Combining Properties 2 and 3: for large nnn, the typical set has cardinality

∣Aϵ(n)∣≈2nH(X),|A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \approx 2^{n H(X)},∣Aϵ(n)​∣≈2nH(X),

up to subexponential factors.


#### Why this matters: a counting picture

The total number of possible sequences of length nnn over an alphabet of size ∣X∣|\mathcal{X}|∣X∣ is ∣X∣n=2nlog⁡∣X∣|\mathcal{X}|^n = 2^{n \log |\mathcal{X}|}∣X∣n=2nlog∣X∣. The typical set has size only 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X). When the source is non-uniform, when H(X)<log⁡∣X∣H(X) < \log |\mathcal{X}|H(X)<log∣X∣, the typical set is an _exponentially small fraction_ of the total space.

For example, with a binary source where p(0)=0.9p(0) = 0.9p(0)=0.9 and p(1)=0.1p(1) = 0.1p(1)=0.1, the entropy is H(X)=Hb(0.1)≈0.469H(X) = H_b(0.1) \approx 0.469H(X)=Hb​(0.1)≈0.469 bits. For n=1000n = 1000n=1000, the total number of sequences is 210002^{1000}21000. The typical set has size approximately 24692^{469}2469. The ratio is 2−5312^{-531}2−531, an absurdly tiny fraction of the total. And yet it contains essentially all the probability.

This is the AEP's deepest content. **The probability mass of long i.i.d. sequences is concentrated on an exponentially small set of "typical" sequences, all of which are roughly equiprobable.**

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
### 3.3 Worked Example: Counting Typical Sequences

Let p(0)=0.8p(0) = 0.8p(0)=0.8, p(1)=0.2p(1) = 0.2p(1)=0.2. The entropy is Hb(0.2)=−0.2log⁡0.2−0.8log⁡0.8≈0.722H_b(0.2) = -0.2 \log 0.2 - 0.8 \log 0.8 \approx 0.722Hb​(0.2)=−0.2log0.2−0.8log0.8≈0.722 bits.

For n=100n = 100n=100, what does the typical set look like?

A typical sequence has roughly np(0)=80np(0) = 80np(0)=80 zeros and np(1)=20np(1) = 20np(1)=20 ones (by the law of large numbers). The number of such sequences is (10020)≈5.36×1020\binom{100}{20} \approx 5.36 \times 10^{20}(20100​)≈5.36×1020.

The probability of each such sequence is 0.880⋅0.220≈1.86×10−220.8^{80} \cdot 0.2^{20} \approx 1.86 \times 10^{-22}0.880⋅0.220≈1.86×10−22, so the total probability is about (10020)⋅0.880⋅0.220≈0.0993\binom{100}{20} \cdot 0.8^{80} \cdot 0.2^{20} \approx 0.0993(20100​)⋅0.880⋅0.220≈0.0993, which is about a tenth.

The dominant typical set actually consists of sequences with a _range_ of compositions (say, 70 to 90 zeros), and the total probability over this range is close to one for large enough nnn. The number of such sequences is approximately 2nH(X)=272.2≈5.4×10212^{n H(X)} = 2^{72.2} \approx 5.4 \times 10^{21}2nH(X)=272.2≈5.4×1021, comparable to our binomial coefficient.

The total number of length-100 binary sequences is 2100≈1.27×10302^{100} \approx 1.27 \times 10^{30}2100≈1.27×1030. The typical set is roughly 10−910^{-9}10−9 of the total. Yet it carries essentially all the probability.

The picture in one diagram:
    
    
       sequence space  (size 2^n  ≈ 10^30 for n = 100)
       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │                                                      │
       │                                                      │
       │      ┌───── typical set ──────┐                      │
       │      │  size ≈ 2^{nH}  ≈ 10^21│                      │
       │      │  probability mass ≈ 1  │                      │
       │      │  each member: prob     │                      │
       │      │    ≈ 2^{-nH} ≈ 10^-22  │                      │
       │      └────────────────────────┘                      │
       │                                                      │
       │   atypical: 10^30 sequences but total prob → 0       │
       │                                                      │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    

The two facts to internalize: the typical set is an _exponentially small island_ in the ambient space (its size relative to 2n2^n2n shrinks as 2−n(log⁡∣X∣−H)2^{-n(\log|\mathcal{X}| - H)}2−n(log∣X∣−H)), yet it carries _essentially all_ the probability. Compression works precisely because we can throw away addresses for everything outside the island.


### 3.4 The High-Probability Set and the Smallest Set Argument

Property 1 says the typical set captures almost all the probability. But is the typical set the _smallest_ set that captures almost all the probability? Almost.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
#### Theorem (Smallest set of high probability)

Let Bn⊂XnB_n \subset \mathcal{X}^nBn​⊂Xn be any set with Pr⁡(Bn)≥1−δ\Pr(B_n) \geq 1 - \deltaPr(Bn​)≥1−δ for some fixed δ<1\delta < 1δ<1. Then for sufficiently large nnn,

∣Bn∣≥2n(H(X)−ϵ)|B_n| \geq 2^{n(H(X) - \epsilon)}∣Bn​∣≥2n(H(X)−ϵ)

for any ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0.

In plain language, this means: any set that captures a constant fraction of the probability must have size at least 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X). The typical set is essentially optimal.

**Proof sketch** : Consider Bn∩Aϵ(n)B_n \cap A_\epsilon^{(n)}Bn​∩Aϵ(n)​. By the AEP, Pr⁡(Aϵ(n))≥1−ϵ\Pr(A_\epsilon^{(n)}) \geq 1 - \epsilonPr(Aϵ(n)​)≥1−ϵ, so Pr⁡(Bn∩Aϵ(n))≥1−δ−ϵ\Pr(B_n \cap A_\epsilon^{(n)}) \geq 1 - \delta - \epsilonPr(Bn​∩Aϵ(n)​)≥1−δ−ϵ. Each sequence in Bn∩Aϵ(n)B_n \cap A_\epsilon^{(n)}Bn​∩Aϵ(n)​ has probability at most 2−n(H(X)−ϵ)2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)}2−n(H(X)−ϵ) (by typicality). So

1−δ−ϵ≤Pr⁡(Bn∩Aϵ(n))≤∣Bn∩Aϵ(n)∣⋅2−n(H(X)−ϵ)≤∣Bn∣⋅2−n(H(X)−ϵ),1 - \delta - \epsilon \leq \Pr(B_n \cap A_\epsilon^{(n)}) \leq |B_n \cap A_\epsilon^{(n)}| \cdot 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)} \leq |B_n| \cdot 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)},1−δ−ϵ≤Pr(Bn​∩Aϵ(n)​)≤∣Bn​∩Aϵ(n)​∣⋅2−n(H(X)−ϵ)≤∣Bn​∣⋅2−n(H(X)−ϵ),

giving ∣Bn∣≥(1−δ−ϵ)⋅2n(H(X)−ϵ)|B_n| \geq (1 - \delta - \epsilon) \cdot 2^{n(H(X) - \epsilon)}∣Bn​∣≥(1−δ−ϵ)⋅2n(H(X)−ϵ). For sufficiently large nnn, the leading constant is positive, and we get the bound. □\square□

This is the converse to the AEP: not only does the typical set capture most of the probability with about 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X) sequences, but no other set can do substantially better.


### 3.5 The Counting Implication for Source Coding

We can already preview the source coding theorem of Chapter 4.

Suppose we want to losslessly encode a long i.i.d. source sequence into binary. A naïve encoding uses ⌈log⁡∣X∣⌉\lceil \log |\mathcal{X}| \rceil⌈log∣X∣⌉ bits per symbol, regardless of the source distribution. This is wasteful when H(X)<log⁡∣X∣H(X) < \log |\mathcal{X}|H(X)<log∣X∣.

Better strategy: index only the typical sequences. There are about 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X) typical sequences, so we can index them with nH(X)n H(X)nH(X) bits, i.e., about H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol. For atypical sequences (occurring with probability less than ϵ\epsilonϵ), we use a fallback, longer encoding.

The expected length per symbol is then approximately

(1−ϵ)⋅H(X)+ϵ⋅log⁡∣X∣→H(X) as ϵ→0.(1 - \epsilon) \cdot H(X) + \epsilon \cdot \log |\mathcal{X}| \to H(X) \text{ as } \epsilon \to 0.(1−ϵ)⋅H(X)+ϵ⋅log∣X∣→H(X) as ϵ→0.

This is the **achievability** part of the source coding theorem: we can compress to within H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol by indexing the typical set. The **converse** , that we cannot do better on average, is the smallest-set-of-high-probability theorem.

We will refine this argument in Chapter 4. The point for now is that the AEP _operationalizes_ the entropy: it tells us why H(X)H(X)H(X) is the asymptotic per-symbol description length.

blocks.src:
### 3.6 The AEP Beyond i.i.d.: Stationary Ergodic Sources

The AEP as we have stated it requires the i.i.d. assumption. Real sources (English text, audio signals, video) are not i.i.d. They have temporal correlations that violate the assumption directly.

It turns out, however, that the AEP extends beyond i.i.d. The right generalization is to **stationary ergodic** processes. A stochastic process {Xt}t∈Z\\{X_t\\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}{Xt​}t∈Z​ is stationary if its joint distributions are invariant under time shift. It is ergodic if, roughly, time averages equal ensemble averages — there is no "decomposition" of the process into substantially different sub-processes.

For a stationary ergodic source, the **entropy rate** is

H=lim⁡n→∞1nH(X1,X2,…,Xn)=lim⁡n→∞H(Xn∣Xn−1,Xn−2,…,X1).H = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} H(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} H(X_n \mid X_{n-1}, X_{n-2}, \ldots, X_1).H=n→∞lim​n1​H(X1​,X2​,…,Xn​)=n→∞lim​H(Xn​∣Xn−1​,Xn−2​,…,X1​).

(Both limits exist and are equal for stationary ergodic processes; the equality is non-trivial.)

The **Shannon-McMillan-Breiman theorem** says that for a stationary ergodic source with entropy rate HHH,

−1nlog⁡p(X1,…,Xn)→Halmost surely.-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \to H \quad \text{almost surely}.−n1​logp(X1​,…,Xn​)→Halmost surely.

This is the AEP for general sources. The proof is harder than the i.i.d. case (it uses ergodic theory rather than the law of large numbers), but the conclusion is the same: typical sequences have probability about 2−nH2^{-n H}2−nH, and there are about 2nH2^{n H}2nH of them.

So the operational interpretation of the entropy rate is the same: the asymptotic per-symbol description cost. For English text with entropy rate around 1 bit per character, an asymptotically optimal compressor uses about 1 bit per character. Modern transformer language models, as we will see in Chapter 15, achieve close to this on diverse English.


### 3.7 Joint Typicality

For coding theorems involving channels (Chapter 6), we need a joint version of the AEP. Let (X1,Y1),(X2,Y2),…,(Xn,Yn)(X_1, Y_1), (X_2, Y_2), \ldots, (X_n, Y_n)(X1​,Y1​),(X2​,Y2​),…,(Xn​,Yn​) be i.i.d. samples from a joint distribution p(x,y)p(x, y)p(x,y).

blocks.src:
#### Definition: The Jointly Typical Set

Aϵ(n)(X,Y)={((x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)):∣−1nlog⁡p(x1,…,xn)−H(X)∣≤ϵ,∣−1nlog⁡p(y1,…,yn)−H(Y)∣≤ϵ,∣−1nlog⁡p(x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn)−H(X,Y)∣≤ϵ}.A_\epsilon^{(n)}(X, Y) = \left\\{((x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)) : \begin{array}{l} |-\frac{1}{n} \log p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) - H(X)| \leq \epsilon, \\\ |-\frac{1}{n} \log p(y_1, \ldots, y_n) - H(Y)| \leq \epsilon, \\\ |-\frac{1}{n} \log p(x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_n) - H(X, Y)| \leq \epsilon \end{array}\right\\}.Aϵ(n)​(X,Y)=⎩⎨⎧​((x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​)):∣−n1​logp(x1​,…,xn​)−H(X)∣≤ϵ,∣−n1​logp(y1​,…,yn​)−H(Y)∣≤ϵ,∣−n1​logp(x1​,…,xn​,y1​,…,yn​)−H(X,Y)∣≤ϵ​⎭⎬⎫​.

In plain language: a pair of sequences is jointly typical if both individual sequences are typical and the pair is also typical under the joint distribution.

The properties of the jointly typical set parallel those of the typical set:

  1. Pr⁡(Aϵ(n)(X,Y))→1\Pr(A_\epsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)) \to 1Pr(Aϵ(n)​(X,Y))→1 as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞.
  2. ∣Aϵ(n)(X,Y)∣≤2n(H(X,Y)+ϵ)|A_\epsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)| \leq 2^{n(H(X, Y) + \epsilon)}∣Aϵ(n)​(X,Y)∣≤2n(H(X,Y)+ϵ).
  3. If (X~n,Y~n)(\tilde{X}^n, \tilde{Y}^n)(X~n,Y~n) are independently chosen with X~n∼∏p(xi)\tilde{X}^n \sim \prod p(x_i)X~n∼∏p(xi​) and Y~n∼∏p(yi)\tilde{Y}^n \sim \prod p(y_i)Y~n∼∏p(yi​) (so the _marginals_ are the same as for (Xn,Yn)(X^n, Y^n)(Xn,Yn), but the joint is the product), then

Pr⁡((X~n,Y~n)∈Aϵ(n)(X,Y))≈2−nI(X;Y).\Pr((\tilde{X}^n, \tilde{Y}^n) \in A_\epsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)) \approx 2^{-n I(X; Y)}.Pr((X~n,Y~n)∈Aϵ(n)​(X,Y))≈2−nI(X;Y).

Property 3 is the key for channel coding: if we draw an "independent" pair, the chance it accidentally looks jointly typical is 2−nI(X;Y)2^{-n I(X; Y)}2−nI(X;Y). This exponential is the engine of Shannon's channel coding theorem in Chapter 6.

**Proof of Property 3** : Each "independent" pair (X~n,Y~n)(\tilde{X}^n, \tilde{Y}^n)(X~n,Y~n) where X~n\tilde{X}^nX~n has typical XXX-marginal and Y~n\tilde{Y}^nY~n has typical YYY-marginal has joint probability about 2−nH(X)⋅2−nH(Y)=2−n(H(X)+H(Y))2^{-n H(X)} \cdot 2^{-n H(Y)} = 2^{-n(H(X) + H(Y))}2−nH(X)⋅2−nH(Y)=2−n(H(X)+H(Y)) under the product distribution. The number of jointly typical pairs is ∣Aϵ(n)(X,Y)∣≈2nH(X,Y)|A_\epsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)| \approx 2^{n H(X, Y)}∣Aϵ(n)​(X,Y)∣≈2nH(X,Y). So

Pr⁡indep((X~n,Y~n)∈Aϵ(n)(X,Y))≈2nH(X,Y)⋅2−n(H(X)+H(Y))=2−nI(X;Y),\Pr_{\text{indep}}((\tilde{X}^n, \tilde{Y}^n) \in A_\epsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)) \approx 2^{n H(X, Y)} \cdot 2^{-n(H(X) + H(Y))} = 2^{-n I(X; Y)},indepPr​((X~n,Y~n)∈Aϵ(n)​(X,Y))≈2nH(X,Y)⋅2−n(H(X)+H(Y))=2−nI(X;Y),

using I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y)I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y). □\square□

This identity is the main reason mutual information is the right quantity for channel capacity. Two random sequences "look correlated" with probability 2−nI(X;Y)2^{-n I(X; Y)}2−nI(X;Y); to send a message reliably through a channel, we need to choose codewords that look "more correlated" than this, which restricts us to about 2nI(X;Y)2^{n I(X; Y)}2nI(X;Y) distinguishable codewords. We will make this precise in Chapter 6.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
### 3.8 An AI Connection: AEP and the Manifold Hypothesis

Modern machine learning often invokes the "manifold hypothesis": the observation that natural data (images, speech, text) lies on or near a low-dimensional manifold in the much higher-dimensional ambient space of pixel values, audio samples, or character sequences. Why is this hypothesis even plausible?

The AEP gives one answer. Natural sources have entropy rates much smaller than the maximum entropy on their alphabets. English has entropy around 1 bit per character versus a maximum of about 6.5 bits per byte. Natural images have entropy estimates of perhaps 1 to 2 bits per pixel versus 8 bits per channel for raw pixel values. The "typical set" of a natural image distribution is therefore an exponentially small fraction of the ambient space — exactly what one means by "the data lies on a low-dimensional manifold."

This is not the whole story (the manifold hypothesis usually invokes geometric structure beyond the counting argument) but the AEP is the underlying probabilistic reason. _Most_ sequences from a low-entropy source are typical; _most_ sequences in the ambient space are atypical. Modern generative models like diffusion models, in some sense, learn to output samples that fall on the typical set of natural images, while never explicitly enumerating it.

There is also a beautiful connection to language models. When a language model generates text by sampling from its predicted distribution at each step, it produces sequences that lie in the typical set of its learned distribution. The diversity of plausible model outputs is bounded by 2nHmodel2^{n H_{\text{model}}}2nHmodel​, which is a rough proxy for "how many different sentences the model considers plausible." Highly entropic models produce more varied output; sharply peaked models produce more deterministic output. Sampling temperature in transformer inference is essentially a knob on the model's entropy, and through it on the size of the typical set the model is willing to sample from.

We will return to this circle of ideas in Chapter 15.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
### 3.9 Historical Note: McMillan, Breiman, and the Bell Labs Years

Shannon's 1948 proof of the AEP was the i.i.d. case, the easy half. Real sources are not i.i.d., and Shannon knew it: his 1951 paper on the entropy of English explicitly used n-gram statistics for n up to 8. But proving the AEP for general stationary ergodic sources required machinery he did not have on hand.

Brockway McMillan, a younger Bell Labs colleague, supplied the first half of the generalization in 1953, extending the AEP to stationary ergodic processes via direct calculation. Leo Breiman, then a Berkeley statistician, sharpened McMillan's result in 1957 from convergence in probability to almost-sure convergence using the Birkhoff ergodic theorem. The combined result is what we now call the _Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem_.

Bell Labs in the 1950s was an unusual place. Shannon worked alongside John Tukey (who would later coin "bit" and "software"), Richard Hamming (Chapter 7), David Slepian (Chapter 12), and Claude Berrou's intellectual ancestors. The labs paid for fundamental research with no immediate application, and the AEP, useless for any product the company was making in 1953, was nevertheless taken seriously enough that McMillan got six months of free time to work on it. The institutional patience that produced these foundational results is largely gone from corporate research; almost all subsequent extensions of the AEP have come from academic settings.


### Common Misconception

Two stumbles are common in interpreting the AEP.

* **Misconception** : "Typical sequences are the most probable sequences."

No. The single most probable sequence of nnn i.i.d. flips of a coin with p(heads)=0.7p(\text{heads}) = 0.7p(heads)=0.7 is "all heads," with probability 0.7n0.7^n0.7n. This sequence is _atypical_ : it has empirical log-probability −nlog⁡0.7≈0.515n-n \log 0.7 \approx 0.515 n−nlog0.7≈0.515n bits, while the entropy is Hb(0.7)≈0.881H_b(0.7) \approx 0.881Hb​(0.7)≈0.881 bits. The atypicality arises because "all heads" has too few tails to match the expected fraction.

Typical sequences are not maximally probable; they are _close to the average log-probability_. The most probable single sequence may be far from typical.

* **Misconception** : "All typical sequences are equally likely."

Approximately, yes, within a factor of 2n⋅2ϵ2^{n \cdot 2 \epsilon}2n⋅2ϵ. But not exactly. The typical set contains sequences with slightly different probabilities, all clustered near 2−nH(X)2^{-n H(X)}2−nH(X). The "equipartition" in AEP is asymptotic and approximate, not literal.

These misconceptions are not catastrophic, but they trip up readers who skim the theorem statements. The slogan to remember is: **typical = average log-probability ≈ H(X)H(X)H(X), not maximum probability**.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Asymptotic Equipartition and Typical Sets
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

The Asymptotic Equipartition Property is the bridge between the abstract definition of entropy and its operational meaning. For i.i.d. sources, the empirical log-probability of a long sequence concentrates on the entropy: −1nlog⁡p(X1,…,Xn)→H(X)-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \to H(X)−n1​logp(X1​,…,Xn​)→H(X) in probability. This implies that long sequences are concentrated on a "typical set" of about 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X) sequences, all roughly equiprobable, capturing almost all the probability.

The typical set is essentially the smallest high-probability set: any set that captures a constant fraction of the probability must have size at least 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X). This already foreshadows the source coding theorem of Chapter 4: H(X)H(X)H(X) is the per-symbol cost of describing the source.

The joint version of the AEP, joint typicality, gives Property 3, that an "independent" pair of marginals looks jointly typical with probability 2−nI(X;Y)2^{-n I(X; Y)}2−nI(X;Y). This exponential is the engine of Shannon's channel coding theorem in Chapter 6.

We sketched the AI angle: natural data sources have low entropy rates, so their typical sets are exponentially small fractions of the ambient space: the underlying probabilistic reason behind the manifold hypothesis. Sampling from a generative model is, in essence, sampling from the typical set of a learned distribution.

The next chapter, on source coding, makes the operational meaning of H(X)H(X)H(X) precise. We will see that no compression scheme can do better than H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol on average, and that Huffman and arithmetic coding asymptotically achieve this bound.

**Answer:** For non-uniform distributions, H(X)<log⁡∣X∣H(X) < \log |\mathcal{X}|H(X)<log∣X∣. blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The AEP says "typical sequences are exponentially fewer than total sequences but contain essentially all the probability." This is not how the human mind tends to think about probabilities. Why is the AEP often counterintuitive on first encounter?

**Discussion:** Several reasons.

First, our intuition tends to conflate "the most likely thing" with "what we will see." For a coin with p(heads)=0.7p(\text{heads}) = 0.7p(heads)=0.7, the most likely single sequence in 100 flips is "all heads." But you will essentially never see this sequence; you will see one of the many sequences with about 70 heads and 30 tails. The notion that "what we see is rarely the most likely thing, but is one of many roughly equiprobable typical things" runs against our usual heuristic.

Second, the exponential gap between typical-set size and total-set size is hard to picture. Saying that the typical set is 10−10010^{-100}10−100 of the total feels like saying it is "vanishingly small," yet it captures essentially all the probability. The mind wants to ascribe positive probability to the rest of the space, and quickly drops a vast amount of it.

Third, the AEP's _uniformity_ over typical sequences is unintuitive. We expect probability to be concentrated on a few "very likely" outcomes, and rare outcomes to be a long tail. The AEP says: there are no especially likely outcomes; the probability is spread evenly over the typical set.

This last point is the deepest. Take 1000 fair coin flips: the probability of any specific sequence is 2−10002^{-1000}2−1000, exactly. The typical set is "all sequences," each equally likely. There is no concentration of probability mass on a small set of "favored" sequences; there is just a ferocious geometric uniformity. Every "typical" outcome is equally surprising in isolation but typical as a class.

The AEP is the precise statement of this fact for non-uniform distributions: the typical set is the _almost_ -uniform region of probability mass.

**Q2.** The AEP's proof relies on the law of large numbers. What goes wrong if the variance of log⁡p(X)\log p(X)logp(X) is infinite? Are there pathological distributions for which the AEP fails?

**Discussion:** The classical (i.i.d.) AEP is a direct corollary of the law of large numbers applied to the random variable log⁡p(X)\log p(X)logp(X). For convergence in probability (the weak AEP), it suffices that E[log⁡p(X)]=−H(X)\mathbb{E}[\log p(X)] = -H(X)E[logp(X)]=−H(X) is finite — which is automatic for finite alphabets. The AEP holds for any i.i.d. source over a finite alphabet without further assumption.

Pathologies arise for _infinite_ alphabets (countably infinite sources). If ppp has infinite entropy, the AEP statement becomes vacuous. If ppp has finite entropy but log⁡p(X)\log p(X)logp(X) has infinite variance, the convergence rate slows but the limit still holds (the law of large numbers is robust here).

For continuous random variables, the analog is the differential AEP: −1nlog⁡f(X1,…,Xn)→h(X)-\frac{1}{n} \log f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \to h(X)−n1​logf(X1​,…,Xn​)→h(X) in probability, where fff is the density and hhh is differential entropy. This holds under regularity conditions on fff.

For non-stationary or non-ergodic processes, the AEP fails. A source that is "two different sources" depending on a hidden mixture component (say, with probability 1/21/21/2 it emits an i.i.d. Bernoulli(0.1) sequence and with probability 1/21/21/2 an i.i.d. Bernoulli(0.5) sequence — has overall per-symbol entropy

H=Hb(0.5)+12Hb(0.1)+12Hb(0.5)=1+12(0.469)+12(1)≈1.74 bits,H = H_b(0.5) + \tfrac{1}{2} H_b(0.1) + \tfrac{1}{2} H_b(0.5) = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.469) + \tfrac{1}{2}(1) \approx 1.74 \text{ bits},H=Hb​(0.5)+21​Hb​(0.1)+21​Hb​(0.5)=1+21​(0.469)+21​(1)≈1.74 bits,

but the empirical log-probability of any one realization concentrates on either Hb(0.1)≈0.469H_b(0.1) \approx 0.469Hb​(0.1)≈0.469 or Hb(0.5)=1H_b(0.5) = 1Hb​(0.5)=1 bit per symbol — _never_ on the average 1.74. The two ergodic components have different per-symbol log-probabilities, so the AEP holds _within_ each component but not over the mixture. The Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem requires ergodicity for exactly this reason: it forbids the "two sources in a trench coat" failure mode.

**Q3.** Modern generative models (diffusion models, large language models) sample from learned distributions. In the AEP picture, they are sampling from "typical sets" of their learned distributions. What does this say about the kinds of outputs they produce — and the kinds they almost never produce?

**Discussion:** A generative model represents an estimated distribution p^\hat{p}p^​ over data. When it samples, it is producing sequences from the typical set of p^\hat{p}p^​. For language models, this means: the model produces sentences whose empirical log-probability matches the model's entropy rate. Sentences with much higher (more probable) or much lower (more surprising) log-probability are not in the typical set and are essentially never sampled.

This explains several empirical phenomena.

First, language models tend to produce "average" text, specifically fluent, plausible, and often somewhat bland. Truly creative or unexpected outputs (the equivalents of "all heads" in our coin example) are atypical and are sampled with vanishing probability under the model's distribution. Sampling tricks like temperature scaling, top-k, or top-p filtering manipulate the model's distribution to bias toward or against the typical set's "edges," giving the user some control over diversity vs. determinism.

Second, language models almost never output sequences that have very high probability under the data distribution but were not seen in training. This is because the model's typical set reflects what was in the training corpus; sequences outside that distribution are atypical relative to the model.

Third, the "mode-collapse" failure mode of generative models (where the model produces only a small subset of possible outputs) is a failure of the typical set to span the data distribution. The model has learned a distribution whose typical set covers only part of the data's typical set.

This circle of ideas runs through Chapter 14 (the InfoNCE and contrastive learning losses are designed to align typical sets) and Chapter 18 (the capstone trains a small model and verifies that its samples match the data distribution's typical set). Information theory provides a rigorous way to talk about what generative models do and do not produce.

blocks.src:
### Connections to Subsequent Chapters

The AEP and its joint cousin are the engine room of all subsequent coding theorems.

* **Chapter 4** uses the typical set to construct compression schemes that achieve H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol; Huffman, arithmetic, and block-coding constructions all rest on the AEP picture.
* **Chapter 5** defines channel capacity CCC using the formula C=max⁡p(X)I(X;Y)C = \max_{p(X)} I(X; Y)C=maxp(X)​I(X;Y), and the operational meaning of CCC (Chapter 6) uses joint typicality directly.
* **Chapter 6** proves Shannon's channel coding theorem by random coding, decoding by joint typicality, and Property 3 of joint typicality (probability of accidental joint typicality is 2−nI(X;Y)2^{-n I(X; Y)}2−nI(X;Y)).
* **Chapters 11, 18** use rate-distortion versions of the AEP, where typical pairs replace typical sequences as the central object.

A reader who has internalized the AEP — typical set size, the smallest-set-of-high-probability theorem, joint typicality, and Property 3 — has the bedrock for the rest of the book.

* * *

---

In Chapter 3 we saw that long sequences from an i.i.d. source are concentrated on a typical set of about 2nH(X)2^{n H(X)}2nH(X) sequences. From this counting fact we can already imagine an asymptotically efficient encoding: index the typical set with ⌈nH(X)⌉\lceil n H(X) \rceil⌈nH(X)⌉ bits and use a longer fallback for the (rare) atypical sequences. This chapter makes that intuition into a constructive theory of compression.

The central result is **Shannon's Source Coding Theorem** , which states that the entropy H(X)H(X)H(X) is the fundamental limit of lossless compression: no scheme can use fewer than H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol on average, and one can come arbitrarily close. We will state and prove the theorem in two flavors (variable-length coding and block coding), and we will see two algorithms (Huffman and arithmetic coding) that approach this bound in practice.

The chapter ends with the most important AI connection in the book: language model perplexity is a compression rate, and modern large language models are world-class compressors of text. When GPT predicts your next sentence, it is, mathematically, performing source coding on the universe of plausible sentences.


### 4.1 Codes and Code Trees

We begin with the building blocks. A **source code** CCC for a random variable XXX on alphabet X\mathcal{X}X is a mapping from X\mathcal{X}X to a set of finite-length binary strings {0,1}∗\\{0, 1\\}^*{0,1}∗. The code assigns to each symbol xxx a **codeword** C(x)C(x)C(x) of length ℓ(x)\ell(x)ℓ(x).

The **expected codeword length** is

L(C)=E[ℓ(X)]=∑xp(x)ℓ(x).L(C) = \mathbb{E}[\ell(X)] = \sum_x p(x) \ell(x).L(C)=E[ℓ(X)]=x∑​p(x)ℓ(x).

We want L(C)L(C)L(C) as small as possible.

For a code to be useful for transmission, we need to be able to _decode_ it. The simplest sufficient condition is that the code be **prefix-free** (also called instantaneous): no codeword is a prefix of another. With this property, a stream of concatenated codewords can be decoded by reading bits one at a time and stopping at the first complete codeword.

Prefix-free codes correspond to leaves of binary trees: assign 0 to "go left" and 1 to "go right"; each codeword is the path from root to leaf. The prefix-free property says that no leaf is on the path to another leaf; leaves are the terminal nodes.


#### Worked Example: A Prefix-Free Code

Let X={a,b,c,d}\mathcal{X} = \\{a, b, c, d\\}X={a,b,c,d} with codewords C(a)=0C(a) = 0C(a)=0, C(b)=10C(b) = 10C(b)=10, C(c)=110C(c) = 110C(c)=110, C(d)=111C(d) = 111C(d)=111. Visualizing as a tree: root has left child aaa (leaf at depth 1) and right child to internal node, which has left child bbb (leaf at depth 2) and right child to internal node with left child ccc and right child ddd (both leaves at depth 3). No codeword is a prefix of another.

The string 010110111010110111010110111 decodes uniquely as 0⋅10⋅110⋅1110 \cdot 10 \cdot 110 \cdot 1110⋅10⋅110⋅111, or a,b,c,da, b, c, da,b,c,d.


### 4.2 The Kraft Inequality

How short can the codeword lengths be? The **Kraft inequality** answers exactly.

#### Theorem (Kraft Inequality)

For any prefix-free binary code with codeword lengths ℓ1,ℓ2,…,ℓn\ell_1, \ell_2, \ldots, \ell_nℓ1​,ℓ2​,…,ℓn​,

∑i=1n2−ℓi≤1.\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\ell_i} \leq 1.i=1∑n​2−ℓi​≤1.

Conversely, given any positive integers ℓ1,…,ℓn\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_nℓ1​,…,ℓn​ satisfying the inequality, there exists a prefix-free binary code with these codeword lengths.

In plain language, this means: the lengths of a prefix-free code cannot be arbitrarily short, but if they satisfy the Kraft inequality, a code with those lengths exists.

**Proof of forward direction** : Consider the binary tree of depth ℓmax⁡=max⁡iℓi\ell_{\max} = \max_i \ell_iℓmax​=maxi​ℓi​. It has 2ℓmax⁡2^{\ell_{\max}}2ℓmax​ leaves. Each codeword of length ℓi\ell_iℓi​ "claims" 2ℓmax⁡−ℓi2^{\ell_{\max} - \ell_i}2ℓmax​−ℓi​ of these leaves (all the descendants). Because the code is prefix-free, the claimed sets are disjoint. So

∑i2ℓmax⁡−ℓi≤2ℓmax⁡,\sum_i 2^{\ell_{\max} - \ell_i} \leq 2^{\ell_{\max}},i∑​2ℓmax​−ℓi​≤2ℓmax​,

which gives the inequality on dividing by 2ℓmax⁡2^{\ell_{\max}}2ℓmax​. □\square□

**Proof of converse** : Sort the lengths ℓ1≤ℓ2≤⋯≤ℓn\ell_1 \leq \ell_2 \leq \cdots \leq \ell_nℓ1​≤ℓ2​≤⋯≤ℓn​. Build a tree of depth ℓmax⁡\ell_{\max}ℓmax​. Greedily assign each codeword to a leaf, removing all descendants of that leaf from availability. The Kraft inequality guarantees that at each step there is an available node. □\square□

The Kraft inequality is the universal constraint on prefix-free codes. Whenever we ask "can we have a code with lengths ℓ1,…,ℓn\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_nℓ1​,…,ℓn​?" the answer is exactly: yes, iff ∑2−ℓi≤1\sum 2^{-\ell_i} \leq 1∑2−ℓi​≤1.


### 4.3 Shannon's Source Coding Theorem (Variable-Length)

Now we prove the central result.

#### Theorem (Shannon's Source Coding Theorem, variable-length form)

For any prefix-free code CCC for a random variable XXX with distribution ppp,

L(C)≥H(X).L(C) \geq H(X).L(C)≥H(X).

Conversely, there exists a prefix-free code with

L(C)<H(X)+1.L(C) < H(X) + 1.L(C)<H(X)+1.

In plain language: H(X)H(X)H(X) is the lower bound on average codeword length, and we can come within one bit of it.

**Proof of converse (achievability)** : For each xxx, choose ℓ(x)=⌈−log⁡p(x)⌉\ell(x) = \lceil -\log p(x) \rceilℓ(x)=⌈−logp(x)⌉. Then

∑x2−ℓ(x)≤∑x2log⁡p(x)=∑xp(x)=1,\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \leq \sum_x 2^{\log p(x)} = \sum_x p(x) = 1,x∑​2−ℓ(x)≤x∑​2logp(x)=x∑​p(x)=1,

so the Kraft inequality is satisfied and a prefix-free code with these lengths exists. The expected length is

L=∑xp(x)ℓ(x)=∑xp(x)⌈−log⁡p(x)⌉<∑xp(x)(−log⁡p(x)+1)=H(X)+1.□L = \sum_x p(x) \ell(x) = \sum_x p(x) \lceil -\log p(x) \rceil < \sum_x p(x) (-\log p(x) + 1) = H(X) + 1. \squareL=x∑​p(x)ℓ(x)=x∑​p(x)⌈−logp(x)⌉<x∑​p(x)(−logp(x)+1)=H(X)+1.□

This construction, the **Shannon code** with codeword length ⌈−log⁡p(x)⌉\lceil -\log p(x) \rceil⌈−logp(x)⌉, is not optimal (Huffman is the optimum, as we show in §4.5), but it suffices for the asymptotic argument.

**Proof of forward direction (converse)** : We will use the Kraft inequality and Gibbs' inequality (which we will prove formally as a property of KL divergence in Chapter 8). Define q(x)=2−ℓ(x)/∑y2−ℓ(y)q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)} / \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)}q(x)=2−ℓ(x)/∑y​2−ℓ(y), which is a probability distribution. Then

L(C)−H(X)=∑xp(x)ℓ(x)−H(X)=−∑xp(x)log⁡2−ℓ(x)−H(X).L(C) - H(X) = \sum_x p(x) \ell(x) - H(X) = -\sum_x p(x) \log 2^{-\ell(x)} - H(X).L(C)−H(X)=x∑​p(x)ℓ(x)−H(X)=−x∑​p(x)log2−ℓ(x)−H(X).

Substituting 2−ℓ(x)=q(x)⋅∑y2−ℓ(y)2^{-\ell(x)} = q(x) \cdot \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)}2−ℓ(x)=q(x)⋅∑y​2−ℓ(y):

L(C)−H(X)=−∑xp(x)log⁡q(x)−log⁡∑y2−ℓ(y)−H(X)=D(p∥q)−log⁡∑y2−ℓ(y).L(C) - H(X) = -\sum_x p(x) \log q(x) - \log \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)} - H(X) = D(p \| q) - \log \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)}.L(C)−H(X)=−x∑​p(x)logq(x)−logy∑​2−ℓ(y)−H(X)=D(p∥q)−logy∑​2−ℓ(y).

Since the Kraft inequality gives ∑y2−ℓ(y)≤1\sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)} \leq 1∑y​2−ℓ(y)≤1, we have −log⁡∑y2−ℓ(y)≥0-\log \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)} \geq 0−log∑y​2−ℓ(y)≥0. And D(p∥q)≥0D(p \| q) \geq 0D(p∥q)≥0 by Gibbs' inequality. So L(C)−H(X)≥0L(C) - H(X) \geq 0L(C)−H(X)≥0, i.e., L(C)≥H(X)L(C) \geq H(X)L(C)≥H(X). □\square□

The proof tells us _when_ equality holds: when D(p∥q)=0D(p \| q) = 0D(p∥q)=0 (i.e., p=qp = qp=q) and when the Kraft sum equals 1 (i.e., the code uses up all the tree). This requires p(x)=2−ℓ(x)p(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}p(x)=2−ℓ(x); the probabilities must be inverse powers of 2 (a "dyadic" distribution).


#### The 1-bit gap

The variable-length theorem leaves a gap of up to one bit per symbol. Where does it come from? The integer-rounding step ⌈−log⁡p(x)⌉\lceil -\log p(x) \rceil⌈−logp(x)⌉. In the worst case, every ℓ(x)\ell(x)ℓ(x) is rounded up by nearly 1.

Two strategies close this gap:

  1. **Block coding** : encode blocks of nnn symbols at a time. The 1-bit gap is amortized over nnn, so the per-symbol gap shrinks to 1/n1/n1/n. For large nnn, the rate approaches H(X)H(X)H(X).
  2. **Arithmetic coding** : a single code that effectively does block coding for arbitrary block lengths, achieving a gap of O(1/n)O(1/n)O(1/n) bits per symbol.

We treat block coding next, then Huffman (the optimal variable-length code for a symbol-at-a-time scheme), then arithmetic coding.

### 4.4 Block Coding and the Asymptotic Bound

If we treat nnn source symbols as a single "super-symbol" XnX^nXn and apply Shannon's variable-length theorem to XnX^nXn, we get

H(Xn)≤Ln<H(Xn)+1,H(X^n) \leq L_n < H(X^n) + 1,H(Xn)≤Ln​<H(Xn)+1,

### 4.5 Huffman Coding

Shannon's variable-length theorem says we can achieve L<H(X)+1L < H(X) + 1L<H(X)+1 by a particular construction. It does not say this construction is optimal. The optimal symbol-at-a-time prefix-free code is **Huffman's code** , devised by David Huffman as a class assignment in 1951.


#### The Huffman Algorithm

Given a probability distribution p(x1),…,p(xn)p(x_1), \ldots, p(x_n)p(x1​),…,p(xn​):

  1. Treat each xix_ixi​ as a leaf with weight p(xi)p(x_i)p(xi​).
  2. Find the two leaves with smallest weight; combine them into an internal node with weight equal to their sum.
  3. Repeat until only one node (the root) remains.
  4. Assign 0 and 1 arbitrarily to the two children of each internal node. The codeword of xix_ixi​ is the bitstring on the root-to-leaf path.

#### Optimality of Huffman

**Theorem** : Huffman's code minimizes the expected codeword length among all prefix-free codes for a given distribution.

The proof uses two lemmas:

  1. In any optimal code, the two least-probable symbols have the same length and differ only in the last bit.
  2. Huffman's tree-merging rule preserves optimality: an optimal code on the (n-1)-symbol distribution (with the two smallest probabilities merged) extends to an optimal code on the original n-symbol distribution.

A formal induction on nnn gives the full theorem.

The optimality is per-symbol, not asymptotic. Huffman achieves the best possible rate among symbol-at-a-time prefix-free codes; for very skewed distributions (one symbol with probability 0.99), it may be much worse than the entropy because integer rounding hurts. To get arbitrarily close to entropy, we either use block coding or move to arithmetic coding.

#### Limitations of Huffman

* **Integer-length problem** : codeword lengths are integers, but −log⁡p(x)-\log p(x)−logp(x) is not. The rounding loss can be significant when one symbol has probability close to 1.
* **Two-pass requirement** : Huffman needs the distribution; in practice this means either training the encoder on representative data or making two passes over the source (one to estimate p(x)p(x)p(x), one to encode).
* **Adaptive Huffman** : a variant that updates the tree as it encodes, eliminating the two-pass requirement, used in some classical compression schemes.
* **Block-coded Huffman** : encode nnn-symbol blocks. The rate gap shrinks to 1/n1/n1/n per symbol, but the alphabet size grows to ∣X∣n|\mathcal{X}|^n∣X∣n, making the algorithm expensive.


### 4.6 Arithmetic Coding

Arithmetic coding solves Huffman's integer-length problem. Instead of assigning codewords to symbols, it represents an entire message as a single number in the unit interval [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1).


#### The Idea

Start with the interval [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1). For each symbol in the message, partition the current interval into subintervals proportional to the symbol probabilities, and select the subinterval corresponding to the actual symbol. After encoding the entire message, the final interval is some range [a,b)[a, b)[a,b). The encoded output is any number in this interval, transmitted as a binary fraction with as few bits as possible.

The number of bits needed to specify a number in an interval of width www is ⌈−log⁡2w⌉\lceil -\log_2 w \rceil⌈−log2​w⌉. After encoding nnn i.i.d. symbols, the interval width is ∏ip(xi)=p(message)\prod_i p(x_i) = p(\text{message})∏i​p(xi​)=p(message), so the encoding uses about −log⁡p(message)=∑i−log⁡p(xi)-\log p(\text{message}) = \sum_i -\log p(x_i)−logp(message)=∑i​−logp(xi​) bits — exactly the self-information of the message.

The expected encoding length per symbol is

1nE[−log⁡p(Xn)]+O(1/n)=H(X)+O(1/n),\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X^n)] + O(1/n) = H(X) + O(1/n),n1​E[−logp(Xn)]+O(1/n)=H(X)+O(1/n),

### 4.7 Universal Source Coding: gzip and Friends

So far we have assumed the source distribution p(x)p(x)p(x) is known. In practice, the source is often unknown; we want to compress a file without knowing what kind of data it contains. **Universal source coding** addresses this: a single algorithm that achieves near-entropy compression on a wide class of sources without knowing the distribution.

The Lempel-Ziv family (LZ77, LZ78, and their many descendants) is the dominant paradigm. The idea: build a dictionary of substrings seen so far, and encode each new substring as a reference to its earlier occurrence.

For LZ77 (used in gzip, deflate, zip):

  1. Maintain a sliding window of the last WWW symbols.
  2. At each position, find the longest match between the upcoming text and a substring in the window.
  3. Encode the match as a (distance, length) pair, plus the next non-matching symbol.

The Lempel–Ziv family was introduced by Ziv and Lempel (LZ77 in 1977, LZ78 in 1978). For an i.i.d. source with entropy rate HHH, LZ77 achieves a rate approaching HHH as the window grows. The full asymptotic-optimality proof for stationary ergodic sources — that the per-symbol rate of LZ77 converges to the entropy rate HHH almost surely — was given by Wyner and Ziv in 1994. So universal coders achieve the entropy bound asymptotically _without knowing_ the source distribution; they learn it implicitly from the data.

In practice, gzip on English text achieves about 60% compression, a ratio of 1/0.4 = 2.5:1. The entropy of English at the character level is around 1 bit per byte (8 bits per byte raw), giving an asymptotic best of about 12% — much better than gzip. The gap is partly because LZ77's window is finite, partly because English has long-range correlations gzip cannot exploit, and partly because gzip is tuned for speed, not maximum compression.

xz (LZMA) and Brotli, more modern compressors, do better: about 40-45% of original size for English. Still well above the entropy floor.

To approach the entropy floor on natural language, you need a much more sophisticated model. Modern transformer language models, used as compressors, do exactly this. We will return to this in §4.8 and Chapter 15.

### 4.8 The AI Connection: Language Models as Compressors

Now we make the connection that defines the AI half of this book.

A language model is a probability distribution pθ(xt∣x1,…,xt−1)p_\theta(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1})pθ​(xt​∣x1​,…,xt−1​) over the next token given the history. Its training objective is to minimize the cross-entropy

L=−1n∑t=1nlog⁡pθ(xt∣x1,…,xt−1)\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1})L=−n1​t=1∑n​logpθ​(xt​∣x1​,…,xt−1​)

on a corpus. By the chain rule, this is

L=−1nlog⁡pθ(x1,…,xn).\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{n} \log p_\theta(x_1, \ldots, x_n).L=−n1​logpθ​(x1​,…,xn​).

If we use this language model as a probability distribution in arithmetic coding, the expected encoding length per token is approximately L\mathcal{L}L bits. So:

**The cross-entropy of a language model on text is exactly the per-symbol bit cost of using that model as the source distribution in arithmetic coding.**

This is not a metaphor. It is an exact mathematical identity.

Consequently, **a language model that achieves cross-entropy L\mathcal{L}L bits per token compresses text at rate L\mathcal{L}L bits per token using arithmetic coding.**

How does this compare to gzip? On large English corpora:

* gzip (LZ77-based): about 2.0-2.5 bits per character (1.6:1 to 2.5:1 compression).
* xz / LZMA: about 1.5-2.0 bits per character.
* A small transformer (124M parameters, GPT-2 small): about 1.0-1.2 bits per character on diverse English.
* Frontier models: about 0.7-0.9 bits per character on diverse English.

The frontier numbers are within a factor of two of Shannon's 1951 estimate of the entropy of English (about 0.7-1.5 bits per character based on human prediction experiments). Modern language models are pushing the empirical entropy estimate down — they predict English better than humans do for many subsamples.

**Perplexity** is a closely related metric: 2L2^{\mathcal{L}}2L. It measures the "effective vocabulary size" the model is choosing from at each step. A perplexity of 32 means the model is, on average, distributing probability as if choosing among 32 equally likely tokens. Frontier perplexities on Wikipedia or web text are now in the single digits; for raw byte-level prediction, frontier models achieve about 1.5-2 effective choices per byte.

The deep claim, and this is what makes information theory the mathematics of modern AI: **prediction and compression are the same problem**. If you have a model that predicts well, you have a model that compresses well, and vice versa. The cross-entropy training of language models is, mathematically, training arithmetic coders to compress text well. The "scaling laws" of language modeling (Hoffmann, Chinchilla; Kaplan) describe how compression rate improves with model size and data — they are scaling laws for an entropy estimator.

We will return to this in Chapter 15 and verify it experimentally in Chapter 18.

### Common Misconception

* **Misconception** : "Compression is impossible past a certain point because the message has a fixed length."

No. Lossless compression is bounded only by entropy, not by message length. A message with low entropy (e.g., "00000...") can be compressed to near zero bits, regardless of its length. The fundamental limit is the entropy of the source distribution.

* **Misconception** : "Huffman is always optimal."

Huffman is optimal _among symbol-at-a-time prefix codes for a given distribution_. For block-coded or arithmetic-coded schemes, you can do better — closer to entropy. For unknown sources, universal coders (LZ77) approach entropy asymptotically.

* **Misconception** : "Compression below the original size requires losing information."

No. Lossless compression preserves all information. The compressed file is shorter only because the original had redundancy (the source was not uniform). A genuinely random file (entropy = original length × log alphabet size) cannot be compressed at all; this is why archived data, encrypted data, or already-compressed data does not benefit from re-compression.


### Chapter Summary

The Source Coding Theorem establishes H(X)H(X)H(X) as the fundamental limit of lossless compression. We saw three achievability constructions:

* **Shannon code** : codeword length ⌈−log⁡p(x)⌉\lceil -\log p(x) \rceil⌈−logp(x)⌉, achieving L<H(X)+1L < H(X) + 1L<H(X)+1.
* **Huffman code** : optimal symbol-at-a-time prefix-free code, achieving LLL within 1 bit of entropy.
* **Arithmetic coding** : amortizes the integer-length problem over the entire message, achieving L=H(X)+O(1/n)L = H(X) + O(1/n)L=H(X)+O(1/n) per symbol for blocks of nnn symbols.

For unknown sources, universal coders (LZ77 family, used in gzip and friends) achieve entropy rates without knowing the distribution. They are practical workhorses but often well above the entropy floor on highly-structured data like natural language.

The deepest connection is to AI: language models trained to minimize cross-entropy are, mathematically, learning compressors. Their cross-entropy in bits per token is exactly the rate at which they compress text using arithmetic coding. Modern frontier models compress English to within a factor of two of Shannon's 1951 entropy estimate, and they continue to improve.

The next chapter shifts from source to channel: rather than asking how compactly a source can be encoded, we ask how reliably a noisy channel can transmit information. The two halves — source coding and channel coding — together constitute the classical theory.

**Q2.** Suppose you compress a file twice using gzip. Will the second compression reduce the size further? Explain.

Hint

The output of a good compressor looks like random bits. What is the entropy of random bits?

**Answer:** No, the second compression will not significantly reduce the size; it may even slightly increase the size (due to header overhead).

A good compressor produces output that is close to the entropy of its input. For a well-compressed file, the output has entropy close to its length × 1 bit/bit (i.e., looks like uniformly random bits). A second compression cannot reduce a file with maximum entropy — the entropy bound H(X)=log⁡2=1H(X) = \log 2 = 1H(X)=log2=1 bit per bit means the compressor cannot find more redundancy.

In practice, gzip on a gzip'd file may do nothing or slightly inflate due to format headers. This is one of the more robust intuitions for understanding what compression does: it removes redundancy, and once the redundancy is gone, there is no more to remove.

This connects to a classical theorem: there exists no algorithm that compresses _every_ file. By a counting argument, if all files of length nnn could be compressed to length less than nnn, there would be more "compressed" files than "compressed forms" — contradiction. Compression works precisely because most real-world data is far from the worst-case high-entropy file.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Shannon's source coding theorem says H(X)H(X)H(X) is the fundamental limit of lossless compression. But in practice, we use _lossy_ compression for images (JPEG), audio (MP3), and video (H.264). What governs the limits of lossy compression? Hint: it is rate-distortion, and we will treat it in Chapter 11.

**Discussion:** Lossless compression is bounded by entropy. Lossy compression is bounded by the _rate-distortion function_ R(D)R(D)R(D), which says: at distortion level DDD, the minimum bit rate needed is R(D)=min⁡p(X^∣X):E[d(X,X^)]≤DI(X;X^)R(D) = \min_{p(\hat{X} \mid X) : \mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat{X})] \leq D} I(X; \hat{X})R(D)=minp(X^∣X):E[d(X,X^)]≤D​I(X;X^).

The intuition: with a tolerable distortion, we can use fewer bits than entropy because we are allowed to confuse "close" outcomes. For continuous-source problems (like image compression), this is essential — you cannot compress a continuous-valued image to finite bits losslessly, but you can to within any prescribed distortion.

For most practical lossy compression, the rate-distortion bound is far below the lossless entropy. JPEG at modest quality compresses images by a factor of 10 or 20, yet the residual distortion is imperceptible to most viewers. That is because human perception tolerates significant pixel-level distortion as long as global structure is preserved.

Chapter 11 develops rate-distortion theory in full. The connection to deep learning is that modern neural compression schemes (autoencoders trained on rate-distortion losses) achieve close-to-optimal compression for natural images, and the rate-distortion view gives a unified framework for understanding why.

**Q2.** Universal compression (gzip, LZMA) achieves entropy rates without knowing the source distribution. What is the price paid for not knowing the distribution? Is there a "no-free-lunch" theorem here?

**Discussion:** The price paid is finite-sample overhead. A universal compressor learns the source distribution implicitly from the data; for short messages, this learning is incomplete, and the compression rate is worse than entropy by a "redundancy" term that decreases as the message grows.

For an i.i.d. source over an ∣X∣|\mathcal{X}|∣X∣-symbol alphabet, the minimax redundancy is asymptotically ∣X∣−12log⁡n\frac{|\mathcal{X}| - 1}{2} \log n2∣X∣−1​logn extra bits over the optimal-knowledge code, where nnn is the message length. So as nnn grows, the per-symbol overhead vanishes (O(log⁡n/n)O(\log n / n)O(logn/n)).

For more complex source classes (Markov, stationary ergodic), the redundancy grows with the parametric complexity of the class, but the asymptotic claim still holds: as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞, the per-symbol rate of the universal coder approaches the entropy rate.

This is the closest analog to a "free lunch": universality is asymptotically free, but you pay a small overhead at finite block lengths.

**Q3.** Cross-entropy minimization is the training objective of every modern language model. By the source coding theorem, the achievable cross-entropy is bounded below by the entropy of natural language. Modern frontier models are at about 0.7 bits per character on English. What does this say about the entropy of English, and where might the next decade of improvements come from?

**Discussion:** If frontier models achieve 0.7 bits per character, the entropy of English is at most 0.7 bits per character (perhaps a bit less, since the model could improve with more data and parameters). Shannon's 1951 estimate via human prediction was 0.6-1.3 bits per character on average passages. So we are likely close to the entropy floor for "natural" English in some statistical sense.

Where do further improvements come from?

  1. **Better data** : training on more diverse, higher-quality data may reveal lower entropy on specific genres. Code, for example, is much more compressible than prose because of its regularity.
  2. **Larger models with more capacity** : the scaling laws (Chinchilla, Kaplan) show that bigger models with more data continue to reduce cross-entropy, though at diminishing returns.
  3. **Better tokenization** : byte-level or character-level modeling may have more headroom than subword tokenization.
  4. **Beyond i.i.d. models** : language has rich long-range structure that even transformers may not fully capture. New architectures (state space models, mixture-of-experts) may extract more.
  5. **Multi-modal grounding** : text alone has a certain entropy. Text grounded in vision/audio/structure may be more predictable, lowering effective per-token cost.

The fundamental limit, the entropy of language, is fixed by the language itself, and we are approaching it. Beyond a point, further "improvements" mean either changing the data distribution (curated, multi-modal) or accepting that we are bumping against an entropy floor. The next decade's debates will likely include the question: _what does it mean for a language model to be "near entropy"?_ Whether this signals true linguistic understanding or merely strong statistical compression is one of the central conceptual questions in modern AI.

We will return to this in Chapter 15.

The first half of this book, Chapters 1 through 4, has been about a single object: an information source, characterized by a probability distribution, sending symbols. We learned how to measure the information of a single outcome (self-information), of a distribution (entropy), of a pair (joint, conditional, mutual information), and of long sequences (the Asymptotic Equipartition Property). We saw how to compress a source losslessly down to its entropy.

The other half of Shannon's framework concerns _channels_ : the noisy media over which messages are transmitted. Telephone wires, radio links, optical fibers, magnetic tapes, neural synapses, the human ear-brain system — all of these are channels. Each one corrupts what is sent in some characteristic way: bits flip, samples blur, signals fade.

The deep question Shannon answered in 1948 is: _given a noisy channel, what is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably across it?_ The answer, given by the **channel capacity** CCC, is shockingly simple: CCC is the maximum mutual information I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) over all input distributions p(X)p(X)p(X). Below this rate, arbitrarily reliable communication is achievable. Above it, no scheme can avoid a fixed positive error rate.

This chapter sets up the machinery. We define channels, give the canonical examples (BSC, BEC, Z-channel, Gaussian), define capacity, and compute it for the canonical cases. The next chapter (Chapter 6) proves Shannon's coding theorem — the deepest theorem in the book.

The AI angle in this chapter is the _noisy channel model_ of decoding: machine translation, speech recognition, even modern denoising diffusion can be viewed as channel-decoding problems. The noisy channel framework is older than the field of natural language processing, and it has resurfaced in modern guise as foundational to LLM-based decoding.

A **discrete memoryless channel** (DMC) consists of:

### 5.4 Channel Capacity


#### Definition: Channel Capacity

The **capacity** of a discrete memoryless channel with transition matrix p(y∣x)p(y \mid x)p(y∣x) is

C=max⁡p(x)I(X;Y),C = \max_{p(x)} I(X; Y),C=p(x)max​I(X;Y),

where the maximum is over all input probability distributions on X\mathcal{X}X.

In plain language, this means: capacity is the highest mutual information achievable by choosing the input distribution. It is the _supremum_ of bits-per-channel-use that can be reliably transmitted.

The operational meaning of capacity will be made precise in Chapter 6 (Shannon's channel coding theorem). For now, take as a slogan: **rates below CCC are achievable; rates above CCC are not**.

#### Properties

  1. **Non-negativity** : C≥0C \geq 0C≥0 (since I(X;Y)≥0I(X; Y) \geq 0I(X;Y)≥0 always).
  2. **Bounding** : C≤min⁡(log⁡∣X∣,log⁡∣Y∣)C \leq \min(\log |\mathcal{X}|, \log |\mathcal{Y}|)C≤min(log∣X∣,log∣Y∣). The channel cannot transmit more bits per use than its alphabets allow.
  3. **Concavity** : I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) is a concave function of p(x)p(x)p(x) for fixed p(y∣x)p(y \mid x)p(y∣x). The maximum over a convex set is attained, and the optimization is convex.

The concavity property is what makes capacity computation tractable: any local maximum is a global maximum, and standard convex-optimization techniques (Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions, the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm) compute capacity exactly.

For the BSC, by symmetry (the channel is invariant under 0↔10 \leftrightarrow 10↔1), the capacity-achieving input distribution is uniform: p(0)=p(1)=1/2p(0) = p(1) = 1/2p(0)=p(1)=1/2. Then

CBSC=1−Hb(ϵ).C_{\text{BSC}} = 1 - H_b(\epsilon).CBSC​=1−Hb​(ϵ).

* ϵ=0\epsilon = 0ϵ=0: C=1C = 1C=1 bit per use (noiseless).
* ϵ=1/2\epsilon = 1/2ϵ=1/2: C=0C = 0C=0 (random output).
* ϵ=1\epsilon = 1ϵ=1: C=1C = 1C=1 (deterministic flip).
