**Answer:** δ(p,q)≤1⋅ln⁡2/2≈0.347≈0.589\delta(p, q) \leq \sqrt{1 \cdot \ln 2 / 2} \approx \sqrt{0.347} \approx 0.589δ(p,q)≤1⋅ln2/2​≈0.347​≈0.589.

So if KL is 1 bit, total variation is at most 0.589, meaning no event differs in probability by more than 58.9 percentage points between ppp and qqq. This is a substantial gap but well below the maximum total variation of 1.

For comparison: KL of 0.1 bit gives δ≤0.186\delta \leq 0.186δ≤0.186; KL of 0.01 bit gives δ≤0.059\delta \leq 0.059δ≤0.059. The bound tightens roughly with the square root of KL.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A classifier outputs probability 0.70.70.7 on the correct class, 0.20.20.2 on a competitor, and 0.10.10.1 on a third class. The true distribution is one-hot on the correct class. What is the cross-entropy loss?

Hint

For a one-hot true distribution, cross-entropy collapses to the negative log-probability of the true label.

**Answer:** Cross-entropy: H(p,q)=−∑yp(y)log⁡q(y)=−1⋅log⁡0.7−0⋅log⁡0.2−0⋅log⁡0.1=−log⁡20.7≈0.515H(p, q) = -\sum_y p(y) \log q(y) = -1 \cdot \log 0.7 - 0 \cdot \log 0.2 - 0 \cdot \log 0.1 = -\log_2 0.7 \approx 0.515H(p,q)=−∑y​p(y)logq(y)=−1⋅log0.7−0⋅log0.2−0⋅log0.1=−log2​0.7≈0.515 bits.

This is also the self-information of the true label under the model's distribution. Minimizing this loss pushes q(correct)q(\text{correct})q(correct) toward 1, where the loss vanishes.

**Q2.** Two language models are evaluated on the same English test set. Model A achieves cross-entropy of 1.2 bits per character; Model B achieves 1.0 bits per character. (a) Which is better? (b) What is the relative compression efficiency? (c) If the entropy of English is approximately 0.9 bits per character, what KL divergence does each model have from the true distribution?

**Answer:** (a) Model B is better: lower cross-entropy means closer to the true distribution.

(b) Compression: Model A uses 1.2 bits/char; Model B uses 1.0 bits/char. Model B is 16.7% more efficient per character.

(c) KL = cross-entropy - entropy. Model A: D≈1.2−0.9=0.3D \approx 1.2 - 0.9 = 0.3D≈1.2−0.9=0.3 bits/char. Model B: D≈1.0−0.9=0.1D \approx 1.0 - 0.9 = 0.1D≈1.0−0.9=0.1 bits/char.

Both models are within a fraction of a bit of the true entropy. The gap from Model A to Model B is the same as the remaining gap from Model B to the entropy floor — meaningful but small in absolute terms.

**Q3.** Two reinforcement-learning policies, πold\pi_{\text{old}}πold​ and πnew\pi_{\text{new}}πnew​, are compared at one state. πold(a)=(0.4,0.3,0.3)\pi_{\text{old}}(a) = (0.4, 0.3, 0.3)πold​(a)=(0.4,0.3,0.3); πnew(a)=(0.7,0.2,0.1)\pi_{\text{new}}(a) = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1)πnew​(a)=(0.7,0.2,0.1). Compute their KL divergence (in nats). Is the new policy a "small" or "large" change?

Hint

D(πnew∥πold)=∑aπnew(a)log⁡[πnew(a)/πold(a)]D(\pi_{\text{new}} \| \pi_{\text{old}}) = \sum_a \pi_{\text{new}}(a) \log [\pi_{\text{new}}(a) / \pi_{\text{old}}(a)]D(πnew​∥πold​)=∑a​πnew​(a)log[πnew​(a)/πold​(a)].

**Answer:** D(πnew∥πold)=0.7ln⁡(0.7/0.4)+0.2ln⁡(0.2/0.3)+0.1ln⁡(0.1/0.3)D(\pi_{\text{new}} \| \pi_{\text{old}}) = 0.7 \ln(0.7/0.4) + 0.2 \ln(0.2/0.3) + 0.1 \ln(0.1/0.3)D(πnew​∥πold​)=0.7ln(0.7/0.4)+0.2ln(0.2/0.3)+0.1ln(0.1/0.3) =0.7⋅0.5596+0.2⋅(−0.4055)+0.1⋅(−1.0986)= 0.7 \cdot 0.5596 + 0.2 \cdot (-0.4055) + 0.1 \cdot (-1.0986)=0.7⋅0.5596+0.2⋅(−0.4055)+0.1⋅(−1.0986) ≈0.3917−0.0811−0.1099\approx 0.3917 - 0.0811 - 0.1099≈0.3917−0.0811−0.1099 ≈0.201\approx 0.201≈0.201 nats.

For PPO/TRPO with a typical KL bound of δ≈0.01\delta \approx 0.01δ≈0.01 (a small fraction of a nat), this is a _large_ update — about twenty times the trust-region threshold. PPO would scale back the update or apply clipping to constrain to within the trust region.

**Q4.** Knowledge distillation trains a student model to match a teacher's soft distribution. If the teacher outputs (0.5,0.3,0.2)(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)(0.5,0.3,0.2) and the student outputs (0.4,0.4,0.2)(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)(0.4,0.4,0.2), what is the distillation loss (KL of teacher from student)?

**Answer:** D(teacher∥student)=0.5log⁡(0.5/0.4)+0.3log⁡(0.3/0.4)+0.2log⁡(0.2/0.2)D(\text{teacher} \| \text{student}) = 0.5 \log(0.5/0.4) + 0.3 \log(0.3/0.4) + 0.2 \log(0.2/0.2)D(teacher∥student)=0.5log(0.5/0.4)+0.3log(0.3/0.4)+0.2log(0.2/0.2) =0.5⋅0.322+0.3⋅(−0.415)+0= 0.5 \cdot 0.322 + 0.3 \cdot (-0.415) + 0=0.5⋅0.322+0.3⋅(−0.415)+0 ≈0.161−0.124+0≈0.037\approx 0.161 - 0.124 + 0 \approx 0.037≈0.161−0.124+0≈0.037 bits.

The student is close to the teacher (KL of about 0.04 bits). Further training would push this toward zero. In practice, distillation losses are computed at every input across a training set and averaged.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** KL divergence is asymmetric. When would you use D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q) versus D(q∥p)D(q \| p)D(q∥p)?

**Discussion:** The choice depends on which distribution you regard as "true."

D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q) ("forward KL") penalizes assignments of low qqq-probability to outcomes with high ppp-probability. It says: "data comes from ppp; how badly does qqq describe it?" Used in maximum likelihood, language modeling, and most supervised learning.

D(q∥p)D(q \| p)D(q∥p) ("reverse KL") penalizes assignments of high qqq-probability to outcomes with low ppp-probability. It says: "model qqq generates samples; how often do they fall in regions ppp considers unlikely?" Used in variational inference (where qqq is the variational distribution and ppp is the true posterior).

The two have qualitatively different optima. Forward KL favors qqq that is "broad" (covers all of ppp's support). Reverse KL favors qqq that is "narrow" (concentrates on a single mode of ppp). For multimodal targets, this matters: forward KL produces averaged solutions; reverse KL produces single-mode solutions.

This asymmetry has practical consequences for variational autoencoders (Chapter 10): VAEs use a reverse-KL term in their loss, which is why they tend to produce somewhat blurry images (single-mode collapse) compared to GANs (which use a different divergence and tend to produce sharper but less diverse images).

**Q2.** Cross-entropy minimization is "the only natural training objective." Yet many alternatives exist (squared error, hinge loss, contrastive loss). When is cross-entropy _not_ the right choice?

**Discussion:** Cross-entropy is the right choice when:

  1. The model outputs a probability distribution.
  2. The objective is to match this distribution to the true distribution.
  3. The training data are i.i.d. samples from the true distribution.

It is _not_ the right choice when:

* The model outputs a regression value (continuous prediction). Then squared error or absolute error is natural.
* The training objective is task-specific and not a probability match. E.g., ranking losses, hinge losses for classification with margin, contrastive losses for similarity.
* The model is non-probabilistic by design (decision tree, kNN). Cross-entropy needs a probability output.

For probabilistic models with i.i.d. data, cross-entropy is essentially the only natural loss because it is equivalent to maximum likelihood. Other losses correspond to different statistical assumptions.

In modern deep learning, cross-entropy is so dominant for classification and language modeling that it is sometimes treated as the default. But for representation learning (contrastive learning), generation (GAN losses), and reinforcement learning (policy gradients), other objectives are needed and used.

**Q3.** KL divergence is one of many divergences. Why is it the "most natural"?

**Discussion:** Several axiomatic justifications exist.

  1. **Information geometry** : KL is the unique divergence (under mild conditions) that is invariant under reparametrization of the probability space. Other divergences are not so well-behaved under change of variables.

  2. **Bayesian updating** : Bayes' rule p(θ∣x)∝p(x∣θ)p(θ)p(\theta \mid x) \propto p(x \mid \theta) p(\theta)p(θ∣x)∝p(x∣θ)p(θ) is the operation that minimizes KL between prior and posterior subject to consistency with data.

3. **Maximum entropy** : distributions of maximum entropy subject to constraints are KL projections from a uniform reference. KL is the natural notion of "distance from uniform" given constraints.

  4. **Coding theory** : D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q) is exactly the redundancy of using a code optimized for qqq on data from ppp. This direct operational meaning is unique to KL.

  5. **Asymptotic statistics** : Stein's lemma in hypothesis testing identifies KL as the unique exponent governing how distinguishable two distributions are with many samples.

These are different angles on the same fact: KL is the central divergence because it has a direct operational meaning (in coding, hypothesis testing, Bayesian updating, and reparametrization invariance) that other divergences lack.

For specific applications, other divergences may be preferable. Wasserstein for optimal transport. Total variation for hypothesis testing with finite samples. χ2\chi^2χ2 for goodness-of-fit testing. But KL is the natural default in most information-theoretic and machine-learning settings.


### Connections to Subsequent Chapters

KL divergence is the central object of the rest of the book.

* **Chapter 9** generalizes KL to other divergences (Wasserstein, χ2\chi^2χ2, Hellinger) and develops information geometry.
* **Chapter 10** treats variational inference, where KL is the workhorse.
* **Chapter 11** uses KL in rate-distortion theory.
* **Chapter 13** uses KL in the information bottleneck.
* **Chapter 14** uses KL bounds in mutual information estimation.
* **Chapter 15** computes cross-entropy of language models on text.
* **Chapter 18** uses cross-entropy as the training loss of the capstone model.

A reader who has internalized this chapter — KL divergence, cross-entropy, Gibbs' inequality, Pinsker — has the foundation for all of modern machine learning theory.

* * *

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
KL divergence is the most important divergence in information theory, but it is not the only one. Different applications call for different notions of "distance" between probability distributions. Total variation is natural for hypothesis testing. Wasserstein distance underlies optimal transport and modern generative models. Hellinger distance arises in statistics. χ2\chi^2χ2 divergence appears in goodness-of-fit tests. Each of these has its own strengths, and choosing the right one for an application is a non-trivial modeling decision.

This chapter surveys the main divergences, develops the **f-divergence** framework that unifies many of them, sketches the **Wasserstein distance** and its connection to optimal transport, and outlines **information geometry** — the view that distributions form a Riemannian manifold whose local distance is given by the Fisher information metric.

The AI angle is the rise of Wasserstein distances in modern generative modeling: Wasserstein GANs by Arjovsky and collaborators in 2017 showed that distance choice has profound consequences for training stability and gradient quality, and the broader field of optimal transport has emerged as a major tool in modern ML.


### 9.1 Total Variation Distance

We met total variation in Chapter 8 in the context of Pinsker's inequality. Recall:

δ(p,q)=12∑x∣p(x)−q(x)∣=max⁡A⊆X∣p(A)−q(A)∣.\delta(p, q) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_x |p(x) - q(x)| = \max_{A \subseteq \mathcal{X}} |p(A) - q(A)|.δ(p,q)=21​x∑​∣p(x)−q(x)∣=A⊆Xmax​∣p(A)−q(A)∣.

Total variation is a true metric: symmetric, definite, satisfies the triangle inequality. It is bounded between 0 (identical distributions) and 1 (disjoint supports).


#### Operational meaning

The total variation between ppp and qqq is the maximum probability difference that any event can have. Equivalently, it is the optimal probability of correctly distinguishing ppp from qqq given a single sample, minus 1/2:

δ(p,q)=2⋅(optimal accuracy of distinguisher)−1.\delta(p, q) = 2 \cdot (\text{optimal accuracy of distinguisher}) - 1.δ(p,q)=2⋅(optimal accuracy of distinguisher)−1.

So small TV means the two distributions are statistically indistinguishable from a single sample.


#### Use cases

* **Hypothesis testing** : TV bounds the error of any test that distinguishes ppp from qqq.
* **Convergence to stationary distribution** : in Markov chain theory, TV measures how close the time-ttt distribution is to the stationary distribution. Mixing times are typically defined in terms of TV.
* **Differential privacy** : the privacy guarantee (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon, \delta)(ϵ,δ)-DP includes a TV-like term.
* **Statistical distance between datasets** : when comparing the distributions of two datasets, TV is the most directly interpretable.


### 9.2 The f-Divergence Framework

Many divergences fit into a unified framework discovered by Csiszár and Ali-Silvey in the 1960s.

#### Definition: f-Divergence

For a convex function f:(0,∞)→Rf: (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}f:(0,∞)→R with f(1)=0f(1) = 0f(1)=0, the **f-divergence** of qqq from ppp is

Df(p∥q)=∑xq(x)f(p(x)q(x)).D_f(p \| q) = \sum_x q(x) f\left(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right).Df​(p∥q)=x∑​q(x)f(q(x)p(x)​).

Choices of fff recover many familiar divergences:

Divergence | f(t)f(t)f(t)  
---|---  
KL: D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q) | tlog⁡tt \log ttlogt  
Reverse KL: D(q∥p)D(q \| p)D(q∥p) | −log⁡t-\log t−logt  
Total variation 2δ2 \delta2δ | 12∥t−1∥\frac{1}{2}\|t - 1\|21​∥t−1∥  
Jensen-Shannon | 12(tlog⁡t−(t+1)log⁡t+12)\frac{1}{2}(t \log t - (t+1) \log \frac{t+1}{2})21​(tlogt−(t+1)log2t+1​)

Hellinger squared | (t−1)2/2(\sqrt{t} - 1)^2 / 2(t​−1)2/2  
  
All f-divergences share several key properties:

  1. **Non-negativity** : Df(p∥q)≥0D_f(p \| q) \geq 0Df​(p∥q)≥0, with equality iff p=qp = qp=q (if fff is strictly convex at 1).
  2. **Joint convexity** : Df(p∥q)D_f(p \| q)Df​(p∥q) is jointly convex in (p,q)(p, q)(p,q).
  3. **Data-processing inequality** : Df(Ph(p)∥Ph(q))≤Df(p∥q)D_f(P_h(p) \| P_h(q)) \leq D_f(p \| q)Df​(Ph​(p)∥Ph​(q))≤Df​(p∥q) for any (deterministic or stochastic) post-processing hhh.
  4. **Scaling invariance** : Dcf(p∥q)=cDf(p∥q)D_{cf}(p \| q) = c D_f(p \| q)Dcf​(p∥q)=cDf​(p∥q) for c>0c > 0c>0.

These properties hold for _any_ choice of convex fff — they are structural facts about the framework, not specific to KL.


#### Hellinger distance

Hellinger distance is

dH(p,q)=12∑x(p(x)−q(x))2.d_H(p, q) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} \sum_x (\sqrt{p(x)} - \sqrt{q(x)})^2}.dH​(p,q)=21​x∑​(p(x)​−q(x)​)2​.

It is a true metric (unlike KL). It is bounded between 0 and 1. It enters statistics through likelihood theory: the Hellinger affinity ∑xp(x)q(x)\sum_x \sqrt{p(x) q(x)}∑x​p(x)q(x)​ is the inner product of likelihood roots and underlies hypothesis testing bounds.


#### χ2\chi^2χ2 divergence

χ2\chi^2χ2-divergence is ∑x(p(x)−q(x))2/q(x)\sum_x (p(x) - q(x))^2 / q(x)∑x​(p(x)−q(x))2/q(x). It is widely used in goodness-of-fit testing (Pearson's χ2\chi^2χ2 test) and in concentration inequalities. It is generally larger than KL.

The χ2\chi^2χ2 and KL divergences satisfy

D(p∥q)≤log⁡(1+χ2(p∥q))≤χ2(p∥q).D(p \| q) \leq \log(1 + \chi^2(p \| q)) \leq \chi^2(p \| q).D(p∥q)≤log(1+χ2(p∥q))≤χ2(p∥q).

So χ2\chi^2χ2 bounds KL from above, and small χ2\chi^2χ2 implies small KL.

Three lessons jump out. (i) **KL is asymmetric.** D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q) is much larger than D(q∥p)D(q \| p)D(q∥p) because qqq puts only 0.10.10.1 mass on the outcome where ppp puts 0.50.50.5; KL severely punishes qqq for being light where ppp is heavy. (ii) **χ 2\chi^2χ2 explodes when qqq is small.** The 0.10.10.1 mass in the denominator dominates the sum. (iii) **Wasserstein equals TV on a two-point space** , but they part ways the moment geometry enters: shift qqq to (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) and TV stays at 0.50.50.5 while W1W_1W1​ reflects the actual "transport distance" 0.5⋅1=0.50.5 \cdot 1 = 0.50.5⋅1=0.5; now embed the same atoms in R\mathbb{R}R at distance d(0,1)=100d(0, 1) = 100d(0,1)=100 and W1W_1W1​ jumps to 505050 while TV is unchanged. f-divergences ignore the metric on X\mathcal{X}X; Wasserstein does not.


### 9.3 Wasserstein Distance and Optimal Transport

A different family of distances arises from the geometric question: how much "work" does it take to transform one distribution into another?


#### The Earth Mover's Intuition

Imagine ppp as a pile of dirt distributed over points {x1,…,xn}\\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\\}{x1​,…,xn​} according to ppp. You want to rearrange the dirt to form a pile distributed according to qqq. The Wasserstein-1 distance is the minimum total work — total mass moved times distance moved.


#### Definition: Wasserstein-1 Distance

For distributions p,qp, qp,q on a metric space (X,d)(\mathcal{X}, d)(X,d),

W1(p,q)=inf⁡π∈Π(p,q)E(x,y)∼π[d(x,y)],W_1(p, q) = \inf_{\pi \in \Pi(p, q)} \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \pi}[d(x, y)],W1​(p,q)=π∈Π(p,q)inf​E(x,y)∼π​[d(x,y)],

where Π(p,q)\Pi(p, q)Π(p,q) is the set of all couplings — joint distributions on X×X\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X}X×X with marginals ppp and qqq.

In plain language: W1W_1W1​ is the minimum expected transport distance over all valid coupling plans.

blocks.src:
#### The Kantorovich-Rubinstein Duality

W1W_1W1​ has an elegant dual formulation:

W1(p,q)=sup⁡f:∣f∣L≤1[Ep[f(X)]−Eq[f(X)]],W_1(p, q) = \sup_{f: |f|_L \leq 1} [\mathbb{E}_p[f(X)] - \mathbb{E}_q[f(X)]],W1​(p,q)=f:∣f∣L​≤1sup​[Ep​[f(X)]−Eq​[f(X)]],

where the supremum is over all 1-Lipschitz functions fff. That is, W1W_1W1​ is the maximum difference in expected values across 1-Lipschitz observers.

This duality is the key to **Wasserstein GANs** (§9.5).


#### Wasserstein-2 and beyond

WpW_pWp​ for general p≥1p \geq 1p≥1 uses d(x,y)pd(x, y)^pd(x,y)p and a final root: Wp(p,q)=(inf⁡E[d(X,Y)p])1/pW_p(p, q) = (\inf \mathbb{E}[d(X, Y)^p])^{1/p}Wp​(p,q)=(infE[d(X,Y)p])1/p. W2W_2W2​ (squared distance) is particularly important for connections to PDEs (gradient flows in distribution space) and to optimization.


#### Why Wasserstein matters

Wasserstein has properties that f-divergences lack:

* **Behaves well with disjoint supports** : KL between two delta distributions is infinite (or undefined); Wasserstein is the distance between their supports. This makes Wasserstein useful for cases where ppp and qqq live on submanifolds that don't overlap.
* **Continuous in the geometry** : a small shift of all points in ppp yields a small Wasserstein change. KL can change discontinuously under such shifts.
* **Captures geometric structure** : Wasserstein incorporates the metric structure of the underlying space, which f-divergences do not.


### 9.4 Information Geometry

Information geometry, developed by Shun-ichi Amari starting in the 1980s, treats the space of probability distributions as a differentiable manifold and applies the tools of differential geometry.


#### The Statistical Manifold

A parametric family of distributions {pθ}θ∈Θ\\{p_\theta\\}_{\theta \in \Theta}{pθ​}θ∈Θ​ (e.g., the family of Gaussians parametrized by mean and variance) forms a manifold of dimension equal to the number of parameters. Points on the manifold are distributions; coordinates are the parameters θ\thetaθ.

The natural Riemannian metric on this manifold is the **Fisher information matrix** :

gij(θ)=Epθ[∂log⁡pθ∂θi⋅∂log⁡pθ∂θj].g_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}\left[\frac{\partial \log p_\theta}{\partial \theta_i} \cdot \frac{\partial \log p_\theta}{\partial \theta_j}\right].gij​(θ)=Epθ​​[∂θi​∂logpθ​​⋅∂θj​∂logpθ​​].

The Fisher matrix gives the local distance between nearby distributions:

D(pθ∥pθ+dθ)≈12∑i,jgij(θ) dθi dθj.D(p_{\theta} \| p_{\theta + d\theta}) \approx \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i, j} g_{ij}(\theta) \, d\theta_i \, d\theta_j.D(pθ​∥pθ+dθ​)≈21​i,j∑​gij​(θ)dθi​dθj​.

So KL divergence is the Fisher metric in infinitesimal form.


#### The Cramér-Rao Bound

A celebrated consequence of information geometry: any unbiased estimator θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ of θ\thetaθ satisfies

Var(θ^)≥1I(θ),\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \geq \frac{1}{I(\theta)},Var(θ^)≥I(θ)1​,

where I(θ)I(\theta)I(θ) is the Fisher information (the matrix gijg_{ij}gij​ collapsed for a one-parameter family). The bound is achievable: maximum-likelihood estimators saturate it asymptotically.

This is the statistical version of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle: the Fisher information bounds the precision of any unbiased estimator. It is the rigorous foundation of asymptotic statistics.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
#### The Natural Gradient

Standard gradient descent on a parametrized model uses the Euclidean gradient. The **natural gradient** developed by Amari in 1998 preconditions the gradient by the inverse Fisher matrix:

Δθnatural=−η F−1∇θL(θ),\Delta \theta_{\text{natural}} = -\eta \, F^{-1} \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta),Δθnatural​=−ηF−1∇θ​L(θ),

where FFF is the Fisher matrix at θ\thetaθ. The natural gradient is invariant under reparametrization: changing parameters does not change the optimization trajectory.

In deep learning, the natural gradient is impractically expensive to compute exactly (the Fisher matrix has dimension equal to the square of the parameter count, which is 101210^{12}1012 or more for frontier models). Approximations such as K-FAC (Kronecker-factored approximate curvature), Shampoo, and AdaHessian capture some of its benefits and are used in production systems for very large models.


#### The Bregman Divergence Picture

Many divergences (including KL) are special cases of **Bregman divergences** , defined for a convex function ϕ\phiϕ:

Dϕ(p∥q)=ϕ(p)−ϕ(q)−∇ϕ(q)⋅(p−q).D_\phi(p \| q) = \phi(p) - \phi(q) - \nabla \phi(q) \cdot (p - q).Dϕ​(p∥q)=ϕ(p)−ϕ(q)−∇ϕ(q)⋅(p−q).

KL corresponds to ϕ(p)=∑pilog⁡pi\phi(p) = \sum p_i \log p_iϕ(p)=∑pi​logpi​ (the negative entropy). Squared Euclidean distance corresponds to ϕ(p)=12∥p∥2\phi(p) = \frac{1}{2} \|p\|^2ϕ(p)=21​∥p∥2. χ2\chi^2χ2 corresponds to a different convex function.

Bregman divergences have the geometric interpretation as the gap between a convex function and its tangent hyperplane. They are not in general symmetric and do not satisfy the triangle inequality, but they are well-behaved in many other ways.

The Bregman divergence framework unifies information theory (KL), classical statistics (squared error), and convex optimization. It is one of the deepest organizing concepts in machine learning theory.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
### 9.5 An AI Connection: Wasserstein GANs and the Distance Choice

Generative adversarial networks introduced by Goodfellow and collaborators in 2014 train two neural networks against each other: a **generator** that produces fake samples, and a **discriminator** that distinguishes real from fake. The original GAN (vanilla GAN) implicitly minimizes Jensen-Shannon divergence between the generator distribution and the data distribution.

Vanilla GANs are notoriously unstable to train. The discriminator's gradient often vanishes — when the discriminator becomes too good, it provides no useful signal to the generator. The mathematical reason: when the generator and data distributions have disjoint supports (which happens when the generator is poorly initialized or stuck in a bad mode), JS divergence is locally constant (saturates at log⁡2\log 2log2), so its gradient is zero.

**Wasserstein GANs** by Arjovsky and collaborators in 2017 solve this by replacing JS with the Wasserstein-1 distance. By the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, training a Wasserstein GAN amounts to finding the 1-Lipschitz function fff (parametrized by the discriminator) that maximizes Epdata[f]−Epgen[f]\mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{data}}}[f] - \mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{gen}}}[f]Epdata​​[f]−Epgen​​[f]. Because Wasserstein distance does not saturate when supports are disjoint, the generator always has a meaningful gradient to follow.

The change of distance fundamentally changes training dynamics. WGANs are vastly more stable than vanilla GANs, and the gradient norm of the loss is meaningful (it correlates with image quality).

The lesson: **the choice of divergence is a modeling decision with real consequences**. Different divergences emphasize different aspects of distribution-matching, and using the wrong one for your problem can derail training entirely.

This was a watershed moment in modern generative modeling. The community started thinking carefully about what it meant to "match distributions" and how the choice of distance affected the resulting models. Variational autoencoders use a (reverse) KL term in their loss; vanilla GANs use JS; Wasserstein GANs use W1W_1W1​; diffusion models use a denoising score-matching objective that, under interpretation, minimizes a particular divergence in the score-function space.

In summary: **modern generative modeling is, in large part, the engineering of divergence-minimization at scale**.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
### Common Misconception

* **Misconception** : "All divergences are essentially equivalent."

No. Different divergences have different topologies, different asymptotic behaviors, and different gradient properties. The choice matters significantly in practice.

* **Misconception** : "Wasserstein distance is just a metric — there is nothing 'information theoretic' about it."

Wasserstein has deep connections to information theory through its dual formulation (Kantorovich-Rubinstein) and through its appearance in rate-distortion theory (Chapter 11). It is _not_ a member of the f-divergence family. f-divergences and integral probability metrics (IPMs, of which Wasserstein-1 is the canonical example) are two distinct frameworks, with the only divergence in their intersection being total variation up to a constant. The information-theoretic content of Wasserstein lives in the IPM side: it is the supremum of mean differences over a class of test functions, which itself has hypothesis-testing interpretations.

* **Misconception** : "Information geometry is just abstract math without practical consequences."

Information geometry directly informs the natural gradient, used in many practical training schemes. The Cramér-Rao bound is the foundation of asymptotic statistics. Modern deep learning optimizers (K-FAC, Shampoo) are direct descendants of natural-gradient ideas.


### Chapter Summary

This chapter widened the divergence toolkit beyond KL:

* **Total variation** : a true metric; bounds the error of any hypothesis test.
* **f-divergences** : the unifying framework (KL, JS, χ2\chi^2χ2, Hellinger, TV are all instances). Share key properties (non-negativity, joint convexity, data-processing inequality).
* **Wasserstein** : optimal-transport distance; geometric in nature; well-behaved when supports are disjoint.
* **Information geometry** : distributions as Riemannian manifolds; Fisher information as local metric; natural gradient as reparametrization-invariant optimization.
* **Bregman divergences** : unify KL, squared error, and many others under convex-function gaps.

The AI angle: Wasserstein GANs showed that divergence choice matters profoundly for training stability. Modern generative modeling is engineering of divergence-minimization at scale.

The next chapter applies KL and divergences to variational inference: the engine of Bayesian deep learning.

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Compute the Hellinger distance between p=(0.5,0.5)p = (0.5, 0.5)p=(0.5,0.5) and q=(0.9,0.1)q = (0.9, 0.1)q=(0.9,0.1).

**Q3.** State the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. Why is it useful for training Wasserstein GANs?

**Answer:** W1(p,q)=sup⁡∣f∣L≤1[Epf−Eqf]W_1(p, q) = \sup_{|f|_L \leq 1} [\mathbb{E}_p f - \mathbb{E}_q f]W1​(p,q)=sup∣f∣L​≤1​[Ep​f−Eq​f].

Useful for Wasserstein GANs because the supremum can be approximated by parametrizing fff as a neural network with Lipschitz constraints (typically enforced via gradient penalty or weight clipping). The discriminator becomes the Lipschitz function fff, and the generator is trained to minimize Epf−Eqf\mathbb{E}_p f - \mathbb{E}_q fEp​f−Eq​f. This avoids the saturation problem of JS-based GANs.

**Q4.** What is the Fisher information of a Gaussian N(μ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)N(μ,σ2) with respect to μ\muμ?

Hint

I(μ)=E[(∂log⁡p/∂μ)2]I(\mu) = \mathbb{E}[(\partial \log p / \partial \mu)^2]I(μ)=E[(∂logp/∂μ)2].

**Answer:** For p(x;μ)=12πσ2exp⁡(−(x−μ)2/(2σ2))p(x; \mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp(-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2))p(x;μ)=2πσ2​1​exp(−(x−μ)2/(2σ2)): ∂log⁡p/∂μ=(x−μ)/σ2\partial \log p / \partial \mu = (x - \mu) / \sigma^2∂logp/∂μ=(x−μ)/σ2. I(μ)=E[(X−μ)2/σ4]=σ2/σ4=1/σ2I(\mu) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2 / \sigma^4] = \sigma^2 / \sigma^4 = 1/\sigma^2I(μ)=E[(X−μ)2/σ4]=σ2/σ4=1/σ2.

The Fisher information is the inverse variance. The Cramér-Rao bound says any unbiased estimator of μ\muμ has variance at least σ2/n\sigma^2 / nσ2/n for nnn samples — exactly what the sample mean achieves. So the sample mean is asymptotically efficient (saturates the CR bound).

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Consider two normal distributions N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0, 1)N(0,1) and N(μ,1)\mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)N(μ,1). Compute the KL divergence and the Wasserstein-2 distance.

Hint

KL: D(N(μ1,σ12)∥N(μ2,σ22))=12[σ12σ22+(μ2−μ1)2σ22−1+log⁡(σ22/σ12)]D(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2) \| \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)) = \frac{1}{2}[\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_2^2} + \frac{(\mu_2 - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma_2^2} - 1 + \log(\sigma_2^2/\sigma_1^2)]D(N(μ1​,σ12​)∥N(μ2​,σ22​))=21​[σ22​σ12​​+σ22​(μ2​−μ1​)2​−1+log(σ22​/σ12​)]. **Q2.** A goodness-of-fit test computes χ2(pempirical∥pmodel)\chi^2(p_{\text{empirical}} \| p_{\text{model}})χ2(pempirical​∥pmodel​) for an empirical histogram of 1000 samples versus a hypothesized uniform distribution on 10 categories. Two settings: (a) pempiricalp_{\text{empirical}}pempirical​ matches the uniform exactly. (b) pempiricalp_{\text{empirical}}pempirical​ has counts (200, 100, 100, ..., 100). What is χ2\chi^2χ2 in each case?

**Answer:** (a) χ2=0\chi^2 = 0χ2=0 (perfect match: every observed probability equals the model's 0.1).

(b) Read the question's "(200, 100, 100, ..., 100)" as cell counts that have been _renormalized_ to sum to 1000 — concretely, 200 in one cell and 800/9≈88.89800/9 \approx 88.89800/9≈88.89 in each of the remaining nine. The probability vector is then pobs=(0.2,800/9000,…)≈(0.2,0.0889,…)p_{\text{obs}} = (0.2, 800/9000, \ldots) \approx (0.2, 0.0889, \ldots)pobs​=(0.2,800/9000,…)≈(0.2,0.0889,…). χ2(pobs∥pmodel)=∑i(pobs,i−0.1)20.1=(0.2−0.1)20.1+9⋅(0.0889−0.1)20.1≈0.1+0.0011≈0.101.\chi^2(p_{\text{obs}} \| p_{\text{model}}) = \sum_i \frac{(p_{\text{obs}, i} - 0.1)^2}{0.1} = \frac{(0.2 - 0.1)^2}{0.1} + 9 \cdot \frac{(0.0889 - 0.1)^2}{0.1} \approx 0.1 + 0.0011 \approx 0.101.χ2(pobs​∥pmodel​)=i∑​0.1(pobs,i​−0.1)2​=0.1(0.2−0.1)2​+9⋅0.1(0.0889−0.1)2​≈0.1+0.0011≈0.101.

Multiplied by the sample size n=1000n = 1000n=1000, the scaled Pearson statistic is nχ2≈101n \chi^2 \approx 101nχ2≈101. With 9 degrees of freedom, this rejects the uniform null at any reasonable significance level. The empirical distribution deviates substantially from uniform — driven almost entirely by the one over-represented cell.

**Q3.** A neural network has 100 million parameters. The Fisher information matrix is 101610^{16}1016 entries. Why is exact natural gradient infeasible, and what approximations are used?

**Answer:** Exact natural gradient requires inverting (or solving with) a 108×10810^8 \times 10^8108×108 matrix at each step. Storage is 101610^{16}1016 numbers (e.g., 64 PB), and inversion is O(n3)=1024O(n^3) = 10^{24}O(n3)=1024 operations — infeasible.

Practical approximations:

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
* **Diagonal Fisher** : approximate FFF by its diagonal (Adam, RMSprop). Cheap but loses cross-parameter curvature.
* **Block-diagonal Fisher (K-FAC)** : approximate FFF by Kronecker factors per layer. Captures within-layer curvature.
* **Shampoo, AdaHessian** : use higher-order moments and Kronecker factors.
* **Gauss-Newton approximation** : for least-squares losses, replaces Hessian with Jacobian-products.

These approximations make natural-gradient-style methods practical at scale and yield consistent improvements in convergence speed for many models.

**Q4.** Compare KL and Wasserstein for distributions concentrated on disjoint supports: ppp is a delta on 0, qqq is a delta on 1. What does each give?

**Answer:** KL: D(p∥q)=∞D(p \| q) = \inftyD(p∥q)=∞ (since ppp puts mass on 0 where qqq is zero). D(q∥p)=∞D(q \| p) = \inftyD(q∥p)=∞ similarly.

Wasserstein-1: W1(p,q)=∣0−1∣=1W_1(p, q) = |0 - 1| = 1W1​(p,q)=∣0−1∣=1 (transport one unit of mass over distance 1).

Wasserstein gives a finite, sensible answer. KL refuses to compare. This is why Wasserstein is preferred when distributions may be on submanifolds with disjoint or near-disjoint supports — exactly the situation in early GAN training, where the generator distribution is a manifold of dimension less than the ambient image space.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** When should you prefer Wasserstein over KL?

**Discussion:** Use Wasserstein when:

* Distributions have disjoint or near-disjoint supports.
* The geometric structure of the space matters (a small spatial shift should yield a small distance).
* You need a true metric (Wasserstein satisfies the triangle inequality).
* You want stable gradients in adversarial training.

Use KL when:

* You are doing maximum likelihood.
* You want an information-theoretic interpretation (bits).
* The distributions have the same support.
* You need analytical tractability (KL has nice closed forms for Gaussians, exponential families).

In modern ML, both are used heavily. The pragmatic question is often: which gives stable training and good final performance for my specific task? Empirical comparison often resolves the question.

**Q2.** Information geometry treats distributions as a Riemannian manifold. What is gained, philosophically, by this perspective?

**Discussion:** Several gains.

  1. **Coordinate independence** : a result expressed in terms of intrinsic geometric quantities (geodesics, curvature) does not depend on the choice of parametrization. A natural gradient method, for instance, gives the same trajectory regardless of how the parameters are reparametrized.

  2. **Conceptual clarity** : many results that look ad hoc in coordinates become natural in geometry. The Cramér-Rao bound is the statement that the variance of an estimator is bounded by the inverse local metric.

  3. **Algorithm design** : optimization algorithms that respect the manifold structure (like the natural gradient) often outperform those that don't.

  4. **Cross-disciplinary connections** : information geometry connects to physics (statistical mechanics), economics (decision theory), and biology (replicator dynamics), revealing that diverse fields are studying aspects of the same Riemannian structure.

The downside: information geometry is mathematically demanding, and many practitioners can do their work without it. It is more of an organizing perspective than a daily tool.

**Q3.** Wasserstein GANs solved the gradient saturation problem of vanilla GANs. But they introduced new challenges. What are they?

**Discussion:** Wasserstein GANs require the discriminator (now called the "critic") to be 1-Lipschitz. Enforcing this constraint is non-trivial. Original WGAN used **weight clipping** : bound the absolute value of every weight by a small constant. This is crude and limits the critic's expressiveness.

WGAN-GP Gulrajani and collaborators in 2017 introduced a **gradient penalty** : add a term to the loss that penalizes the norm of the critic's gradient at random interpolated points. This is a cleaner enforcement of Lipschitzness and is the standard technique today.

Other challenges:

* **Critic convergence** : WGAN requires the critic to be near-optimal at each generator step. This needs more critic updates per generator update than vanilla GAN.
* **Computational cost** : gradient penalty requires extra backward passes through the critic.
* **Mode collapse** : while WGAN reduces mode collapse, it doesn't eliminate it; some architectures and training tricks remain necessary.

The lesson: solving one problem (gradient saturation) often introduces others (Lipschitz enforcement). The art of generative modeling is largely the engineering of trade-offs between these issues.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Information Geometry and Other Divergences
blocks.src:
### Connections to Subsequent Chapters

This chapter widened the divergence toolkit. The next chapter applies it.

* **Chapter 10** : variational inference uses KL (and ELBO maximization).
* **Chapter 11** : rate-distortion uses Wasserstein-like arguments for continuous distortion.
* **Chapter 13** : information bottleneck uses mutual information (a KL).
* **Chapter 14** : MI estimation uses lower bounds on KL.

A reader who has finished this chapter has the divergence vocabulary needed for the rest of the book.

* * *

---

Bayesian probabilistic modeling has a beautiful structure but a hard computational core. Given a model with latent variables zzz and observed data xxx, the posterior p(z∣x)p(z \mid x)p(z∣x) is the object we want: the distribution over the unknowns given what we have seen. By Bayes' rule, p(z∣x)=p(x,z)/p(x)p(z \mid x) = p(x, z) / p(x)p(z∣x)=p(x,z)/p(x), and the denominator p(x)=∫p(x,z) dzp(x) = \int p(x, z) \, dzp(x)=∫p(x,z)dz is, in general, intractable.

The history of computational Bayesian statistics is, in large part, the history of approximations to this intractable integral. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approximates by sampling. **Variational inference** approximates by optimization: find a tractable distribution qϕ(z)q_\phi(z)qϕ​(z) that is "as close as possible" to the true posterior p(z∣x)p(z \mid x)p(z∣x), where "as close as possible" means minimizing a KL divergence.

This chapter develops the variational framework, derives the **Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)** , and applies it to a classic example (Gaussian mixture inference) and a modern one (the variational autoencoder). The connection to information theory is direct: variational inference is KL minimization, and the ELBO decomposes into reconstruction (cross-entropy) and regularization (KL) terms.

The AI angle is the central role variational methods play in modern Bayesian deep learning. VAEs, normalizing flows, Bayesian neural networks, and many other techniques all rest on the variational framework.


### 10.1 The Setup: Latent-Variable Models

A latent-variable model has:

* **Observed variables** xxx: what we measure.
* **Latent variables** zzz: hidden quantities we want to infer.
* **Joint distribution** p(x,z)=p(z)p(x∣z)p(x, z) = p(z) p(x \mid z)p(x,z)=p(z)p(x∣z), specified by: 
    * **Prior** p(z)p(z)p(z): our beliefs about zzz before seeing xxx.
    * **Likelihood** p(x∣z)p(x \mid z)p(x∣z): how xxx depends on zzz.

By Bayes' rule, the posterior is

p(z∣x)=p(x∣z)p(z)p(x)=p(x,z)p(x),p(z \mid x) = \frac{p(x \mid z) p(z)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(x, z)}{p(x)},p(z∣x)=p(x)p(x∣z)p(z)​=p(x)p(x,z)​,

and the **evidence** (marginal likelihood) is

p(x)=∫p(x,z) dz.p(x) = \int p(x, z) \, dz.p(x)=∫p(x,z)dz.

For most interesting models, this integral is intractable: the latent space is high-dimensional, or the likelihood is non-conjugate to the prior, or the joint involves a neural network that defies analytical integration.


#### Examples

* **Gaussian mixture model** : zzz is the cluster index (categorical), xxx is the observation (Gaussian conditional on cluster). Inference: which cluster does each observation belong to?
* **Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)** : zzz is the topic distribution per document and topic per word. Inference: what topics are present in this document?
* **Variational autoencoder (VAE)** : zzz is a continuous latent code; xxx is an image. Inference: what code generated this image?
* **Bayesian neural network** : zzz are the network weights; xxx is the data. Inference: what weight distribution is consistent with the data?

In all cases, the marginal p(x)p(x)p(x) is the key intractable object.

### 10.2 The Variational Framework

The variational approach: instead of computing p(z∣x)p(z \mid x)p(z∣x) directly, find a tractable distribution qϕ(z)q_\phi(z)qϕ​(z) (parametrized by ϕ\phiϕ) that approximates it.

The "tractable" family is chosen for computational convenience: typically a factorized distribution (mean-field), a Gaussian, or a neural-network-parametrized distribution.

We want qϕ(z)q_\phi(z)qϕ​(z) to be as close to p(z∣x)p(z \mid x)p(z∣x) as possible. The natural distance is KL:

ϕ∗=arg⁡min⁡ϕD(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣x)).\phi^* = \arg\min_\phi D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z \mid x)).ϕ∗=argϕmin​D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z∣x)).

But p(z∣x)p(z \mid x)p(z∣x) is intractable, so we cannot compute this KL directly. The variational trick: **rewrite the KL using the joint distribution**.

D(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣x))=Eqϕ[log⁡qϕ(z)−log⁡p(z∣x)]=Eqϕ[log⁡qϕ(z)−log⁡p(x,z)+log⁡p(x)].D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z \mid x)) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log q_\phi(z) - \log p(z \mid x)] = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log q_\phi(z) - \log p(x, z) + \log p(x)].D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z∣x))=Eqϕ​​[logqϕ​(z)−logp(z∣x)]=Eqϕ​​[logqϕ​(z)−logp(x,z)+logp(x)].

Rearranging:

log⁡p(x)=D(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣x))+Eqϕ[log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qϕ(z)].\log p(x) = D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z \mid x)) + \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p(x, z) - \log q_\phi(z)].logp(x)=D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z∣x))+Eqϕ​​[logp(x,z)−logqϕ​(z)].

Define the **Evidence Lower Bound** :

ELBO(qϕ)=Eqϕ[log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qϕ(z)]=log⁡p(x)−D(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣x)).\text{ELBO}(q_\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p(x, z) - \log q_\phi(z)] = \log p(x) - D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z \mid x)).ELBO(qϕ​)=Eqϕ​​[logp(x,z)−logqϕ​(z)]=logp(x)−D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z∣x)).

Two crucial observations:

This is the variational trick: the intractable problem (minimize KL to the true posterior) becomes the tractable problem (maximize the ELBO).


#### Decomposition of the ELBO

ELBO(qϕ)=Eqϕ[log⁡p(x∣z)]−D(qϕ(z)∥p(z)).\text{ELBO}(q_\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p(x \mid z)] - D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z)).ELBO(qϕ​)=Eqϕ​​[logp(x∣z)]−D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z)).

This decomposes the ELBO into:

* **Reconstruction term** Eqϕ[log⁡p(x∣z)]\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p(x \mid z)]Eqϕ​​[logp(x∣z)]: how well the latent code zzz (sampled from qϕq_\phiqϕ​) explains the data xxx. This is the negative cross-entropy of the model's likelihood under the variational posterior.
* **Regularization term** D(qϕ(z)∥p(z))D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z))D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z)): how far the variational posterior is from the prior. This is a KL divergence from the prior.

The first term encourages the variational posterior to put mass on codes that explain the data well. The second penalizes deviation from the prior. The trade-off is the rate-distortion view of the problem (which we will see explicitly in Chapter 11).

#### When the variational family doesn't include the truth

For a non-conjugate model where the true posterior is, say, a mixture of Gaussians, the variational family of single Gaussians cannot match it. The ELBO maximum gives the "best Gaussian approximation" to the true posterior — a single Gaussian centered on one of the modes, typically. This **mode-seeking** behavior is a characteristic of the reverse-KL objective and is one of the practical tradeoffs of variational inference.

### 10.4 The Variational Autoencoder

The Variational Autoencoder (VAE), introduced by Kingma and Welling in 2013, is the canonical modern application of variational inference.


#### Setup

* Observed: an image xxx (e.g., 28x28 MNIST digit).
* Latent: a low-dimensional code zzz (e.g., z∈R10z \in \mathbb{R}^{10}z∈R10).
* Prior: p(z)=N(0,I)p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)p(z)=N(0,I) standard Gaussian.
* Likelihood: pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x \mid z)pθ​(x∣z) is a neural network ("decoder") mapping zzz to a distribution over images.
* Variational posterior: qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x) is a neural network ("encoder") mapping xxx to a distribution over codes (typically Gaussian: qϕ(z∣x)=N(μϕ(x),σϕ2(x))q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \sigma_\phi^2(x))qϕ​(z∣x)=N(μϕ​(x),σϕ2​(x))).


#### Training objective

The ELBO per data point:

ELBO(x;θ,ϕ)=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]−D(qϕ(z∣x)∥p(z)).\text{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - D(q_\phi(z \mid x) \| p(z)).ELBO(x;θ,ϕ)=Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]−D(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)).

Maximize this over (θ,ϕ)(\theta, \phi)(θ,ϕ). The reconstruction term encourages the decoder to reproduce xxx from samples of qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x). The KL term regularizes the encoded distribution toward the prior.

#### The reparametrization trick

A practical issue: sampling z∼qϕ(z∣x)z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)z∼qϕ​(z∣x) is non-differentiable in ϕ\phiϕ, which prevents backpropagation. Solution: rewrite the sample as a deterministic function of ϕ\phiϕ and a noise variable:

z=μϕ(x)+σϕ(x)⋅ϵ,ϵ∼N(0,I).z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \cdot \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).z=μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⋅ϵ,ϵ∼N(0,I).

Now zzz is differentiable in ϕ\phiϕ, and the gradient flows through. This **reparametrization trick** proposed independently by Kingma in 2013 and Rezende and colleagues in 2014 is what makes VAE training practical.


#### Operational view: a learned compressor

The VAE can be understood as a learned compression scheme. The encoder maps an image to a compact code (with some uncertainty); the decoder reconstructs from the code. The rate is the KL term (in bits, this is the average number of bits per example to specify the code in the prior). The distortion is the reconstruction error.

This is an explicit rate-distortion picture, which Chapter 11 will treat in full. For now, note that the VAE is solving a rate-distortion problem at the population level: minimize total loss = rate + distortion, with the trade-off implicit.


#### β\betaβ-VAE

A modification introduced by Higgins and collaborators in 2017 introduces a hyperparameter β\betaβ:

L=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]−β⋅D(qϕ(z∣x)∥p(z)).\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - \beta \cdot D(q_\phi(z \mid x) \| p(z)).L=Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]−β⋅D(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)).

For β=1\beta = 1β=1, this is the standard VAE. For β>1\beta > 1β>1, more weight on regularization; for β<1\beta < 1β<1, more weight on reconstruction.

The β\betaβ-VAE is a Lagrangian view of the rate-distortion trade-off. Different β\betaβ yield different points on the rate-distortion curve. Empirically, larger β\betaβ tends to produce more disentangled latent representations.


### 10.5 Beyond VAE: Modern Variational Methods

The variational framework extends well beyond the VAE.


#### Normalizing flows

A normalizing flow proposed by Rezende in 2015 and Dinh and collaborators in 2016 parametrizes a complex distribution as a sequence of invertible transformations of a simple base distribution (typically Gaussian). The change of variables formula gives

log⁡pθ(x)=log⁡pbase(z)−∑ilog⁡∣det⁡Ji∣,\log p_\theta(x) = \log p_{\text{base}}(z) - \sum_i \log |\det J_i|,logpθ​(x)=logpbase​(z)−i∑​log∣detJi​∣,

where z=f−1(x)z = f^{-1}(x)z=f−1(x) and JiJ_iJi​ are the Jacobians of each layer.

This gives a tractable density model with exact likelihoods — no ELBO bound needed. Architectures like RealNVP, Glow, and various neural ODE flows have produced strong density estimators. For images, however, GANs and diffusion models have surpassed flows in sample quality.

#### Bayesian deep learning

A Bayesian neural network treats the network weights as random variables with a prior. The posterior over weights given data is intractable, but variational approximations make Bayesian inference at neural-network scale tractable.

The "weight uncertainty" in Bayesian neural networks gives calibrated predictive uncertainty: the model knows what it doesn't know. This is valuable for safety-critical applications (medical imaging, autonomous driving) where overconfident wrong predictions are costly.

Practical Bayesian neural networks: variational Bayes (Bayes by Backprop), Monte Carlo Dropout, deep ensembles. Each is a variational approximation of a different form.


#### Diffusion models as variational

Modern diffusion models can be derived as variational models with a specific (fixed) forward noising process and a learned reverse process. The training objective is a hierarchical ELBO summed over noise levels. The connection between diffusion and variational methods is recent and elegantly unifies these two streams of generative modeling.


### 10.6 An AI Connection: ELBO as Information Theory

The ELBO has a clean information-theoretic reading.

Decomposed as ELBO=Eq[log⁡p(x∣z)]−D(q(z)∥p(z))\text{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x \mid z)] - D(q(z) \| p(z))ELBO=Eq​[logp(x∣z)]−D(q(z)∥p(z)):

* The reconstruction term Eq[log⁡p(x∣z)]\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x \mid z)]Eq​[logp(x∣z)] is the negative cross-entropy of the data given the code.
* The KL term D(q(z)∥p(z))D(q(z) \| p(z))D(q(z)∥p(z)) is the rate at which the code is described, measured against the prior.

So:

**ELBO = -distortion - rate.**

Maximizing the ELBO is minimizing the rate-distortion objective: code data at low rate (close to the prior) while keeping distortion (negative log-likelihood) low.

This is exactly the rate-distortion picture of Chapter 11, and it tells us that variational inference is, at root, lossy compression of the latent code.

For a generic latent-variable model, the maximum ELBO over variational families gives a lower bound on log⁡p(x)\log p(x)logp(x) — i.e., an upper bound on the _unachievable_ compression rate. This is a deep operational interpretation: variational inference quantifies how compressible the data are under a particular model class.

### 10.7 Historical Note: From EM to ELBO

The variational perspective on Bayesian inference has a long pedigree. The expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm of Dempster, Laird, and Rubin (1977) can be read in retrospect as a coordinate-ascent algorithm on the ELBO: the E-step computes the posterior q(z∣x)q(z \mid x)q(z∣x), the M-step maximizes the joint log-likelihood under that posterior. EM was developed for missing-data problems and only later recognized as variational inference avant la lettre.

The modern formulation, calling it "variational" and writing the ELBO explicitly, emerged in the 1990s through the work of Michael Jordan, Tommi Jaakkola, Lawrence Saul, and others, often in the context of graphical models and mean-field approximations. Wainwright and Jordan's 2008 monograph _Graphical Models, Exponential Families, and Variational Inference_ codified the framework as a unified approach to approximate inference.

The variational autoencoder (Kingma and Welling, 2013; Rezende, Mohamed, and Wierstra, 2014) was the breakthrough that brought variational methods into deep learning. Both papers appeared within months of each other and made the same conceptual move: parametrize the variational posterior with a neural network, use the reparametrization trick for stochastic gradient estimation. The VAE became the canonical example of how a 1990s statistical technique could be revived by combining it with neural networks.

A characteristic feature of variational inference's history: the same mathematical structure has been rediscovered in different communities (statistical physics' mean-field theory, control theory's KL-divergence costs, message-passing in coding theory) and only later recognized as one framework. Variational ideas seem to have a habit of being reinvented every fifteen years.


### Common Misconception

* **Misconception** : "Variational inference is just an approximation; MCMC is exact."

Both are approximations in practice. MCMC is asymptotically exact (as samples grow), but with finite samples, it is biased and noisy. Variational inference is structurally biased (constrained to the variational family) but converges quickly. Choose based on what you can afford: VI for fast approximate posteriors at scale; MCMC for high-fidelity inference at smaller scale.

* **Misconception** : "The ELBO is a single number you maximize."

The ELBO is a _function_ of the variational parameters ϕ\phiϕ. You maximize it over ϕ\phiϕ to get a posterior approximation. The maximum value of the ELBO is a lower bound on log-evidence, useful for model selection.

* **Misconception** : "VAEs reconstruct images perfectly."

VAEs typically produce somewhat blurry images. This is a consequence of the variational objective (mode-seeking reverse KL) and the typically Gaussian decoder (which is L2-loss equivalent). For sharp images, GANs or diffusion models are preferred.

### Chapter Summary

Variational inference is the optimization-based approach to Bayesian computation. It approximates the intractable posterior p(z∣x)p(z \mid x)p(z∣x) by a tractable variational distribution qϕ(z)q_\phi(z)qϕ​(z), found by maximizing the ELBO:

ELBO(qϕ)=Eqϕ[log⁡p(x∣z)]−D(qϕ(z)∥p(z))=log⁡p(x)−D(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣x)).\text{ELBO}(q_\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p(x \mid z)] - D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z)) = \log p(x) - D(q_\phi(z) \| p(z \mid x)).ELBO(qϕ​)=Eqϕ​​[logp(x∣z)]−D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z))=logp(x)−D(qϕ​(z)∥p(z∣x)).

Maximizing the ELBO equals minimizing KL to the true posterior. The decomposition is rate-distortion in disguise: the reconstruction term is negative distortion; the KL term is rate.

Modern variational methods include the variational autoencoder (VAE), normalizing flows, Bayesian neural networks, and (in a recent unification) diffusion models. All rest on the same ELBO machinery introduced here.

The next chapter develops rate-distortion theory in full, making the rate-distortion view of VAE explicit and connecting to lossy compression.

KL term D(qϕ(z∣x)∥p(z))D(q_\phi(z \mid x) \| p(z))D(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)): KL divergence of the encoder's output from the prior. Measures how "different" the encoded distribution is from the prior. Smaller is better.

The trade-off: better reconstruction often requires more "spread" in the encoder distribution (more bits used), which increases the KL. The ELBO chooses the optimal balance.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A VAE is trained on MNIST. The reconstruction loss is 100 nats per image (i.e., Eq[log⁡p(x∣z)]≈−100\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x \mid z)] \approx -100Eq​[logp(x∣z)]≈−100 on the training set). The KL term averages 30 nats per image. What is the ELBO?

**Answer:** ELBO=Eq[log⁡p(x∣z)]−D(q∥p)=−100−30=−130\text{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x \mid z)] - D(q \| p) = -100 - 30 = -130ELBO=Eq​[logp(x∣z)]−D(q∥p)=−100−30=−130 nats per image.

Lower bound on log-evidence: log⁡p(x)≥−130\log p(x) \geq -130logp(x)≥−130 nats. The actual log-evidence is at least -130 nats per image; the gap is the KL of qqq from the true posterior.

**Q2.** Two VAEs are compared. Both achieve the same ELBO of -100 nats. Model A has reconstruction loss -90 nats and KL 10 nats; Model B has reconstruction loss -50 nats and KL 50 nats. Which is better, and for what?

**Answer:** Same ELBO means the same lower bound on log-evidence. They are equivalent in this sense.

But operationally:

* Model A has lower KL — its codes are close to the prior, so sampling from the prior gives codes that the decoder "recognizes." Better for _generation_ (sampling new images).
* Model B has higher KL — its codes are far from the prior. Sampling from the prior may give codes the decoder doesn't reconstruct well. But it has better reconstruction, meaning it captures more of the data's structure in the code. Better for _reconstruction_ (autoencoding existing images).

This trade-off is the rate-distortion view: Model A is at a low-rate, high-distortion point; Model B is at a high-rate, low-distortion point. Both are valid choices depending on the goal.

**Q3.** A Bayesian neural network on a 1000-class classification task uses variational inference with a Gaussian variational posterior over weights. The KL term is enormous (millions of nats). Why? What does this say about the practical trade-off?

**Answer:** The KL term is large because the variational posterior is far from the prior, which is what we want — the data has informed the weights significantly. With a vague prior over millions of weights, the KL grows roughly with the number of weights times their effective shift.

The practical trade-off: a strong prior (small KL allowed) means the posterior stays close to the prior, sacrificing fit to data. A weak prior allows large KL but grants the model flexibility. Hyperparameter tuning involves balancing these effects.

This is a major reason Bayesian neural networks are computationally challenging at scale: getting the prior right and the variational family expressive is a delicate engineering problem.

**Q4.** Describe how to use a trained VAE to (a) reconstruct a test image and (b) generate a new image.

**Answer:** (a) Reconstruction: encode the test image to get μϕ(x),σϕ(x)\mu_\phi(x), \sigma_\phi(x)μϕ​(x),σϕ​(x); sample (or take the mean) zzz from qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x); decode to get reconstructed image x^∼pθ(x∣z)\hat{x} \sim p_\theta(x \mid z)x^∼pθ​(x∣z). The reconstruction is determined by the encoder-decoder pipeline.

(b) Generation: sample z∼p(z)z \sim p(z)z∼p(z) (the prior, e.g., N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I)); decode to get x∼pθ(x∣z)x \sim p_\theta(x \mid z)x∼pθ​(x∣z). The new image is generated from the prior.

For generation to work well, the variational posterior must "match" the prior in some sense (small KL term ensures this). Otherwise, samples from the prior may give codes the decoder hasn't seen and produce poor samples.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Variational inference uses _reverse_ KL: D(q∥p)D(q \| p)D(q∥p). Maximum likelihood and most cross-entropy losses use _forward_ KL: D(p∥q)D(p \| q)D(p∥q). Why the asymmetry?

**Discussion:** The choice is dictated by computability. Forward KL D(p∥q)=Ep[log⁡p−log⁡q]D(p \| q) = \mathbb{E}_p[\log p - \log q]D(p∥q)=Ep​[logp−logq] requires sampling from ppp, but ppp is the unknown true distribution — we have only data samples from it (which is fine for ML, where you're computing an empirical KL).

Reverse KL D(q∥p)=Eq[log⁡q−log⁡p]D(q \| p) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q - \log p]D(q∥p)=Eq​[logq−logp] requires sampling from qqq, which is the _variational_ distribution — easy by construction (you choose qqq to be tractable).

So variational inference uses reverse KL because it is the only computable direction. Maximum likelihood uses forward KL because the data gives empirical samples from the true distribution.

The behavior also differs: forward KL is "mass-covering" (penalizes qqq for missing modes of ppp); reverse KL is "mode-seeking" (penalizes qqq for placing mass where ppp has none). Mode-seeking is the canonical failure mode of VAEs (blurry outputs that average over modes rather than sharply choosing one).

**Q2.** When the variational family does not include the true posterior, the variational solution is biased. How bad is this in practice?

**Discussion:** Highly variable. For convex posteriors (single mode, near-Gaussian), a Gaussian variational family captures most of the posterior. For multimodal posteriors, a single-mode variational family will collapse onto one mode, missing the rest. This is the canonical limitation of mean-field VI.

Practical solutions:

* **Richer variational families** : mixtures of Gaussians, normalizing flows, neural-network-parametrized distributions. More expressive but more expensive.
* **Multiple restarts** : run VI from different initializations and ensemble.
* **MCMC for ground truth** : use VI for fast approximation, MCMC to validate.

In Bayesian deep learning, where the true posterior over millions of weights is unimaginably complex, the variational approximation is necessarily a major simplification. The empirical question is whether the approximation captures enough of the posterior structure to give useful uncertainty estimates and predictions. The honest answer: often it does, sometimes it doesn't, and we are still learning when each happens.

**Q3.** The ELBO is one form of variational bound. Tighter bounds (importance-weighted ELBO, Renyi divergences, ...) exist. When are they worth the cost?

**Discussion:** Tighter bounds give better posterior approximations but at higher computational cost.

Importance-weighted ELBO (IWAE, Burda 2015) uses KKK samples from qqq and weights them by importance ratios. As K→∞K \to \inftyK→∞, the bound becomes tight, and the gradient estimate has lower bias.

In practice:

* For small models and exact log-evidence estimation, IWAE is standard.
* For large models with many parameters, the extra cost of KKK samples per update is prohibitive, and standard ELBO with K=1K = 1K=1 is preferred.
* For uncertainty quantification, tighter bounds give better-calibrated estimates of model evidence.

The general lesson: variational tightness is one knob in a multi-knob system. Tighter bounds matter when the computational budget allows; for very large models, looser bounds with more updates may give better final quality.

Lossless compression, the subject of Chapter 4, is bounded by entropy: no scheme can compress below H(X)H(X)H(X) bits per symbol on average. The fundamental limit of _lossy_ compression is given by **rate-distortion theory** , the subject of this chapter. The rate-distortion function R(D)R(D)R(D) tells you the minimum bit rate needed to compress a source while keeping the average distortion below a level DDD.

### 11.3 Properties of R(D)R(D)R(D)

The rate-distortion function has several elegant properties:

  1. **Monotonically decreasing** : R(D)R(D)R(D) decreases as DDD increases (more distortion allowed → less rate needed).
  2. **Convex** : R(D)R(D)R(D) is a convex function of DDD. The convexity is a consequence of time-sharing arguments.
  3. **R(0)=H(X)R(0) = H(X)R(0)=H(X)** for discrete sources with Hamming distortion: zero distortion means lossless compression, which costs H(X)H(X)H(X) bits.
  4. **R(Dmax⁡)=0R(D_{\max}) = 0R(Dmax​)=0**: at sufficiently high distortion, you can use the constant reproduction (no information at all) and still meet the constraint.

The general shape of R(D)R(D)R(D) is a smooth convex curve dropping from H(X)H(X)H(X) at D=0D = 0D=0 to 000 at some Dmax⁡D_{\max}Dmax​.

### 11.6 The Gaussian Source as a Special Case

The Gaussian source is special in rate-distortion theory in the same way it is special in channel coding: it is the _worst_ source (highest entropy for given variance), and so its rate-distortion function is the most permissive bound. For any source with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and squared-error distortion,

R(D)≥12log⁡σ2D.R(D) \geq \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{\sigma^2}{D}.R(D)≥21​logDσ2​.

The bound is achieved iff the source is Gaussian. For non-Gaussian sources, the rate-distortion function is strictly smaller.

This is a useful baseline: the Gaussian R(D)R(D)R(D) is an upper bound on what's needed for any source with the same variance, and a near-tight bound for sources with low excess kurtosis.


### 11.7 An AI Connection: Neural Compression

Modern neural compression is a direct application of rate-distortion theory. The setup:

* Encoder: a neural network z=fθ(x)z = f_\theta(x)z=fθ​(x) mapping image xxx to a latent zzz.
* Decoder: a neural network x^=gϕ(z)\hat{x} = g_\phi(z)x^=gϕ​(z) mapping zzz back to a reconstructed image.
* Entropy model: a parametric distribution pψ(z)p_\psi(z)pψ​(z) used for arithmetic-coding the latent.

Training objective:

L=−log⁡pψ(z)+λ⋅d(x,x^),\mathcal{L} = -\log p_\psi(z) + \lambda \cdot d(x, \hat{x}),L=−logpψ​(z)+λ⋅d(x,x^),

a Lagrangian rate-distortion loss. The first term is the rate (in bits, modulo a factor); the second is the distortion. λ\lambdaλ controls the trade-off.

This is exactly the rate-distortion view of the variational autoencoder from Chapter 10, with a specific decoder loss (perceptual or pixel-wise) and a specific entropy model (often a hyperprior or autoregressive model over zzz).


#### Performance

Modern neural compressors achieve:

* Better than JPEG: by a wide margin at all bit rates.
* Comparable to BPG (HEVC intra) at moderate rates.
* Better than BPG at very low rates (where neural models can produce sharp, plausible images at rates classical codecs can't match).

For perceptual quality (MS-SSIM, LPIPS), neural compressors are now state of the art on standard image datasets. For PSNR (pixel-wise MSE), they are competitive but not dominant.

The picture: rate-distortion theory was developed in the 1950s for analog signal compression; it now describes the training objective of state-of-the-art image and video compressors using deep neural networks.

#### β\betaβ-VAE

The β\betaβ-VAE objective from Chapter 10:

L=E[log⁡p(x∣z)]−β⋅D(q(z∣x)∥p(z))\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}[\log p(x \mid z)] - \beta \cdot D(q(z \mid x) \| p(z))L=E[logp(x∣z)]−β⋅D(q(z∣x)∥p(z))

is a Lagrangian rate-distortion loss. Different β\betaβ trace out the rate-distortion curve.


#### Diffusion models

Diffusion models can be derived from a hierarchical ELBO with rate-distortion structure at each noise level. The training loss decomposes into a sum of per-noise-level distortion terms.

#### Neural language models

Even text language models have implicit rate-distortion structure. The cross-entropy loss (Chapter 4) is the rate; if we constrain the model's output distribution to a particular family, the achievable cross-entropy is bounded by an information rate-distortion bound.

The general claim: modern generative modeling is rate-distortion theory at scale. The rate is what the model uses to specify each generated example; the distortion is the gap between the generated and ideal distributions.


### 11.9 Historical Note: Berger and the Rate-Distortion Era

Shannon's original 1948 paper introduced entropy and channel capacity, but rate-distortion theory was not fully developed until his 1959 paper _Coding Theorems for a Discrete Source with a Fidelity Criterion_. There Shannon proved the rate-distortion theorem in essentially its modern form and computed R(D)R(D)R(D) for the Gaussian source under squared-error distortion.

The systematic textbook treatment came from Toby Berger, whose 1971 book _Rate Distortion Theory: A Mathematical Basis for Data Compression_ is the canonical reference. Berger spent his career at Cornell and had a knack for finding the right level of generality: his book treats discrete and continuous sources, single-letter and multi-letter distortion measures, and the relationship to channel coding, all in a unified framework. Many later results in network information theory (Chapter 12) trace back to Berger's framing of distributed source coding.

The application of rate-distortion theory to actual codecs — JPEG (1992), MP3 (1993), H.264 (2003) — followed roughly the pattern of Shannon's channel coding theorem and practical codes (Chapter 7): twenty to forty years between theoretical limit and engineering reality. JPEG and MP3 do not literally implement R(D)R(D)R(D)-optimal schemes, but their design (transform coding, scalar quantization, entropy coding) is recognizably _informed_ by rate-distortion intuitions. Modern neural compressors by Ballé, Minnen, and collaborators between 2017 and 2024 come closer to operational optimality.

The deep result is that lossy compression is _fundamentally_ harder than lossless: not only do you need a compression algorithm, you need to know what kind of distortion is acceptable. The choice of distortion measure (MSE? perceptual? task-specific?) is part of the modeling problem. Rate-distortion theory does not tell you what to choose; it tells you what is achievable once you have chosen.

### Common Misconception

* **Misconception** : "Rate-distortion is the same as lossless compression with errors allowed."

Rate-distortion is more refined: it specifies the _type_ of distortion via the distortion measure. Two compressed versions of the same image can have the same MSE but very different perceptual quality. Choosing the right distortion measure is part of the design.

* **Misconception** : "The rate-distortion function is the operational rate at which lossy compression schemes work."

The rate-distortion function is the _fundamental limit_. Practical schemes (JPEG, MP3, neural compressors) operate at points above the curve, with various levels of suboptimality. JPEG, for instance, is far from the rate-distortion optimum at low rates; neural compressors are much closer.

* **Misconception** : "Rate-distortion theory applies only to compression."

The framework applies to any task that trades off "complexity of representation" against "fidelity to source." This includes hashing, summarization, and the information bottleneck (Chapter 13). The rate-distortion formalism is one of the most generally applicable tools in information theory.


### Chapter Summary

Rate-distortion theory gives the fundamental limit of lossy compression. The rate-distortion function R(D)R(D)R(D) is the minimum bit rate to represent a source with distortion at most DDD:

R(D)=min⁡p(x^∣x):E[d]≤DI(X;X^).R(D) = \min_{p(\hat{x} \mid x): \mathbb{E}[d] \leq D} I(X; \hat{X}).R(D)=p(x^∣x):E[d]≤Dmin​I(X;X^).

For the canonical Gaussian source with squared-error distortion, R(D)=12log⁡(σ2/D)R(D) = \frac{1}{2} \log(\sigma^2 / D)R(D)=21​log(σ2/D) — every bit cuts MSE by a factor of 4. For parallel Gaussian sources, the optimal allocation is reverse water-filling: spend bits on high-variance components first.

Modern neural compression is a direct application of rate-distortion theory: train autoencoders with explicit Lagrangian rate-distortion losses to achieve state-of-the-art compression. The same machinery underlies β\betaβ-VAE, diffusion models, and other generative-modeling techniques.

The next chapter generalizes from point-to-point information theory to multi-user network channels.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Rate-distortion theory uses MSE or Hamming distortion as the canonical "distortion measure." But for images, MSE doesn't match human perception. How is this addressed?

**Discussion:** This is a major active research area.

  1. **Better distortion metrics** : SSIM, MS-SSIM, LPIPS, FID. These are designed to better match human perception. Modern neural compressors typically use a combination: MSE + LPIPS (or perceptual + adversarial losses).

  2. **Generative models for distortion** : train a GAN-style discriminator that distinguishes real from compressed images; use the discriminator's output as distortion. This produces visually pleasing reconstructions even when the rate is too low for accurate reconstruction.

  3. **Task-specific distortion** : for downstream tasks (object detection, segmentation), use task accuracy as the distortion measure. The compressor is then tuned to preserve task-relevant information.

The general lesson: rate-distortion theory is a framework, not a prescription. The choice of distortion measure is part of the modeling problem and may itself require deep learning.

**Q2.** Modern neural compression has surpassed classical codecs on perceptual quality. But it has computational costs at decode time. Is this trade-off acceptable?

**Discussion:** Depends on the application.

For _storage_ : training and encoding are one-time costs; decode happens at every view. Decode complexity matters. Neural decoders can require multiple GPU seconds per high-resolution image — orders of magnitude slower than JPEG. For real-time video, this is a serious obstacle.

For _transmission_ : encode complexity matters too. Live broadcast cannot afford slow encoding.

For _archival_ : encode/decode time is irrelevant. Storage cost is what matters. Neural compression saves significant storage at the cost of computational dependencies (you need the trained model to decode).

In practice, neural compression is being deployed in scenarios where its compression efficiency outweighs its computational cost: low-bandwidth video streaming, satellite imagery, medical imaging archives. For everyday image storage and ubiquitous video, classical codecs still dominate due to inertia and computational constraints.

**Q3.** The information bottleneck (Chapter 13) is "rate-distortion in disguise." Sketch the analogy.

**Discussion:** The information bottleneck objective is

min⁡I(X;T)−βI(T;Y)\min I(X; T) - \beta I(T; Y)minI(X;T)−βI(T;Y)

where TTT is a representation of XXX and we want to predict YYY.

Compare to rate-distortion: min⁡I(X;X^)\min I(X; \hat{X})minI(X;X^) subject to E[d(X,X^)]≤D\mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat{X})] \leq DE[d(X,X^)]≤D.

The IB problem replaces the distortion constraint with a "relevance" constraint: instead of "X^\hat{X}X^ should be close to XXX in some distortion sense," it is "TTT should preserve information about YYY." The β\betaβ parameter is the Lagrange multiplier on this constraint.

Both are Lagrangian optimizations of mutual information. Both produce trade-off curves with similar shapes. Both have similar achievability proofs.

The IB formulation is more naturally suited to representation learning (where the goal is task-relevant encoding), while rate-distortion is more naturally suited to compression (where the goal is reproduction).
