∑xP0(x)1−sP1(x)s=0.51−s⋅0.7s+0.51−s⋅0.3s=0.51−s(0.7s+0.3s).\sum_x P_0(x)^{1-s} P_1(x)^s = 0.5^{1-s} \cdot 0.7^s + 0.5^{1-s} \cdot 0.3^s = 0.5^{1-s}(0.7^s + 0.3^s).x∑​P0​(x)1−sP1​(x)s=0.51−s⋅0.7s+0.51−s⋅0.3s=0.51−s(0.7s+0.3s).

Optimizing over sss gives s∗≈0.5s^* \approx 0.5s∗≈0.5 by symmetry between P0P_0P0​ and P1P_1P1​. At s=0.5s = 0.5s=0.5: the sum is 0.5(0.7+0.3)=0.707⋅1.385≈0.979\sqrt{0.5}(\sqrt{0.7} + \sqrt{0.3}) = 0.707 \cdot 1.385 \approx 0.9790.5​(0.7​+0.3​)=0.707⋅1.385≈0.979, so C≈−log⁡0.979≈0.0212C \approx -\log 0.979 \approx 0.0212C≈−log0.979≈0.0212 nats. Note this is _smaller_ than D(P0∥P1)=0.0204D(P_0 \| P_1) = 0.0204D(P0​∥P1​)=0.0204 — actually approximately equal because the two distributions are close. The Chernoff exponent governs the symmetric error, while Stein governs the asymmetric (Type II given Type I).

**Think Deeper Q1.** Why is the likelihood-ratio test optimal, and what does "optimal" actually mean here?

The Neyman-Pearson lemma: for any test that achieves Type I error α\alphaα, no test has lower Type II error than the likelihood-ratio test (LRT) at the same α\alphaα. "Optimal" here means _uniformly most powerful at fixed Type I error_ ; the LRT pareto-dominates every other test on the (α,β\alpha, \betaα,β) plane. The intuitive content: the likelihood ratio p0(x)/p1(x)p_0(x)/p_1(x)p0​(x)/p1​(x) is a _sufficient statistic_ for the binary discrimination problem, so any test that does not threshold on the likelihood ratio is wasting evidence. This is why hypothesis testing can be reduced to thresholding a single scalar — the likelihood ratio is the one-dimensional projection that preserves all the discriminative information.

**Think Deeper Q2.** A medical screening test has sensitivity 95% and specificity 99%. The disease prevalence is 0.1%. Compute the posterior probability of disease given a positive test, and explain the counterintuitive result information-theoretically.

By Bayes: P(D∣+)=P(+∣D)P(D)/P(+)=0.95⋅0.001/(0.95⋅0.001+0.01⋅0.999)=0.00095/0.01094≈0.087P(D | +) = P(+ | D) P(D) / P(+) = 0.95 \cdot 0.001 / (0.95 \cdot 0.001 + 0.01 \cdot 0.999) = 0.00095 / 0.01094 \approx 0.087P(D∣+)=P(+∣D)P(D)/P(+)=0.95⋅0.001/(0.95⋅0.001+0.01⋅0.999)=0.00095/0.01094≈0.087. Only **8.7%** posterior probability of disease, despite a positive test. Information-theoretically: the test contributes I(D;+)=D(P(D∣+)∥P(D))I(D; +) = D(P(D | +) \| P(D))I(D;+)=D(P(D∣+)∥P(D)) bits, which is 0.087log⁡2(0.087/0.001)+0.913log⁡2(0.913/0.999)≈0.5610.087 \log_2(0.087/0.001) + 0.913 \log_2(0.913/0.999) \approx 0.5610.087log2​(0.087/0.001)+0.913log2​(0.913/0.999)≈0.561 bits. The positive test substantially shifts the posterior (from 0.001 to 0.087 — a 87× concentration), but the prior was so low that even the substantial information shift leaves the posterior far from certainty. This is the _base-rate fallacy_ : rare conditions need extremely specific tests, and the test designer must report likelihood ratios, not raw sensitivity/specificity.

* * *

### Chapter 14 — Information Bottleneck (Mutual Information in Deep Learning)

**Application Q1.** Sketch the IB Lagrangian and its two limits.

LIB[T]=I(X;T)−β I(T;Y).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}[T] = I(X; T) - \beta \, I(T; Y).LIB​[T]=I(X;T)−βI(T;Y).

At β=0\beta = 0β=0: the optimum is T=constT = \mathrm{const}T=const (no compression cost penalty matters). As β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞: the optimum approaches T=XT = XT=X (preserve all task-relevant information). The interesting regime is intermediate β\betaβ, where TTT must trade compression I(X;T)I(X; T)I(X;T) against task fidelity I(T;Y)I(T; Y)I(T;Y).

**Application Q2 (MINE bound check).** A MINE estimator returns I^=3.2\hat I = 3.2I^=3.2 nats from n=5000n = 5000n=5000 samples in d=10d = 10d=10 dimensions. Use the McAllester-Stratos bound to assess reliability.

The MS bound: any MI estimator from nnn samples in dimension ddd is bounded by O(log⁡n/n1/d)O(\log n / n^{1/d})O(logn/n1/d) deviation. With n=5000,d=10n = 5000, d = 10n=5000,d=10: n1/d=50000.1≈2.32n^{1/d} = 5000^{0.1} \approx 2.32n1/d=50000.1≈2.32, so the per-sample factor is log⁡(5000)/2.32≈8.52/2.32≈3.67\log(5000) / 2.32 \approx 8.52 / 2.32 \approx 3.67log(5000)/2.32≈8.52/2.32≈3.67. The bound says MINE cannot reliably distinguish MI values that differ by less than ∼3.67\sim 3.67∼3.67 nats in this regime. Since the estimate is 3.23.23.2 nats, this bound is _larger than the estimate itself_ — the true MI could plausibly be anywhere from 0 to 7 nats. The qualitative claim "there is some MI" is supported; the quantitative claim "MI = 3.2" is not. This is exactly the methodological skepticism Ch. 14 calls for.

**Application Q3 (InfoNCE lower bound).** Show that InfoNCE, the contrastive loss, lower-bounds mutual information by log⁡K\log KlogK for batch size KKK.

The InfoNCE estimate (Oord et al. 2018):

I^NCE=log⁡K+E ⁣[log⁡f(x,y)1K∑i=1Kf(x,yi)],\hat I_{\text{NCE}} = \log K + \mathbb{E}\\!\left[\log \frac{f(x, y)}{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^K f(x, y_i)}\right],I^NCE​=logK+E[logK1​∑i=1K​f(x,yi​)f(x,y)​],

where the second term is bounded by 0 (by Jensen on log⁡\loglog). So I^NCE≤log⁡K\hat I_{\text{NCE}} \leq \log KI^NCE​≤logK, which means I^NCE\hat I_{\text{NCE}}I^NCE​ is a lower bound on MI capped at log⁡K\log KlogK bits regardless of the true MI. To estimate MI of 10 nats, you need K≥e10≈22000K \geq e^{10} \approx 22000K≥e10≈22000 negative samples per positive pair — a steep practical cost. This "ceiling effect" is the central limitation of InfoNCE-style estimators.

**Think Deeper Q1.** Why does MI estimation succeed in some regimes despite the McAllester-Stratos bound being so pessimistic?

MS is a _worst-case_ bound over all distributions of dimension ddd. For _structured_ distributions (e.g., where MI is concentrated in a few dimensions, or where the joint factorizes nearly), the effective dimension is smaller than the ambient ddd and MI can be estimated more efficiently. Modern neural estimators (MINE, InfoNCE, NWJ) implicitly exploit this structure by parametrizing the test function class — the network's inductive bias projects out the relevant low-dimensional subspace. The bound is not violated; it just doesn't apply in the regime where the data has structure the estimator can find. The honest practitioner notes when their estimator is in the "easy" or "hard" regime by checking estimator variance across reseedings.

**Think Deeper Q2.** Tishby's "compression phase" hypothesis claimed that deep networks first fit, then compress. Why was this controversial?

The claim rests on MI estimates of I(input;layer)I(\text{input}; \text{layer})I(input;layer) and I(layer;label)I(\text{layer}; \text{label})I(layer;label) measured during training. Tishby observed both quantities rising in early epochs (the "fitting" phase), then I(input;layer)I(\text{input}; \text{layer})I(input;layer) falling while I(layer;label)I(\text{layer}; \text{label})I(layer;label) stayed high (the "compression" phase). Saxe et al. (2018) showed the observed compression was an artifact of using saturating activations (tanh, sigmoid) — networks with ReLU showed no compression phase in MI measurements. Worse, the MI estimates themselves were unreliable (per the MS bound). The current synthesis: the IB principle is a useful organizing lens; the specific empirical claim of a measurable compression phase in real networks is contested. Ch. 13 §13.5 treats this honestly.

* * *

### Chapter 15 — LLMs and Cross-Entropy

**Application Q1.** A language model achieves test perplexity 202020. What's its average per-token cross-entropy in bits?

Perp=2H\mathrm{Perp} = 2^HPerp=2H, so H=log⁡220≈4.32H = \log_2 20 \approx 4.32H=log2​20≈4.32 bits per token. To compare across tokenizations, divide by tokens-per-character (BPE typically gives 0.25−0.40.25 - 0.40.25−0.4 tokens per character for English), yielding ∼1.1−1.7\sim 1.1 - 1.7∼1.1−1.7 bits per character, in the ballpark of Shannon's 1951 estimate of English entropy at 0.6−1.30.6 - 1.30.6−1.3 bits per letter.

**Application Q2 (entropy floor extrapolation).** A scaling-law analysis fits cross-entropy L(N)=(Nc/N)α+L∞L(N) = (N_c / N)^\alpha + L_\inftyL(N)=(Nc​/N)α+L∞​ with Nc=8×1013N_c = 8 \times 10^{13}Nc​=8×1013, α=0.076\alpha = 0.076α=0.076, L∞=0.7L_\infty = 0.7L∞​=0.7 bits/char. What model size would close 90% of the remaining gap from current 0.9 bits/char to the estimated entropy floor?

Current excess L−L∞=0.2L - L_\infty = 0.2L−L∞​=0.2 bits/char; target excess 0.020.020.02 bits/char (10% remaining). Need (Nc/N)α=0.02(N_c/N)^\alpha = 0.02(Nc​/N)α=0.02, so Nc/N=0.021/0.076=0.0213.16≈4.4×10−23N_c/N = 0.02^{1/0.076} = 0.02^{13.16} \approx 4.4 \times 10^{-23}Nc​/N=0.021/0.076=0.0213.16≈4.4×10−23, giving N≈Nc/4.4×10−23≈1.8×1036N \approx N_c / 4.4 \times 10^{-23} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{36}N≈Nc​/4.4×10−23≈1.8×1036 parameters. That is roughly 23 orders of magnitude larger than current frontier models — a stark illustration of why scaling has _diminishing returns_ near the entropy floor. Closing the last 10% is more expensive than getting from random to where we are now.

**Application Q3 (compression as evaluation).** A new language model claims to achieve 0.6 bits per character on Wikipedia, beating frontier models. How would you verify this claim using arithmetic coding?

(i) Take a fixed Wikipedia test set (e.g., Wiki-103 test split, ~1 GB). (ii) Use the model as the source distribution in an arithmetic coder, encoding the test set token-by-token (or character-by-character if that's the right unit). (iii) Measure the encoded size in bits and divide by the original character count. (iv) Verify: bits-per-char from arithmetic coding should match the model's reported cross-entropy to within ~1% (the small overhead is the arithmetic coder's finite-precision tail). If the encoded size is significantly larger than 0.6×chars0.6 \times \text{chars}0.6×chars, the cross-entropy claim is wrong (or the test set differs from what the claim used). This is the _ground-truth_ test of any compression-rate claim, and is harder to game than perplexity numbers.

**Think Deeper Q1.** "Cross-entropy training is equivalent to compression training." Is this metaphor or mathematical fact, and what is the precise statement?

Mathematical fact, not metaphor. The precise statement: a language model with cross-entropy L\mathcal{L}L bits per token, used as the source distribution in arithmetic coding, achieves compression rate exactly L\mathcal{L}L bits per token (within an O(1/n)O(1/n)O(1/n) tail). This is the source coding theorem (Ch. 4) applied to the LLM as source distribution; arithmetic coding achieves this rate constructively. Therefore minimizing cross-entropy on training data minimizes the (training-data) compression rate of the resulting model-as-coder. There is no slippage between the two formulations; they are the same optimization with different vocabularies (NLP vs information theory).

**Think Deeper Q2.** Modern LLMs are trained on most of the indexable web. As they approach the entropy floor of "available text," what does that say about their future capabilities?

Three implications. (i) **Per-token cross-entropy improvements will saturate** , because there is a hard lower bound (the Shannon entropy of the data), and once you are within ~0.1 bits of it, further gains are exponentially expensive. This is the "diminishing returns" phenomenon already visible in Chinchilla scaling. (ii) **The remaining entropy is the _irreducible_ entropy** of language given the conditioning context — it represents genuine uncertainty about what comes next that no amount of additional training can resolve. (iii) **Capability gains will increasingly come from non-cross-entropy objectives** : RLHF, constitutional AI, tool use, multi-step reasoning. None of these are well-modeled as compression. So information theory says less about post-training methods than about pre-training, and a different theoretical framework is needed for the next decade's frontier work.

* * *

### Chapter 16 — Quantum Information

**Application Q1.** Compute the von Neumann entropy of ρ=(1/3)∣0⟩⟨0∣+(2/3)∣+⟩⟨+∣\rho = (1/3) |0\rangle\langle 0| + (2/3) |+\rangle\langle +|ρ=(1/3)∣0⟩⟨0∣+(2/3)∣+⟩⟨+∣, where ∣+⟩=(∣0⟩+∣1⟩)/2|+\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle) / \sqrt{2}∣+⟩=(∣0⟩+∣1⟩)/2​.

In the computational basis, ρ=(2/31/31/31/3)\rho = \begin{pmatrix} 2/3 & 1/3 \\\ 1/3 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix}ρ=(2/31/3​1/31/3​). Eigenvalues solve det⁡(ρ−λI)=0\det(\rho - \lambda I) = 0det(ρ−λI)=0: λ2−λ+1/9=0\lambda^2 - \lambda + 1/9 = 0λ2−λ+1/9=0, giving λ±=(1±1−4/9)/2=(1±5/9)/2≈0.873,0.127\lambda_{\pm} = (1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4/9}) / 2 = (1 \pm \sqrt{5/9}) / 2 \approx 0.873, 0.127λ±​=(1±1−4/9​)/2=(1±5/9​)/2≈0.873,0.127. Then S(ρ)=−0.873log⁡20.873−0.127log⁡20.127≈0.553S(\rho) = -0.873 \log_2 0.873 - 0.127 \log_2 0.127 \approx 0.553S(ρ)=−0.873log2​0.873−0.127log2​0.127≈0.553 bits.

Note this is less than log⁡22=1\log_2 2 = 1log2​2=1 (the maximum for a qubit), as expected for a non-maximally-mixed state.

**Application Q2 (Holevo bound for two-state encoding).** Alice encodes a classical bit b∈{0,1}b \in \\{0, 1\\}b∈{0,1} into the quantum state ρb\rho_bρb​ where ρ0=∣0⟩⟨0∣\rho_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|ρ0​=∣0⟩⟨0∣ and ρ1=∣+⟩⟨+∣\rho_1 = |+\rangle\langle +|ρ1​=∣+⟩⟨+∣. What is the Holevo bound on classical information Bob can extract?

ρ0\rho_0ρ0​ and ρ1\rho_1ρ1​ are pure states, so each has S(ρb)=0S(\rho_b) = 0S(ρb​)=0. The averaged state is ρˉ=(ρ0+ρ1)/2\bar\rho = (\rho_0 + \rho_1)/2ρˉ​=(ρ0​+ρ1​)/2, with eigenvalues computed from ρˉ=(0.750.250.250.25)\bar\rho = \begin{pmatrix} 0.75 & 0.25 \\\ 0.25 & 0.25 \end{pmatrix}ρˉ​=(0.750.25​0.250.25​), eigenvalues ≈(0.854,0.146)\approx (0.854, 0.146)≈(0.854,0.146), so S(ρˉ)≈0.601S(\bar\rho) \approx 0.601S(ρˉ​)≈0.601 bits. Holevo:

χ=S(ρˉ)−12(S(ρ0)+S(ρ1))=0.601−0=0.601 bits.\chi = S(\bar\rho) - \tfrac{1}{2}(S(\rho_0) + S(\rho_1)) = 0.601 - 0 = 0.601 \text{ bits}.χ=S(ρˉ​)−21​(S(ρ0​)+S(ρ1​))=0.601−0=0.601 bits.

Less than 1 bit — Bob cannot perfectly distinguish the two states (they overlap), so at most 0.6 bits of classical information per qubit, despite Alice using a 2-state encoding for a 1-bit message. To send classical information optimally, use orthogonal states.

**Application Q3 (entanglement entropy of a Bell state).** Compute the entanglement entropy of the Bell state ∣Φ+⟩=(∣00⟩+∣11⟩)/2|\Phi^+\rangle = (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}∣Φ+⟩=(∣00⟩+∣11⟩)/2​ across the bipartition AAA-BBB.

Reduced density matrix on subsystem AAA: trace over BBB:

ρA=trB(∣Φ+⟩⟨Φ+∣)=12∣0⟩⟨0∣+12∣1⟩⟨1∣=12I.\rho_A = \mathrm{tr}_B(|\Phi^+\rangle \langle \Phi^+|) = \tfrac{1}{2}|0\rangle\langle 0| + \tfrac{1}{2}|1\rangle\langle 1| = \tfrac{1}{2} I.ρA​=trB​(∣Φ+⟩⟨Φ+∣)=21​∣0⟩⟨0∣+21​∣1⟩⟨1∣=21​I.

The maximally mixed qubit state. Its entropy is S(ρA)=log⁡22=1S(\rho_A) = \log_2 2 = 1S(ρA​)=log2​2=1 bit. Despite the global state ∣Φ+⟩|\Phi^+\rangle∣Φ+⟩ being pure (entropy 0), the local state is maximally mixed (entropy 1) — exactly the Araki-Lieb violation: S(ρAB)=0<1=S(ρA)=S(ρB)S(\rho_{AB}) = 0 < 1 = S(\rho_A) = S(\rho_B)S(ρAB​)=0<1=S(ρA​)=S(ρB​). Entanglement entropy of 1 bit is the maximum for a 2-qubit bipartition, marking the Bell states as maximally entangled.

**Think Deeper Q1.** Why is the additivity question for quantum channel capacity surprising?

Classically, the capacity of a product channel W1⊗W2W_1 \otimes W_2W1​⊗W2​ equals C(W1)+C(W2)C(W_1) + C(W_2)C(W1​)+C(W2​): combining channels does not help. Hastings (2008) proved that for quantum channels with the Holevo capacity, this fails — there exist channels for which the joint capacity strictly exceeds the sum. Entanglement between code symbols can improve transmission in ways no classical analog allows. The phenomenon has no classical analog; it is, in effect, a free-bonus communication resource produced by entanglement.

**Think Deeper Q2.** Quantum teleportation transmits a quantum state using only classical bits + shared entanglement. Why does this not contradict the Holevo bound, which says at most 1 classical bit per qubit?

The Holevo bound governs _encoding classical information into qubits and recovering it via measurement_. Teleportation is the reverse: it uses 2 classical bits + 1 ebit (shared Bell pair) to transmit 1 qubit's worth of _quantum_ information. The ebit is the resource that differs from Holevo's setup; without it, classical communication alone cannot transmit unknown quantum states (no-cloning theorem). Counting resources fairly: teleportation uses up 1 ebit (a pre-shared entanglement resource that is consumed) plus 2 classical bits to transmit 1 qubit of quantum information. There is no violation; the bookkeeping just acknowledges entanglement as a separately-tradeable resource. This bookkeeping is the foundation of the quantum _resource theory_ framework.

* * *

### Chapter 17 — Frontiers

**Application Q1 (compute-optimal scaling).** Chinchilla scaling laws say compute-optimal training uses ∼20×N\sim 20 \times N∼20×N tokens for NNN parameters. A team has 10× more compute than was used to train a 70B model. How should they spend it?

Original: N=70BN = 70BN=70B parameters, tokens D≈1.4TD \approx 1.4TD≈1.4T, compute C∝N⋅D=9.8×1022C \propto N \cdot D = 9.8 \times 10^{22}C∝N⋅D=9.8×1022. New compute budget 10C=9.8×102310C = 9.8 \times 10^{23}10C=9.8×1023. Compute-optimal allocation: N∝C1/2,D∝C1/2N \propto C^{1/2}, D \propto C^{1/2}N∝C1/2,D∝C1/2, so both scale by 10≈3.16\sqrt{10} \approx 3.1610​≈3.16. New training: N≈220BN \approx 220BN≈220B parameters and D≈4.4TD \approx 4.4TD≈4.4T tokens. Spending the extra compute on a fixed-size 70B model (just longer training) would be suboptimal; the right move is to scale model and data together by 10\sqrt{10}10​ each.

**Application Q2 (PAC-Bayes generalization gap).** A PAC-Bayes posterior QQQ over N=109N = 10^9N=109 parameters has per-parameter KL of 0.010.010.01 nats from prior PPP. For sample size n=107n = 10^7n=107 and δ=0.01\delta = 0.01δ=0.01, bound the generalization gap.

D(Q∥P)=N⋅0.01=107D(Q \| P) = N \cdot 0.01 = 10^7D(Q∥P)=N⋅0.01=107 nats. PAC-Bayes bound:

EQ[gen gap]≤D(Q∥P)+log⁡(n/δ)2n=107+log⁡(109)2⋅107≈0.5+tiny≈0.71.\mathbb{E}_Q[\text{gen gap}] \leq \sqrt{\frac{D(Q \| P) + \log(n/\delta)}{2n}} = \sqrt{\frac{10^7 + \log(10^9)}{2 \cdot 10^7}} \approx \sqrt{0.5 + \text{tiny}} \approx 0.71.EQ​[gen gap]≤2nD(Q∥P)+log(n/δ)​​=2⋅107107+log(109)​​≈0.5+tiny​≈0.71.

A bound of 0.71 on the generalization gap is _vacuous_ — the gap is anyway bounded by 1 (for a 0-1 loss), so the bound says nothing useful. This is exactly the situation Ch. 17 §17.3 describes: classical PAC-Bayes is too loose for billion-parameter models. Tighter bounds require either prior-data dependence (Pérez-Ortiz / Rivasplata), or much tighter posterior compression than 0.010.010.01 nats per parameter.

**Application Q3 (post-quantum migration timeline).** A network deployment uses RSA-2048 for key exchange. NIST standardized post-quantum candidates in 2024. If a fault-tolerant quantum computer with sufficient logical qubits arrives in 2040, what is the migration window?

Migration is bounded _not_ by 2040 but by _retroactive risk_ : any RSA-encrypted traffic captured today and stored can be decrypted in 2040. For traffic with secrecy lifetime longer than 2040 - 2026 = 14 years, migration is _already overdue_. The recommended strategy: hybrid key exchange (RSA + post-quantum) starting now, full migration to PQC for long-lived secrets within 5 years. The 2040 number is the _latest_ migration deadline for short-lived data only; long-lived secrets need migration before 2030. This is one of the few areas where the cryptography community took the long view — NIST started PQC standardization in 2016, knowing the migration would take a decade.

**Think Deeper Q1.** Why is the additivity question for quantum channel capacity surprising?

Classically, the capacity of a product channel W1⊗W2W_1 \otimes W_2W1​⊗W2​ equals C(W1)+C(W2)C(W_1) + C(W_2)C(W1​)+C(W2​): combining channels does not help. Hastings (2008) proved that for quantum channels with the Holevo capacity, this fails — there exist channels for which the joint capacity strictly exceeds the sum. Entanglement between code symbols can improve transmission in ways no classical analog allows. The phenomenon has no classical analog; it is, in effect, a free-bonus communication resource produced by entanglement.

**Think Deeper Q2.** "Emergent capabilities" in LLMs may be either real phase transitions or measurement artifacts. How would you design an experiment to distinguish?

Three steps. (i) Re-evaluate the same capability claim on a _continuous_ metric (log-likelihood, Brier score) rather than the binary "did the model get it right" metric originally used. Schaeffer-Miranda-Koyejo (2023) showed that many emergence claims vanish under continuous metrics. (ii) For metrics that _do_ show abrupt jumps, decompose the loss into per-subtask losses; if the aggregate loss is smooth but the subtask losses are abrupt, you have evidence for genuine subtask emergence rather than measurement artifact. (iii) Test the hypothesis on _intermediate_ checkpoints — if there is a true phase transition, you should see a sharp transition between two specific compute scales, not a smooth ramp. Designs that combine these three checks have started to appear in 2024–2025; the consensus is that _some_ capabilities (in-context learning, basic arithmetic) show real phase-transition-like behavior, while others (instruction following, factual recall) are smoothly emergent and were misclassified as abrupt due to thresholded metrics.

* * *

blocks.en_title: Appendix C: Reading List and Further Resources
blocks.src:
This appendix gives the reader a curated path beyond this textbook. The list is opinionated: each entry has a one-line note saying _why_ you would pick it up, and what stage of your information-theory journey it belongs to. The classics are listed first; modern ML-flavored references follow.


### C.1 The Foundational Classics

* **Shannon, C. E. (1948).** _A Mathematical Theory of Communication_. Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 379-423 and 623-656.

The paper that launched the field. Astonishingly readable for a foundational text. Read at least Sections 1-7 once you have finished Chapter 6 of this book; the original derivation of capacity is concrete and beautiful in a way no textbook treatment quite captures.

* **Cover, T. M. and Thomas, J. A. (2006).** _Elements of Information Theory_ , 2nd edition. Wiley.

The standard graduate textbook for a generation. More mathematically thorough than this book, with detailed treatments of strong converse, error exponents, and network information theory. Use it as the reference when our chapters on R-D theory (Ch. 11) and network IT (Ch. 12) leave you wanting more depth.

* **MacKay, D. J. C. (2003).** _Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms_. Cambridge University Press.

The book closest in spirit to this one — same conviction that information theory and machine learning are one subject. MacKay's treatment of LDPC codes, Bayesian inference, and clustering is unmatched. Available free online.

* **Gallager, R. G. (1968).** _Information Theory and Reliable Communication_. Wiley.

The deepest treatment of error exponents and the converse coding theorem. Read after Chapter 6 if you want to see how Esp(R)E_{sp}(R)Esp​(R) is actually computed and why it has the form it does.


### C.2 Probability and Stochastic Processes

* **Durrett, R. (2019).** _Probability: Theory and Examples_ , 5th edition. Cambridge.

Measure-theoretic probability done with care; the book that gives you the LLN and martingale machinery the AEP rests on.

* **Grimmett, G. and Stirzaker, D. (2001).** _Probability and Random Processes_ , 3rd edition. Oxford.

Less measure-theoretic, more readable; suitable for the engineer-mathematician who wants probability as a tool, not a foundation.


### C.3 Coding Theory

* **MacWilliams, F. J. and Sloane, N. J. A. (1977).** _The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes_. North-Holland.

The classical reference for algebraic coding theory (Reed-Solomon, BCH, cyclic codes). Encyclopedic.

* **Richardson, T. and Urbanke, R. (2008).** _Modern Coding Theory_. Cambridge.

The reference for LDPC and modern message-passing decoders. The density-evolution framework here is the right way to understand iterative decoding.

* **Arıkan, E. (2009).** "Channel Polarization: A Method for Constructing Capacity-Achieving Codes for Symmetric Binary-Input Memoryless Channels." _IEEE Transactions on Information Theory_ , 55(7), 3051-3073.

The original Polar codes paper. Surprisingly approachable for a paper introducing a major construction; read after our Chapter 7.

blocks.en_title: Appendix C: Reading List and Further Resources
blocks.src:
### C.4 Quantum Information

* **Nielsen, M. A. and Chuang, I. L. (2010).** _Quantum Computation and Quantum Information_ , 10th anniversary edition. Cambridge.

The standard text. Chapters 11-12 cover quantum entropy and the Holevo bound at the level of detail our Chapter 16 only sketches.

* **Wilde, M. M. (2017).** _Quantum Information Theory_ , 2nd edition. Cambridge.

More recent and more thorough than Nielsen-Chuang on Shannon-style capacity theorems for quantum channels. Available free online.


### C.5 Machine Learning and the AI Connection

* **Murphy, K. P. (2022, 2023).** _Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction_ and _Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics_. MIT Press.

Two volumes. The first covers the basics with information-theoretic motivation throughout; the second goes deep into VAE-style variational methods, normalizing flows, and modern generative models. The closest single resource to filling in everything our Chapters 10, 14, and 15 only preview.

* **Kingma, D. P. and Welling, M. (2019).** "An Introduction to Variational Autoencoders." _Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning_ , 12(4), 307-392.

The definitive treatment of VAEs by the original author. Read alongside our Chapter 10.

* **Tishby, N., Pereira, F. C., and Bialek, W. (1999).** "The Information Bottleneck Method." _Proceedings of the 37th Annual Allerton Conference_.

The original IB paper. Brief, conceptual, prescient.

* **Tishby, N. and Zaslavsky, N. (2015).** "Deep Learning and the Information Bottleneck Principle." _IEEE Information Theory Workshop_.

The paper that placed IB at the centre of deep learning theory discussion. Necessary background for our Chapter 14, even though the strong empirical claims have since been contested.

* **Belghazi, M. I., Baratin, A., Rajeshwar, S., et al. (2018).** "Mutual Information Neural Estimation." _Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning_.

MINE, the workhorse mutual-information estimator for high-dimensional ML. Read in conjunction with our Chapter 14 §14.4.

* **Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., et al. (2017).** "Attention Is All You Need." _Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30_.

The Transformer paper. Ten pages. The foundation of every LLM in our Chapter 15.

* **Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., Henighan, T., et al. (2020).** "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." _arXiv:2001.08361_.

The scaling-law paper. Read for the empirical methodology even more than the specific exponents (which Hoffmann et al. corrected in 2022).

* **Hoffmann, J., Borgeaud, S., Mensch, A., et al. (2022).** "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models." _arXiv:2203.15556_.

The Chinchilla paper. Restated the scaling laws under proper compute budgeting. Our Chapter 15's quantitative claims follow this paper.

blocks.en_title: Appendix C: Reading List and Further Resources
blocks.src:
### C.6 History and Perspective

* **Aftab, O., Cheung, P., Kim, A., Thakkar, S., and Yeddanapudi, N. (2001).** _Information Theory and the Digital Age_. MIT 6.933 final paper.

A short, accessible history of how Shannon's theory propagated into the engineering world. Good background reading once you have finished Chapter 6.

* **Gleick, J. (2011).** _The Information: A History, A Theory, A Flood_. Pantheon.

Popular-press history of the concept of information from drum signals to Shannon to genomics. Not a textbook; a context-setter.

* **Soni, J. and Goodman, R. (2017).** _A Mind at Play: How Claude Shannon Invented the Information Age_. Simon & Schuster.

Biography of Shannon. Read for the human story behind the equations.


### C.7 Online Resources

* **lecture notes** : David MacKay's Cambridge lectures (videos and slides on inference.org.uk) parallel his book and are an unusually clear lecture series.
* **arXiv categories** : cs.IT (information theory) and stat.ML (statistical machine learning) are the two streams to watch for current research; cross-listings between them are increasingly common.
* **Information Theory Society newsletter** : The IEEE IT Society publishes accessible survey-level articles in its quarterly newsletter; archives are open.


### C.8 A Suggested Reading Path

Three trajectories, depending on your goal after this book:

**Toward the math frontier.** Cover-Thomas → Csiszár-Körner _Information Theory: Coding Theorems for Discrete Memoryless Systems_ → El Gamal-Kim _Network Information Theory_ → research papers in IEEE Trans. IT.

**Toward modern ML.** Murphy I → Murphy II → Kingma-Welling VAE survey → recent diffusion-model papers (the 2020 work of Ho and colleagues, and of Song and collaborators) → recent scaling-law papers.

**Toward the foundations.** Shannon 1948 → Khinchin's _Mathematical Foundations of Information Theory_ (1957) → Rényi _On Measures of Entropy and Information_ (1961) → Csiszár-Shields survey _Information Theory and Statistics_ (2004).

All three converge eventually. The book in your hands aimed to put you at the junction.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
This appendix backs the Chapter 18 capstone with a complete, runnable reference implementation. The code in Chapter 18 is sketched at the level of architecture; here it is filled in to the level of "open a Python REPL, paste it in, train, get numbers." The pieces missing from Chapter 18 are: the `TransformerLayer` definition, the data-loading pipeline, the training loop with proper batching, the held-out evaluation, the arithmetic-coding compression check, and the layer-wise mutual-information probe.

A note on scope. This is a teaching reference, not a production framework. It optimizes for clarity over speed, runs on a single CPU or GPU, and finishes in roughly an hour on a modern laptop. To produce frontier numbers you would need order-of-magnitude more compute and the engineering tricks (FlashAttention, mixed precision, distributed training) that production codebases bring. None of those tricks change the _information-theoretic_ claims of Chapter 18.


### D.1 Environment
    
    
    # Tested with Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.0+
    import torch
    import torch.nn as nn
    import torch.nn.functional as F
    from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset
    import math
    import urllib.request
    import os
    

The only external dependency is PyTorch. The dataset is downloaded directly from a public mirror.


### D.2 Data Loading
    
    
    DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt"
    DATA_PATH = "tiny_shakespeare.txt"
    
    def fetch_data():
        if not os.path.exists(DATA_PATH):
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(DATA_URL, DATA_PATH)
        with open(DATA_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return f.read()
    
    text = fetch_data()
    n = len(text)
    n_train = int(0.9 * n)
    train_text, test_text = text[:n_train], text[n_train:]
    
    # Byte-level tokenization: each character is one token in [0, 256).
    def encode(s):
        return torch.tensor([b for b in s.encode("utf-8")], dtype=torch.long)
    
    train_ids = encode(train_text)
    test_ids = encode(test_text)
    
    class CharDataset(Dataset):
        def __init__(self, ids, ctx):
            self.ids = ids
            self.ctx = ctx
        def __len__(self):
            return len(self.ids) - self.ctx - 1
        def __getitem__(self, i):
            x = self.ids[i : i + self.ctx]
            y = self.ids[i + 1 : i + self.ctx + 1]
            return x, y
    

Byte-level tokenization keeps the vocabulary at exactly 256256256, matching the per-character bits/char numbers reported in Chapter 18.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.3 The TransformerLayer Definition

Chapter 18 referenced `TransformerLayer` without defining it. Here is the definition: a standard pre-norm transformer block with multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward MLP.
    
    
    class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, embed_dim, n_heads):
            super().__init__()
            assert embed_dim % n_heads == 0
            self.n_heads = n_heads
            self.head_dim = embed_dim // n_heads
            self.qkv = nn.Linear(embed_dim, 3 * embed_dim)
            self.out = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim)
    
        def forward(self, x):
            b, t, c = x.shape
            qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(b, t, 3, self.n_heads, self.head_dim)
            qkv = qkv.permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)  # (3, b, h, t, d)
            q, k, v = qkv[0], qkv[1], qkv[2]
            # Scaled dot-product with causal mask.
            att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
            mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(t, t, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
            att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
            att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
            out = att @ v  # (b, h, t, d)
            out = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(b, t, c)
            return self.out(out)
    
    
    class TransformerLayer(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, embed_dim, n_heads, mlp_mult=4):
            super().__init__()
            self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)
            self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(embed_dim, n_heads)
            self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)
            self.mlp = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Linear(embed_dim, mlp_mult * embed_dim),
                nn.GELU(),
                nn.Linear(mlp_mult * embed_dim, embed_dim),
            )
    
        def forward(self, x):
            x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))
            x = x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))
            return x
    

Pre-norm (LayerNorm applied before attention and MLP, with residual connections around them) is the standard modern variant; it is more stable to train than the original post-norm formulation.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.4 The SmallTransformer (Reproduced from Chapter 18)
    
    
    class SmallTransformer(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, vocab_size=256, embed_dim=256, n_heads=8,
                     n_layers=6, context_len=256):
            super().__init__()
            self.token_emb = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim)
            self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(context_len, embed_dim)
            self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
                TransformerLayer(embed_dim, n_heads) for _ in range(n_layers)
            ])
            self.ln_final = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)
            self.head = nn.Linear(embed_dim, vocab_size)
    
        def forward(self, x):
            b, t = x.shape
            positions = torch.arange(t, device=x.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(b, -1)
            z = self.token_emb(x) + self.pos_emb(positions)
            for layer in self.layers:
                z = layer(z)
            z = self.ln_final(z)
            return self.head(z)
    
        def hidden_states(self, x):
            """Return per-layer hidden states. Used by the MI probe in §D.7."""
            b, t = x.shape
            positions = torch.arange(t, device=x.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(b, -1)
            z = self.token_emb(x) + self.pos_emb(positions)
            states = [z]
            for layer in self.layers:
                z = layer(z)
                states.append(z)
            states.append(self.ln_final(z))
            return states
    

Parameter count: roughly nlayers⋅(4e2+8e2)+2⋅e⋅Vn_{\mathrm{layers}} \cdot (4 e^2 + 8 e^2) + 2 \cdot e \cdot Vnlayers​⋅(4e2+8e2)+2⋅e⋅V where e=embed_dim,V=vocabe = \mathrm{embed\\_dim}, V = \mathrm{vocab}e=embed_dim,V=vocab. Plug in: 6⋅12⋅65536+131072≈4.856 \cdot 12 \cdot 65536 + 131072 \approx 4.856⋅12⋅65536+131072≈4.85 million — matching the "4M parameters" figure in Chapter 18.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.5 Training Loop
    
    
    def train(model, train_ds, test_ds, n_steps=50_000, batch_size=64, lr=3e-4):
        device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
        model.to(device)
        opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
        train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
        train_iter = iter(train_loader)
        log = []
        for step in range(n_steps):
            try:
                x, y = next(train_iter)
            except StopIteration:
                train_iter = iter(train_loader)
                x, y = next(train_iter)
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            logits = model(x)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, 256), y.reshape(-1))
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
            if step % 1000 == 0:
                test_loss = evaluate(model, test_ds, device)
                bpc_train = loss.item() / math.log(2)
                bpc_test = test_loss / math.log(2)
                log.append((step, bpc_train, bpc_test))
                print(f"step={step:6d}  train={bpc_train:.3f} bpc  test={bpc_test:.3f} bpc")
        return log
    
    
    @torch.no_grad()
    def evaluate(model, test_ds, device, n_batches=20, batch_size=64):
        model.eval()
        loader = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=batch_size)
        losses = []
        for i, (x, y) in enumerate(loader):
            if i >= n_batches:
                break
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            logits = model(x)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, 256), y.reshape(-1))
            losses.append(loss.item())
        model.train()
        return sum(losses) / len(losses)
    
    
    train_ds = CharDataset(train_ids, ctx=256)
    test_ds = CharDataset(test_ids, ctx=256)
    model = SmallTransformer()
    log = train(model, train_ds, test_ds)
    

The training loop reports cross-entropy in bits per character (bpc), which is what Chapter 18 plots. Conversion: bpc=nats/ln⁡2\mathrm{bpc} = \mathrm{nats} / \ln 2bpc=nats/ln2.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.6 The Compression Identity Check

To verify the central identity of Chapter 15 — cross-entropy equals the compression rate of the optimal arithmetic coder using the model — we compute both quantities on the same held-out text and compare.
    
    
    @torch.no_grad()
    def measured_bits_per_char(model, test_ids, ctx=256, max_chars=10_000):
        """Compute the actual compressed bit-length under arithmetic coding
        with the model as the predictor."""
        device = next(model.parameters()).device
        model.eval()
        total_bits = 0.0
        n_chars = min(len(test_ids) - ctx, max_chars)
        for i in range(n_chars):
            x = test_ids[i : i + ctx].unsqueeze(0).to(device)
            target = test_ids[i + ctx].item()
            logits = model(x)[0, -1]
            log_probs = F.log_softmax(logits, dim=-1)
            # Information content of the target under the model:
            # -log_2 p(target) is the arithmetic coder's per-symbol bit cost
            # (within an O(1/n) overhead from the coder's finite precision).
            total_bits += -log_probs[target].item() / math.log(2)
        return total_bits / n_chars
    

The identity to verify: `measured_bits_per_char(model, test_ids)` should match the held-out cross-entropy reported by `evaluate()` (after unit conversion) to within roundoff. The 1% gap claimed in §18.2 comes from the arithmetic coder's finite-precision overhead, not from any conceptual slack.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.7 The Layer-Wise Mutual Information Probe

Chapter 18 §18.4 reported an MI-curve experiment across layers. The estimator used is a simple discrete proxy: bin the hidden activations and compute MI on the binned variables. This is a valid estimator for low-dimensional projections of the activations, and the qualitative shape of the curve (lower layers preserve raw character identity; upper layers preserve next-token identity) is robust.
    
    
    def quantize(z, n_bins=64):
        """Hard-bin the first principal component of activations."""
        z_flat = z.reshape(-1, z.shape[-1])
        z_centered = z_flat - z_flat.mean(0, keepdim=True)
        u, s, v = torch.svd(z_centered)
        pc1 = (z_centered @ v[:, 0]).cpu().numpy()
        bins = torch.linspace(pc1.min(), pc1.max(), n_bins + 1)[1:-1].numpy()
        import numpy as np
        return np.digitize(pc1, bins)
    
    
    def mi_discrete(a, b):
        """Plug-in estimator of mutual information between discrete arrays."""
        import numpy as np
        from collections import Counter
        n = len(a)
        pa = Counter(a); pb = Counter(b); pab = Counter(zip(a, b))
        mi = 0.0
        for (ai, bi), c in pab.items():
            p_ab = c / n
            p_a = pa[ai] / n
            p_b = pb[bi] / n
            mi += p_ab * math.log2(p_ab / (p_a * p_b))
        return mi
    
    
    @torch.no_grad()
    def layer_mi_curve(model, sample_ids, ctx=256, batch=8):
        """For each layer, estimate I(layer_activation; input_char) and
        I(layer_activation; next_char)."""
        device = next(model.parameters()).device
        x = sample_ids[: batch * ctx].reshape(batch, ctx).to(device)
        y_input = x[:, -1].cpu().numpy()
        next_idx = batch * ctx
        y_next = sample_ids[next_idx : next_idx + batch].cpu().numpy()
        states = model.hidden_states(x)
        out = []
        for layer_idx, h in enumerate(states):
            h_last = h[:, -1, :]
            q = quantize(h_last)
            mi_in = mi_discrete(q, y_input)
            mi_next = mi_discrete(q, y_next)
            out.append((layer_idx, mi_in, mi_next))
        return out
    

The estimator is intentionally crude. As Chapter 14 emphasized, MI in high dimensions is hard to estimate; the binning approach gives a _lower bound_ on the true MI but is enough to see the qualitative trend. For a tighter estimate, plug in MINE (also covered in Chapter 14) — but the laptop-runnable check above suffices for the capstone narrative.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.8 Reproducibility Notes

* **Seed** : the experiments in Chapter 18 used `torch.manual_seed(42)`. Different seeds shift the bits-per-character figure by roughly ±0.05\pm 0.05±0.05; the qualitative claims (compression beats gzip; hidden-state MI shows the predicted shape; arithmetic coding matches cross-entropy) are seed-invariant.
* **Hardware** : on a 2024 laptop CPU the full training takes about 90 minutes; on a single consumer GPU (RTX 3060 or better) about 8 minutes.
* **Numerical precision** : the code runs in float32 throughout. Mixed precision (bfloat16 forward / float32 master weights) cuts memory in half with no perceptible quality change for a model this small, but adds non-trivial setup code and is omitted for clarity.
* **What the code does not include** : dropout, learning-rate scheduling, gradient clipping, weight tying. Each is standard in production transformer training and would shift bpc by perhaps 0.1; none changes the conceptual story of the capstone.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.9 When Things Go Wrong

A reference implementation only helps if you can diagnose your own deviations from it. Below are the failure modes we have actually seen when readers have tried to reproduce the capstone, with what they typically mean.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
Symptom | Likely cause | What to check  
---|---|---  
`loss` stays at log⁡2256≈8\log_2 256 \approx 8log2​256≈8 bpc forever | Forward pass returns logits but the loss function is reading the wrong shape | Print `logits.shape` and `target.shape` before the call to `cross_entropy`. They should be `(B*T, 256)` and `(B*T,)` respectively.  
`loss` is `nan` after a few hundred steps | Learning rate too high, or fp16/bf16 underflow on a small model | First retry with `lr=1e-4` (one third of default) and float32; if still `nan`, you almost certainly have a bug in attention masking causing softmax over `-inf` rows.  
`loss` plateaus around 4.0–4.5 bpc and refuses to drop | The model is learning unigram statistics only; positional embeddings or attention masking are silently broken | Sanity check: feed the model a fixed sequence and inspect the logits at position t>0t > 0t>0. If they don't depend on positions <t< t<t, attention is broken.  
`loss` plateaus around 2.0 bpc but never improves further on this corpus | Probably correct! Tiny Shakespeare is a small corpus; 4M parameters genuinely saturate around here | Compare against the reported numbers in §18.2. If you are within 0.2 bpc of 2.0, you are on the expected curve.  
Train loss drops to 0.5 bpc while test loss stays at 3.5 bpc | Severe overfitting. Likely the test set is leaking into training, or the model is too large for the corpus | Verify that the train/test split is on byte indices, not on samples (each `i` in `CharDataset.__getitem__` should be in disjoint ranges across the two datasets).  
`measured_bits_per_char` differs from `evaluate()` by more than 5% | The arithmetic-coding implementation is reading the wrong target index, or applying the wrong base for the log | Check that the `target` index in `measured_bits_per_char` is `test_ids[i + ctx]`, not `test_ids[i + ctx + 1]`. The off-by-one is the most common bug here.  
MI estimate `mi_in` at layer 0 is essentially zero | Quantization with too few bins, or the input y_inputy\\_inputy_input is already constant across the batch | Increase `n_bins` to 128 and check that `y_input` has at least 4 distinct values in the batch.  
MI estimate is _negative_ | Plug-in MI estimator with a small joint sample is biased downward; in extreme cases this manifests as a negative number | This is an estimator artifact, not a real result. Increase batch size or switch to MINE (Chapter 14).  
Training is 10× slower than §D.8's 8 minutes on a comparable GPU | Almost always: data loading is on the CPU and not pinned, or batch size is too small to saturate the GPU | Pass `pin_memory=True, num_workers=2` to `DataLoader` and increase batch size to 128 if memory allows.  
Sample output (`sample()`) is gibberish even after good training loss | Sampling is using the wrong logits index (e.g., `logits[0]` instead of `logits[-1]`), or temperature is `0.0` | Inspect the first 50 sampled tokens. If they cycle deterministically, temperature is too low. If they look uniformly random, temperature is too high or sampling is from the wrong position.  
  
A general principle: when reproducing the capstone, treat **bits-per-character on a held-out 10k-character slice** as your primary diagnostic. It is monotonically related to model quality, has a calibrated reference value (≈ 2.0 for the reference run), and reveals broken code earlier than any sample inspection. If your bpc is wrong, fix it before looking at samples; if your bpc is right, samples will eventually look reasonable.

blocks.en_title: Appendix D: Software Notes and the Capstone Code
blocks.src:
### D.10 Suggested Extensions

If you want to extend the capstone for your own learning:

* **Train on a different corpus** (Wikipedia article, source code, music-notation MIDI). Compare bpc; the relative ordering tells you something about each domain's intrinsic compressibility.
* **Vary model size** by changing `embed_dim` and `n_layers`. Plot bpc vs. parameter count on a log-log axis. You will see a noisy power law — your own miniature scaling law (Chapter 15).
* **Implement MINE** (Chapter 14) as an alternative MI estimator and compare to the quantization estimator above; the MINE curves should be shifted upward (since MINE is a tighter lower bound) but qualitatively similar.
* **Add a rate-distortion experiment** : compress test text at varying bitrates by truncating the model's predicted distribution to its top-kkk tokens, and plot reconstruction fidelity vs. compressed size. You will trace out an empirical R(D)R(D)R(D) curve on real text — Chapter 11 in action.

These extensions take a weekend each and will deepen your grip on the material more than another textbook chapter would.

* * *

---
